To my dear husband

George Henry Lewes

> Wishing me like to one more rich in hope,

⋮

Desiring this man’s art and that man’s scope.

With what I most enjoy contented least;

Yet in these thoughts myself almost despising,

Haply I think on thee﻿—and then my state,

Like to the lark at break of day arising

From sullen earth, sings hymns at heaven’s gate;

For thy sweet love remembered such wealth brings,

That then I scorn to change my state with kings.

## Foreword Extracts from a Letter Written Oct. 29, 1876, to Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe / 前言 摘自1876年10月29日致哈丽雅特·比彻·斯托夫人的信
===Original===

“As to the Jewish element in Deronda, I expected from first to last, in writing it, that it would create much stronger resistance and even repulsion than it has actually met with. But precisely because I felt that the usual attitude of Christians towards Jews is﻿—I hardly know whether to say more impious or more stupid when viewed in the light of their professed principles, I therefore felt urged to treat Jews with such sympathy and understanding as my nature and knowledge could attain to. Moreover, not only towards the Jews, but towards all Oriental peoples with whom we English come in contact, a spirit of arrogance and contemptuous dictatorialness is observable which has become a national disgrace to us. There is nothing I should care more to do, if it were possible, than to rouse the imagination of men and women to a vision of human claims in those races of their fellowmen who most differ from them in customs and beliefs. But towards the Hebrews we Western people who have been reared in Christianity have a peculiar debt, and whether we acknowledge it or not, a peculiar thoroughness of fellowship in religious and moral sentiment. Can anything be more disgusting than to hear people called ‘educated’ making small jokes about eating ham, and showing themselves empty of any real knowledge as to the relation of their own social and religious life to the history of the people they think themselves witty in insulting? They hardly know that Christ was a Jew. And I find men, educated, supposing that Christ spoke Greek. To my feeling, this deadness to the history which has prepared half our world for us, this inability to find interest in any form of life that is not clad in the same coattails and flounces as our own, lies very close to the worst kind of irreligion. The best that can be said of it is that it is a sign of the intellectual narrowness﻿—in plain English, the stupidity﻿—which is still the average mark of our culture. Yes, I expected more aversion than I have found. But I was happily independent in material things, and felt no temptation to accommodate my writing to any standard except that of trying to do my best in what seemed to me most needful to be done; and I sum up with the writer of the Book of Maccabees: ‘If I have done well and as befits the subject, it is what I desired; and if I have done ill, it is what I could attain unto.’ ”

===Chinese===

「至于《丹尼尔·德龙达》中的犹太元素，从动笔之初到最后完稿，我都预料到它会遭遇比实际上更强烈的抵制乃至反感。但恰恰因为我感到基督徒对犹太人的一贯态度——在他们的 professed 原则光照之下，我几乎不知道该说是更加亵渎还是更加愚蠢——我才被驱使着以我的天性和学识所能达到的同情与理解去对待犹太人。而且，不仅对犹太人，对我们英国人有所接触的一切东方民族，都可以观察到一种傲慢与轻蔑的发号施令之气，这已成为我们民族的一种耻辱。倘若可能，我最愿意做的事，莫过于唤醒世人的想象力，让他们看见那些在习俗与信仰上与自己最不相同的同类的属人之权利。但对于希伯来人，我们这些在基督教中长大的西方人负有一种特殊的债，并且无论我们承认与否，在宗教与道德情感上都有着一种特殊的、深彻的同伴之情。还有什么比听到所谓『受过教育』的人拿吃火腿开无聊的玩笑，更令人作呕的呢？他们对自己所嘲讽的这个民族的历史与自己社会、宗教生活的关联，其实一无所知。他们几乎不知道基督本人就是犹太人。我还发现有些受过教育的人竟以为基督说的是希腊语。在我感觉中，这种对我们世界得以奠基的历史的麻木，这种对任何不穿着与我们同样的燕尾服和褶裙的生活形态都提不起兴趣的漠然，与最恶劣的不敬神明相去无几。对它至多只能说，这是一种智识狭隘——说白了，愚蠢——的标志，而这也仍然是我们文化的平均水平。是的，我预料到的嫌恶比实际遇到的更多。但幸运的是我在物质上无所依傍，也全然不想让我的写作屈从于任何标准，只求尽我所能去做在我看来最需要做的事；最后，我以《马加比书》作者的话作结：『我若写得好，且合乎题材，那正是我所愿；我若写得不好，那也是我力所能及。』」

That trample on the dead to seize their spoil,

As exhalations laden with slow death,

And o’er the fairest troop of captured joys

===Original===

I The Spoiled Child

===Chinese===

第一卷 被宠坏的孩子

### I / 第一章
===Original===

> Men can do nothing without the make-believe of a beginning. Even science, the strict measurer, is obliged to start with a make-believe unit, and must fix on a point in the stars’ unceasing journey when his sidereal clock shall pretend that time is at Nought. His less accurate grandmother Poetry has always been understood to start in the middle; but on reflection it appears that her proceeding is not very different from his; since Science, too, reckons backward as well as forward, divides his unit into billions, and with his clock-finger at Nought really sets off *in medias res*. No retrospect will take us to the true beginning; and whether our prologue be in heaven or on earth, it is but a fraction of that all-presupposing fact with which our story sets out.

===Chinese===

> 人若不假装有一个开端，便什么事也做不成。就连科学这位一丝不苟的度量者，也不得不从一个假装的单位出发，不得不在星辰无休止的旅程中定下一个点，让他的恒星钟宣称时间归零。他那不如科学精确的老祖母诗歌，向来被认为是从中间开始的；但细想之下，她的做法与他其实相差无几；因为科学也同样往前推算、往后推算，把单位切成亿万份，而当时钟指针指向零时，他实际上也是*从中间开始*（in medias res）的。任何回顾都无法把我们带回真正的开端；无论我们的序幕设在天上还是人间，它都不过是那个为故事预设了一切的事实的一个片段——我们的故事，正是从这个事实出发的。

===Original===

Was she beautiful or not beautiful? and what was the secret of form or expression which gave the dynamic quality to her glance? Was the good or the evil genius dominant in those beams? Probably the evil; else why was the effect that of unrest rather than of undisturbed charm? Why was the wish to look again felt as coercion and not as a longing in which the whole being consents?
She who raised these questions in Daniel Deronda’s mind was occupied in gambling: not in the open air under a southern sky, tossing coppers on a ruined wall, with rags about her limbs; but in one of those splendid resorts which the enlightenment of ages has prepared for the same species of pleasure at a heavy cost of gilt mouldings, dark-toned color and chubby nudities, all correspondingly heavy﻿—forming a suitable condenser for human breath belonging, in great part, to the highest fashion, and not easily procurable to be breathed in elsewhere in the like proportion, at least by persons of little fashion.
It was near four o’clock on a September day, so that the atmosphere was well-brewed to a visible haze. There was deep stillness, broken only by a light rattle, a light chink, a small sweeping sound, and an occasional monotone in French, such as might be expected to issue from an ingeniously constructed automaton. Round two long tables were gathered two serried crowds of human beings, all save one having their faces and attention bent on the tables. The one exception was a melancholy little boy, with his knees and calves simply in their natural clothing of epidermis, but for the rest of his person in a fancy dress. He alone had his face turned toward the doorway, and fixing on it the blank gaze of a bedizened child stationed as a masquerading advertisement on the platform of an itinerant show, stood close behind a lady deeply engaged at the roulette-table.
About this table fifty or sixty persons were assembled, many in the outer rows, where there was occasionally a deposit of newcomers, being mere spectators, only that one of them, usually a woman, might now and then be observed putting down a five-franc with a simpering air, just to see what the passion of gambling really was.

===Chinese===

她美，还是不美？是怎样一种形体或神情的奥秘，赋予她的目光一种摄人的力量？在她那眼波之中，主宰的究竟是善的神灵还是恶的神灵？多半是恶的；否则，那效果为何是不安，而非不容搅扰的魅力？为何再看一眼的愿望，让人感到的是胁迫，而不是整个身心都甘愿沉溺的渴望？

这个在丹尼尔·德龙达（Daniel Deronda）心中激起这些疑问的女子，正沉迷于赌博：不是在南方天空下的露天里，倚着断壁掷铜板、衣衫褴褛的那种；而是在那些华丽的场所之中——历代的文明以昂贵的代价，为同一种享乐备下了鎏金的线脚、暗沉的色调和丰满的小裸像，一切都同样厚重——构成一个适合凝聚人类呼气的容器；这里的呼气，大半属于最上流的时髦人物，而且别处不易吸到同样比例的这种呼气，至少对不那么时髦的人而言是如此。

那是九月里将近四点钟的时候，空气已被充分熬炼成一层看得见的薄雾。四下深寂，只听得见轻轻的骰子声、细细的钱币声、小小的扫币声，以及偶尔一句单调的法语，仿佛出自一架构造精巧的自动木偶。两张长桌四周，挤着两堆密集的人群，除一人而外，全都把脸和注意力伏在桌面上。唯一的例外是一个忧郁的小男孩，膝盖和小腿只裹着天然的皮肤，身上其余部分却穿一件花哨的行头。唯有他把脸朝着门口，像一个被安置在流动戏台平台上充作化装广告的、穿得花里胡哨的孩子那样，呆呆地凝望着，紧站在一位正专注于轮盘赌的贵妇人身后。

这张桌边聚了五六十人，外圈多是偶有新人落座的看客，只除了其中一位——通常是个女人——时不时被瞧见带着傻笑押下一个五法郎，只为见识见识赌博的激情究竟是什么滋味。

===Original===

Those who were taking their pleasure at a higher strength, and were absorbed in play, showed very distant varieties of European type: Livonian and Spanish, Graeco-Italian and miscellaneous German, English aristocratic and English plebeian. Here certainly was a striking admission of human equality. The white bejewelled fingers of an English countess were very near touching a bony, yellow, crab-like hand stretching a bared wrist to clutch a heap of coin﻿—a hand easy to sort with the square, gaunt face, deep-set eyes, grizzled eyebrows, and ill-combed scanty hair which seemed a slight metamorphosis of the vulture. And where else would her ladyship have graciously consented to sit by that dry-lipped feminine figure prematurely old, withered after short bloom like her artificial flowers, holding a shabby velvet reticule before her, and occasionally putting in her mouth the point with which she pricked her card? There too, very near the fair countess, was a respectable London tradesman, blonde and soft-handed, his sleek hair scrupulously parted behind and before, conscious of circulars addressed to the nobility and gentry, whose distinguished patronage enabled him to take his holidays fashionably, and to a certain extent in their distinguished company. Not his the gambler’s passion that nullifies appetite, but a well-fed leisure, which, in the intervals of winning money in business and spending it showily, sees no better resource than winning money in play and spending it yet more showily﻿—reflecting always that Providence had never manifested any disapprobation of his amusement, and dispassionate enough to leave off if the sweetness of winning much and seeing others lose had turned to the sourness of losing much and seeing others win. For the vice of gambling lay in losing money at it. In his bearing there might be something of the tradesman, but in his pleasures he was fit to rank with the owners of the oldest titles. Standing close to his chair was a handsome Italian, calm, statuesque, reaching across him to place the first pile of napoleons from a new bagful just brought him by an envoy with a scrolled mustache. The pile was in half a minute pushed over to an old bewigged woman with eyeglasses pinching her nose.

===Chinese===

那些以更高强度消遣、全神贯注于赌局的人，显示出差别极大的各种欧洲类型：立沃尼亚人和西班牙人，希腊裔意大利人，形形色色的德国人，英国贵族和英国平民。这里无疑是对人类平等的一个惊人认可。一位英国伯爵夫人戴着珠宝的雪白手指，几乎要碰到一只瘦骨嶙峋、蜡黄的蟹爪般的手；那手裸着腕子伸过来抓一把硬币——这样的手，很容易与那张方削、枯瘦的脸、深陷的眼睛、灰白的眉毛和梳理不善的稀疏头发归在一起，那些东西仿佛是秃鹫的一次轻微变形。别处哪里，伯爵夫人会惠然肯与那个干嘴唇的女人形象同坐一处呢？她未老先衰，短暂的花期过后便枯萎了，就像她那些人造花，面前捧着一只寒酸的丝绒网袋，不时把扎牌用的针尖放进嘴里吮着。就在伯爵夫人近旁，还坐着一位体面的伦敦商人，金发白面，手皮柔嫩，油亮的头发在前后都一丝不苟地分出缝来，心里惦着寄给贵族与绅士们的生意通函——正是他们显赫的惠顾，使他得以时髦地度假，而且在某种程度上是置身于显赫人物的圈子里度假。他身上的并非那种令人忘却食欲的赌徒激情，而是一种饱食后的闲暇：在做生意赚钱与大手笔花钱的间隙里，觉得再没有比在赌桌上赢钱、再更大手笔地花钱更好的消遣了——他心里总想着，天意从未对他的这项娱乐表示过任何不悦；而且他也足够冷静，一旦「大赢、看别人输」的甜头变成「大输、看别人赢」的酸涩，他便会罢手。因为赌博之恶，正在于输钱。他的仪态里或许带着商人气，但在享乐上，他尽可与最古老的世家头衔的主人们比肩。紧挨着他的椅子站着一个英俊的意大利人，沉静如雕像，越过他把刚从一袋新筹码里数出的第一摞拿破仑金币码上——那袋钱刚由一个留着卷曲小胡子的信使送到。不出半分钟，那一摞就被推给了旁边一个戴假发的老妇人，她鼻子上夹着夹鼻眼镜。

===Original===

There was a slight gleam, a faint mumbling smile about the lips of the old woman; but the statuesque Italian remained impassive, and﻿—probably secure in an infallible system which placed his foot on the neck of chance﻿—immediately prepared a new pile. So did a man with the air of an emaciated beau or worn-out libertine, who looked at life through one eyeglass, and held out his hand tremulously when he asked for change. It could surely be no severity of system, but rather some dream of white crows, or the induction that the eighth of the month was lucky, which inspired the fierce yet tottering impulsiveness of his play.
But, while every single player differed markedly from every other, there was a certain uniform negativeness of expression which had the effect of a mask﻿—as if they had all eaten of some root that for the time compelled the brains of each to the same narrow monotony of action.
Deronda’s first thought when his eyes fell on this scene of dull, gas-poisoned absorption, was that the gambling of Spanish shepherd-boys had seemed to him more enviable:﻿—so far Rousseau might be justified in maintaining that art and science had done a poor service to mankind. But suddenly he felt the moment become dramatic. His attention was arrested by a young lady who, standing at an angle not far from him, was the last to whom his eyes traveled. She was bending and speaking English to a middle-aged lady seated at play beside her: but the next instant she returned to her play, and showed the full height of a graceful figure, with a face which might possibly be looked at without admiration, but could hardly be passed with indifference.
The inward debate which she raised in Deronda gave to his eyes a growing expression of scrutiny, tending farther and farther away from the glow of mingled undefined sensibilities forming admiration. At one moment they followed the movements of the figure, of the arms and hands, as this problematic sylph bent forward to deposit her stake with an air of firm choice; and the next they returned to the face which, at present unaffected by beholders, was directed steadily toward the game.

===Chinese===

老妇人嘴角掠过一丝微光，一丝含糊的浅笑；那雕像般的意大利人却纹丝不动，而且——多半是倚仗着一套能将机遇踩在脚下的万无一失的体系——立刻又码起一摞新的。另一个男人也如此，他带着憔悴的花花公子或油尽灯枯的浪荡子气派，用单片眼镜看人生，讨找零钱时伸出的手微微发抖。激励他那凶狠而又踉跄的赌劲的，肯定不是什么体系的严密，倒不如说是某种白乌鸦式的迷梦，或是「每月初八吉利」之类的推论。

然而，尽管每个赌客都与其他人截然不同，他们脸上却有一种共同的、茫然无神的表情，其效果如同一副面具——仿佛他们都吃了什么草根，一时之间把每个人的头脑都逼进了同样狭隘单调的动作里。

德龙达的目光落到这幅煤气毒害般的呆滞沉迷图景上时，第一个念头是：西班牙牧童的赌博在他看来反而更令人羡慕——就这一点而论，卢梭断言艺术与科学对人类弊大于利，也许不无道理。但忽然间，他感到这一刻变得富于戏剧性。他的注意力被一位年轻小姐攫住了；她站在离他不远的一个斜角上，是他的目光最后落到的人。她正弯腰用英语对一位坐在她身旁赌局中的中年太太说话；但下一瞬她已回到自己的赌局上，显出优美身材的整个高度，一张脸孔也许不至于引人爱慕，却几乎不可能被人淡然略过。

她向德龙达心中激起的这场内在辩论，使他的眼睛渐渐带上审视的神情，越来越远离那种由种种难以名状的感受混合而成的爱慕之光。这一刻，他的目光追随着那身影、那手臂和手的动作，看这个捉摸不定的精灵如何俯身押下赌注，带着一种斩钉截铁选择的神气；下一刻，目光又回到那张脸上——此刻它未受旁观者影响，正径直对着赌局。

===Original===

The sylph was a winner; and as her taper fingers, delicately gloved in pale-gray, were adjusting the coins which had been pushed toward her in order to pass them back again to the winning point, she looked round her with a survey too markedly cold and neutral not to have in it a little of that nature which we call art concealing an inward exultation.
But in the course of that survey her eyes met Deronda’s, and instead of averting them as she would have desired to do, she was unpleasantly conscious that they were arrested﻿—how long? The darting sense that he was measuring her and looking down on her as an inferior, that he was of different quality from the human dross around her, that he felt himself in a region outside and above her, and was examining her as a specimen of a lower order, roused a tingling resentment which stretched the moment with conflict. It did not bring the blood to her cheeks, but it sent it away from her lips. She controlled herself by the help of an inward defiance, and without other sign of emotion than this lip-paleness turned to her play. But Deronda’s gaze seemed to have acted as an evil eye. Her stake was gone. No matter; she had been winning ever since she took to roulette with a few napoleons at command, and had a considerable reserve. She had begun to believe in her luck, others had begun to believe in it: she had visions of being followed by a cortège who would worship her as a goddess of luck and watch her play as a directing augury. Such things had been known of male gamblers; why should not a woman have a like supremacy? Her friend and chaperon who had not wished her to play at first was beginning to approve, only administering the prudent advice to stop at the right moment and carry money back to England﻿—advice to which Gwendolen had replied that she cared for the excitement of play, not the winnings. On that supposition the present moment ought to have made the flood-tide in her eager experience of gambling. Yet, when her next stake was swept away, she felt the orbits of her eyes getting hot, and the certainty she had (without looking) of that man still watching her was something like a pressure which begins to be torturing. The more reason to her why she should not flinch, but go on playing as if she were indifferent to loss or gain. Her friend touched her elbow and proposed that they should quit the table.

===Chinese===

那精灵是个赢家；当她戴浅灰手套的纤长手指整理着推向她的金币、准备再押回那个赢点上时，她环顾四周，那目光过分地冷淡而中立，反倒显出几分那种我们称之为「艺术」的天性——掩饰着内心的得意。

可在这一环顾之中，她的目光与德龙达的相遇了；她本想移开视线，却不适地发觉自己的目光被钉住了——钉了多久？她心头电光一闪：他正在打量她、俯视她如低人一等；他与她周围那群人类的渣滓不同类；他自觉置身于她之外、高于她的境地，正把她当作一个低等种属的标本来检视——这激起一种刺痛的愤懑，使这一瞬间被争斗拉得悠长。这愤懑没有把血送上她的双颊，却把它从她唇边驱走了。她借着内心的倨傲克制住自己，除嘴唇发白之外不动别的声色，转身回到赌局上。可是德龙达的凝视似乎起了恶眼的作用。她的赌注输掉了。不要紧；自从她凭着几个拿破仑金币的本钱开始玩轮盘赌，她一直在赢，还有一笔可观的后备。她开始相信自己的运气，别人也开始相信了：她幻想有一队人马追随着她，把她当作幸运女神来崇拜，把她的赌法看作指引的占兆。这种事在男赌客中是听闻过的；为什么女人就不能有同样的霸权？她那位起初不愿她下注的伴护女友，如今也开始赞成了，只谨慎地劝她见好就收、把钱带回英国——对此格温多琳（Gwendolen）回答说，她要的是赌的刺激，不是赢的钱。照这个说法，眼下这一刻本该是她赌博经历中涨潮的最高点。然而，当她的下一注又被扫走时，她觉得眼眶发热，而且她确知（不用看也知道）那个男人还在盯着她，那感觉就像一种渐渐变得折磨人的压力。她更有理由不退缩，而要若无其事地继续赌下去，仿佛对输赢无动于衷。她的女友碰碰她的手肘，提议她们离开赌桌。

===Original===

For reply Gwendolen put ten louis on the same spot: she was in that mood of defiance in which the mind loses sight of any end beyond the satisfaction of enraged resistance; and with the puerile stupidity of a dominant impulse includes luck among its objects of defiance. Since she was not winning strikingly, the next best thing was to lose strikingly. She controlled her muscles, and showed no tremor of mouth or hands. Each time her stake was swept off she doubled it. Many were now watching her, but the sole observation she was conscious of was Deronda’s, who, though she never looked toward him, she was sure had not moved away. Such a drama takes no long while to play out: development and catastrophe can often be measured by nothing clumsier than the moment-hand. “*Faites votre jeu, mesdames et messieurs*,” said the automatic voice of destiny from between the mustache and imperial of the croupier: and Gwendolen’s arm was stretched to deposit her last poor heap of napoleons. “*Le jeu ne va plus*,” said destiny. And in five seconds Gwendolen turned from the table, but turned resolutely with her face toward Deronda and looked at him. There was a smile of irony in his eyes as their glances met; but it was at least better that he should have kept his attention fixed on her than that he disregarded her as one of an insect swarm who had no individual physiognomy. Besides, in spite of his superciliousness and irony, it was difficult to believe that he did not admire her spirit as well as her person: he was young, handsome, distinguished in appearance﻿—not one of these ridiculous and dowdy Philistines who thought it incumbent on them to blight the gaming-table with a sour look of protest as they passed by it. The general conviction that we are admirable does not easily give way before a single negative; rather when any of Vanity’s large family, male or female, find their performance received coldly, they are apt to believe that a little more of it will win over the unaccountable dissident. In Gwendolen’s habits of mind it had been taken for granted that she knew what was admirable and that she herself was admired. This basis of her thinking had received a disagreeable concussion, and reeled a little, but was not easily to be overthrown.

===Chinese===

作为回答，格温多琳把十个路易押在同一处：她正处在那种倨傲的对抗情绪之中，心里除了满足被激怒的抵抗之外看不见任何别的目的；在这种支配性冲动的幼稚愚蠢里，连运气也被列为了对抗的对象。既然她不能赢得漂亮，退而求其次，便是输得漂亮。她控制住自己的肌肉，嘴唇和手都不露一丝颤抖。每当赌注被扫走，她便加倍押上。如今许多人都在看她，但她意识到的唯一目光是德龙达的；她从未朝他望去，却确信他没有走开。这样的戏剧用不了多久便会演完：发展与灾变的度量，往往不过是分针那般笨拙的东西。「*各位先生太太，请下注*，」命运那机械的声音从赌场职员的两撇髭和唇须之间发出：格温多琳的手臂伸出去，押上她最后可怜的一小堆拿破仑金币。「*停止下注*，」命运说。五秒钟后，格温多琳从赌桌转过身来，却是毅然转过头，把脸正对着德龙达，直望着他。两人的目光相遇时，他眼中含着一丝讥诮的笑意；但至少，他一直注视着她，总比把她当作没有个体面目的一群飞虫中的一只而弃置不顾要好。况且，尽管他一脸的傲慢与讥诮，还是很难相信他不倾慕她的精神连同她的容貌：他年轻、俊美、气度出众——可不是那种可笑而邋遢的市侩，那种人自以为有责任在走过赌桌时投去一道酸溜溜的抗议神色，让赌桌为之枯萎。我们相信自己可爱，这种普遍的信念不会轻易在单独一个否定面前让步；反倒是这样：当「虚荣」这个庞大家族中的任何一员，无论男女，发现自己的表演受到冷遇，他们总倾向于相信，再多来一点表演就能把这个莫名其妙的异议者争取过来。在格温多琳的思维习惯里，她知道什么可爱、而她自己正被人爱慕，这本是天经地义。她的这个思想根基遭到了不快的撞击，晃了一晃，却不是轻易推得翻的。

===Original===

In the evening the same room was more stiflingly heated, was brilliant with gas and with the costumes of ladies who floated their trains along it or were seated on the ottomans.
The Nereid in sea-green robes and silver ornaments, with a pale sea-green feather fastened in silver falling backward over her green hat and light brown hair, was Gwendolen Harleth. She was under the wing, or rather soared by the shoulder, of the lady who had sat by her at the roulette-table; and with them was a gentleman with a white mustache and clipped hair: solid-browed, stiff and German. They were walking about or standing to chat with acquaintances, and Gwendolen was much observed by the seated groups.
“A striking girl﻿—that Miss Harleth﻿—unlike others.”
“Yes, she has got herself up as a sort of serpent now﻿—all green and silver, and winds her neck about a little more than usual.”
“Oh, she must always be doing something extraordinary. She is that kind of girl, I fancy. Do you think her pretty, Mr. Vandernoodt?”
“Very. A man might risk hanging for her﻿—I mean a fool might.”
“You like a *nez retroussé*, then, and long narrow eyes?”
“When they go with such an *ensemble*.”
“The *ensemble du serpent*?”
“If you will. Woman was tempted by a serpent; why not man?”
“She is certainly very graceful; but she wants a tinge of color in her cheeks. It is a sort of Lamia beauty she has.”
“On the contrary, I think her complexion one of her chief charms. It is a warm paleness; it looks thoroughly healthy. And that delicate nose with its gradual little upward curve is distracting. And then her mouth﻿—there never was a prettier mouth, the lips curled backward so finely, eh, Mackworth?”
“Think so? I cannot endure that sort of mouth. It looks so self-complacent, as if it knew its own beauty﻿—the curves are too immovable. I like a mouth that trembles more.”
“For my part, I think her odious,” said a dowager. “It is wonderful what unpleasant girls get into vogue. Who are these Langens? Does anybody know them?”
“They are quite *comme il faut*. I have dined with them several times at the Russie. The baroness is English. Miss Harleth calls her cousin. The girl herself is thoroughly well-bred, and as clever as possible.”
“Dear me! and the baron?”
“A very good furniture picture.”
“Your baroness is always at the roulette-table,” said Mackworth. “I fancy she has taught the girl to gamble.”

===Chinese===

到了晚上，这间厅房里更加闷热，煤气灯和女士们的衣装使它一片辉煌；她们曳着长裙沿厅游走，或坐在软榻上。

那位身着海绿色长袍、缀银饰、绿帽上用银扣别着一支浅海绿色羽毛、向后披落在浅棕色头发上的水中仙子，正是格温多琳·哈利斯（Gwendolen Harleth）。她偎在那位于轮盘桌旁坐在她身边的那位太太的翼下——或者不如说是翱翔于她的肩头；同他们在一起的还有一位先生，留着白髭、头发剪得短短的：眉骨厚实，举止生硬，是个德国人。他们或走动或站着与熟人交谈，格温多琳颇受坐着的人们注目。

「真出挑的姑娘——那位哈利斯小姐——与众不同。」

「是啊，她如今把自己装扮成一条蛇的模样——通身绿和银，脖子也比平日扭动得多一些。」

「哦，她总得做出些不寻常的事来。我想她就是那种姑娘。范德努特先生，您觉得她美吗？」

「很美。一个男人可能为她冒绞刑的危险——我是说，一个傻瓜可能。」

「那么您喜欢翘鼻子，配上又长又窄的眼睛？」

「当它们与这样的整体（ensemble）相配的时候。」

「蛇的整体？」

「随您怎么说。女人是被蛇引诱的；男人为什么不能？」

「她确实很优雅；只是两颊缺点血色。她那种美，是拉弥亚式的美。」

「恰恰相反，我认为那肤色正是她主要的魅力之一。那是一种暖调的苍白，看上去十分健康。那只小巧的鼻子、那道渐渐微微上翘的弧线，真叫人心荡神驰。还有她的嘴——再没有更美的嘴了，双唇那样纤巧地向后卷曲，是吧，麦克沃思？」

「是吗？我可受不了那种嘴。它显得那样自鸣得意，仿佛自知其美——那弧线太僵死了。我喜欢颤动多一些的嘴。」

「依我看，她讨厌极了，」一位半老夫人说，「如今什么样的讨厌姑娘都能行时，真是奇了。这些朗根家的人是谁？有谁知道吗？」

「他们相当合乎体统（comme il faut）。我在俄国旅馆同他们吃过好几回饭。男爵夫人是英国人。哈利斯小姐管她叫表姨。那姑娘很有教养，而且聪明极了。」

「哎呀！那么男爵呢？」

「一幅很不错的家具画。」

「你们那位男爵夫人总泡在轮盘桌旁，」麦克沃思说，「我看是她教坏了那姑娘，让她赌起钱来。」

===Original===

“Oh, the old woman plays a very sober game; drops a ten-franc piece here and there. The girl is more headlong. But it is only a freak.”
“I hear she has lost all her winnings today. Are they rich? Who knows?”
“Ah, who knows? Who knows that about anybody?” said Mr. Vandernoodt, moving off to join the Langens.
The remark that Gwendolen wound her neck about more than usual this evening was true. But it was not that she might carry out the serpent idea more completely: it was that she watched for any chance of seeing Deronda, so that she might inquire about this stranger, under whose measuring gaze she was still wincing. At last her opportunity came.
“Mr. Vandernoodt, you know everybody,” said Gwendolen, not too eagerly, rather with a certain languor of utterance which she sometimes gave to her clear soprano. “Who is that near the door?”
“There are half a dozen near the door. Do you mean that old Adonis in the George the Fourth wig?”
“No, no; the dark-haired young man on the right with the dreadful expression.”
“Dreadful, do you call it? I think he is an uncommonly fine fellow.”
“But who is he?”
“He is lately come to our hotel with Sir Hugo Mallinger.”
“Sir Hugo Mallinger?”
“Yes. Do you know him?”
“No.” (Gwendolen colored slightly.) “He has a place near us, but he never comes to it. What did you say was the name of that gentleman near the door?”
“Deronda﻿—Mr. Deronda.”
“What a delightful name! Is he an Englishman?”
“Yes. He is reported to be rather closely related to the baronet. You are interested in him?”
“Yes. I think he is not like young men in general.”
“And you don’t admire young men in general?”
“Not in the least. I always know what they will say. I can’t at all guess what this Mr. Deronda would say. What *does* he say?”
“Nothing, chiefly. I sat with his party for a good hour last night on the terrace, and he never spoke﻿—and was not smoking either. He looked bored.”
“Another reason why I should like to know him. I am always bored.”
“I should think he would be charmed to have an introduction. Shall I bring it about? Will you allow it, baroness?”
“Why not?﻿—since he is related to Sir Hugo Mallinger. It is a new role of yours, Gwendolen, to be always bored,” continued Madame von Langen, when Mr. Vandernoodt had moved away. “Until now you have always seemed eager about something from morning till night.”
“That is just because I am bored to death.

===Chinese===

「哦，那老妇人赌得很谨慎；零零星星押个十法郎。那姑娘可鲁莽多了。不过只是一时兴之所至。」

「听说她今天把赢的全输光了。他们家有钱吗？谁知道呢？」

「啊，谁知道呢？谁又知道谁的底细呢？」范德努特先生说罢走开，朝朗根一家那边去了。

说格温多琳今晚脖子扭动得比往常更多，这话不假。但那并不是为了把蛇的构思贯彻得更彻底：而是她在留心一切机会，想瞧见德龙达，好打听这个陌生人的底细——他那打量的目光至今仍让她隐隐作痛。机会终于来了。

「范德努特先生，您谁都认得，」格温多琳说，口气不算急切，倒是带着一种她有时会赋予她清亮女高音的慵懒。「门口附近那个人是谁？」

「门口附近有半打人呢。您是指那个戴乔治四世式假发的老阿多尼斯吗？」

「不，不；右边那个黑头发的年轻人，一脸怕人的表情。」

「怕人？您管那叫怕人？我看他是个非凡的美男子。」

「可他是谁呢？」

「他最近同雨果·马林格爵士（Sir Hugo Mallinger）一起住进我们旅馆的。」

「雨果·马林格爵士？」

「是的。您认识他？」

「不认识。」（格温多琳微微红了脸。）「他的府邸在我们家附近，可他从不来住。您刚才说，门边那位先生叫什么名字？」

「德龙达——德龙达先生。」

「多好听的名字！他是英国人吗？」

「是。据说他与那位从男爵关系相当近。您对他有兴趣？」

「有。我觉得他不像一般的年轻人。」

「那么您不欣赏一般的年轻人喽？」

「一点也不。他们要说什么我总能料到。这位德龙达先生会说什么，我可完全猜不出。他都说些什么？」

「多半什么都不说。昨晚我在露台上同他们一伙坐了足足一个钟头，他一言不发——也没抽烟。看样子是腻烦了。」

「这就更是我想认识他的理由了。我总是腻烦。」

「我想他会很高兴有人引见的。要我来促成吗？男爵夫人，您允许吗？」

「为什么不呢？——既然他是雨果·马林格爵士的亲戚。倒是你这新角色演得怪，格温多琳，居然『总是腻烦』，」范德努特先生走开后，冯·朗根夫人接着说，「直到如今，你从早到晚好像总在盼着什么似的。」

「那恰恰是因为我烦得要死。

===Original===

If I am to leave off play I must break my arm or my collarbone. I must make something happen; unless you will go into Switzerland and take me up the Matterhorn.”
“Perhaps this Mr. Deronda’s acquaintance will do instead of the Matterhorn.”

But Gwendolen did not make Deronda’s acquaintance on this occasion. Mr. Vandernoodt did not succeed in bringing him up to her that evening, and when she reentered her own room she found a letter recalling her home.

===Chinese===

要是叫我不再赌，除非我摔断胳膊或锁骨。我总得弄出点事来；除非您肯去瑞士，带我登马特洪峰。」

「也许认识这位德龙达先生，可以代替马特洪峰。」

「也许吧。」

然而这一次格温多琳并没有结识德龙达。范德努特先生当晚没能把他领到她跟前；而当她回到自己房间里时，她发现了一封信，召她回家。

### II / 第二章
===Original===

> This man contrives a secret ’twixt us two,

That he may quell me with his meeting eyes

Like one who quells a lioness at bay.

This was the letter Gwendolen found on her table:

===Chinese===

> 这人暗中设下机密横在我们之间，
> 好用他逼视的目光将我镇住，
> 像镇住一头困兽的母狮。

格温多琳在桌上看到的是这样一封信：

===Original===

> Dearest Child.﻿—I have been expecting to hear from you for a week. In your last you said the Langens thought of leaving Leubronn and going to Baden. How could you be so thoughtless as to leave me in uncertainty about your address? I am in the greatest anxiety lest this should not reach you. In any case, you were to come home at the end of September, and I must now entreat you to return as quickly as possible, for if you spent all your money it would be out of my power to send you any more, and you must not borrow of the Langens, for I could not repay them. This is the sad truth, my child﻿—I wish I could prepare you for it better﻿—but a dreadful calamity has befallen us all. You know nothing about business and will not understand it; but Grapnell & Co. have failed for a million, and we are totally ruined﻿—your aunt Gascoigne as well as I, only that your uncle has his benefice, so that by putting down their carriage and getting interest for the boys, the family can go on. All the property our poor father saved for us goes to pay the liabilities. There is nothing I can call my own. It is better you should know this at once, though it rends my heart to have to tell it you. Of course we cannot help thinking what a pity it was that you went away just when you did. But I shall never reproach you, my dear child; I would save you from all trouble if I could. On your way home you will have time to prepare yourself for the change you will find. We shall perhaps leave Offendene at once, for we hope that Mr. Haynes, who wanted it before, may be ready to take it off my hands. Of course we cannot go to the rectory﻿—there is not a corner there to spare. We must get some hut or other to shelter us, and we must live on your uncle Gascoigne’s charity, until I see what else can be done. I shall not be able to pay the debts to the tradesmen besides the servants’ wages. Summon up your fortitude, my dear child; we must resign ourselves to God’s will. But it is hard to resign one’s self to Mr. Lassman’s wicked recklessness, which they say was the cause of the failure. Your poor sisters can only cry with me and give me no help. If you were once here, there might be a break in the cloud﻿—I always feel it impossible that you can have been meant for poverty. If the Langens wish to remain abroad, perhaps you can put yourself under someone else’s care for the journey.

===Chinese===

> 最亲爱的孩子——我等你的信已经等了一个星期。你上一封信里说，兰根一家打算离开卢布隆（Leubronn）去巴登。你怎么这样粗心，让我连你的地址都不得而知？我焦虑万分，唯恐这封信到不了你手里。无论如何，你本来九月底就该回家的，如今我必须恳请你尽快回来，因为倘若你把钱花光了，我是再也无法寄钱给你的，你也万万不可向兰根家借钱，因为我无力偿还。这是惨痛的事实，我的孩子——但愿我能更好地让你有个准备——可是一场可怕的灾祸降临到了我们全家头上。你不懂生意上的事，也不会明白：格拉普内尔公司破产了，负债一百万，我们彻底完了——你的加斯科因姨妈和我一样，只是你姨父还有圣俸，只要把马车退了，再给男孩子们张罗点利息收入，那一家人还过得下去。我们可怜的父亲为我们攒下的全部家产，都要拿去抵债了。我再没有一样东西可以称为自己的。这个你还是立刻知道的好，虽然说出这话来，我的心都要碎了。当然，我们不免要想，你偏偏在那个节骨眼上出门，实在太可惜了。可我永远不会责怪你，亲爱的孩子；只要能够，我情愿替你担下一切苦难。在回家的路上，你有时间让自己对将要面对的变化做好心理准备。我们也许马上就得离开奥芬迪恩（Offendene），因为海恩斯先生先前想要这房子，我们盼着他如今肯从我手里接过去。当然我们不能住到教区牧师宅去——那里连一个空角落也没有。我们得随便找个栖身的小屋，靠你加斯科因姨父的接济过活，再看还有什么别的办法。除了仆人的工资，那些欠店铺的账我是还不起的了。鼓起勇气来吧，亲爱的孩子；我们只能顺从上帝的旨意。可是要顺从拉斯曼先生那种恶劣的莽撞，实在太难了——听说破产就是他一手造成的。你可怜的姐姐们只会陪着我哭，一点也帮不上忙。你若回来了，这乌云里也许还能透出一线光——我始终觉得，你生来就不该受穷。要是兰根一家想留在国外，也许你可以托旁人照应着上路。

===Original===

But come as soon as you can to your afflicted and loving mamma,
> Fanny Davilow.

The first effect of this letter on Gwendolen was half-stupefying. The implicit confidence that her destiny must be one of luxurious ease, where any trouble that occurred would be well clad and provided for, had been stronger in her own mind than in her mamma’s, being fed there by her youthful blood and that sense of superior claims which made a large part of her consciousness. It was almost as difficult for her to believe suddenly that her position had become one of poverty and of humiliating dependence, as it would have been to get into the strong current of her blooming life the chill sense that her death would really come. She stood motionless for a few minutes, then tossed off her hat and automatically looked in the glass. The coils of her smooth light-brown hair were still in order perfect enough for a ballroom; and as on other nights, Gwendolen might have looked lingeringly at herself for pleasure (surely an allowable indulgence); but now she took no conscious note of her reflected beauty, and simply stared right before her as if she had been jarred by a hateful sound and was waiting for any sign of its cause. By-and-by she threw herself in the corner of the red velvet sofa, took up the letter again and read it twice deliberately, letting it at last fall on the ground, while she rested her clasped hands on her lap and sat perfectly still, shedding no tears. Her impulse was to survey and resist the situation rather than to wail over it. There was no inward exclamation of “Poor mamma!” Her mamma had never seemed to get much enjoyment out of life, and if Gwendolen had been at this moment disposed to feel pity she would have bestowed it on herself﻿—for was she not naturally and rightfully the chief object of her mamma’s anxiety too? But it was anger, it was resistance that possessed her; it was bitter vexation that she had lost her gains at roulette, whereas if her luck had continued through this one day she would have had a handsome sum to carry home, or she might have gone on playing and won enough to support them all. Even now was it not possible?

===Chinese===

> 但求你尽快回到你痛苦的、爱你的妈妈身边
> 范妮·戴维洛

这封信给格温多琳的头一阵影响几乎是令她麻木的。她心中素来确信自己的命运必定是优裕安逸的，纵有烦恼也是衣食无忧、早有安排的——这份信心在她自己心里比在她母亲心里还要牢固，因为她的青春热血，还有那种自命不凡的优越感（这占据了她意识的很大一部分），都在滋养着它。要她一下子相信自己沦落到了贫穷和屈辱的仰人鼻息之地，几乎就像要她那生机勃发的生命里忽然渗进死亡当真会来临的寒意一样难。她一动不动地站了几分钟，然后甩掉帽子，下意识地照了照镜子。她那浅褐色光滑的发卷依旧纹丝不乱，整齐得可以进舞厅；若在别的夜晚，格温多琳也许会顾影自怜地流连一番（这总归是情有可原的癖好）；可此刻她对自己的美貌浑然不觉，只是直愣愣地望着前方，仿佛被什么可憎的声响震了一下，正等着查明那声响的来由。过了一会儿，她一头倒在红丝绒沙发的角落里，重新拿起那封信，不慌不忙地读了两遍，随后任它落在地上，双手交叠搁在膝头，端坐不动，也不落泪。她的本能是要审视这处境、与之对抗，而不是对着它哀哭。她心里并没有一声「可怜的妈妈！」她妈妈从来不曾显得从生活里得到多少乐趣，即使此刻格温多琳想发慈悲，那慈悲也多半会落到自己身上——因为她岂不也是母亲心头天然的、名正言顺的第一牵挂？此刻占据她的是愤怒，是抗拒；她懊恼不已的是自己竟把轮盘赌赢来的钱又输掉了，倘若这一天的手气再延续一下，她本可以带一大笔钱回家，或者索性赌下去，赢个够全家吃用。即便是现在，难道就没有可能了吗？

===Original===

She had only four napoleons left in her purse, but she possessed some ornaments which she could sell: a practice so common in stylish society at German baths that there was no need to be ashamed of it; and even if she had not received her mamma’s letter, she would probably have decided to get money for an Etruscan necklace which she happened not to have been wearing since her arrival; nay, she might have done so with an agreeable sense that she was living with some intensity and escaping humdrum. With ten louis at her disposal and a return of her former luck, which seemed probable, what could she do better than go on playing for a few days? If her friends at home disapproved of the way in which she got the money, as they certainly would, still the money would be there. Gwendolen’s imagination dwelt on this course and created agreeable consequences, but not with unbroken confidence and rising certainty as it would have done if she had been touched with the gambler’s mania. She had gone to the roulette-table not because of passion, but in search of it: her mind was still sanely capable of picturing balanced probabilities, and while the chance of winning allured her, the chance of losing thrust itself on her with alternate strength and made a vision from which her pride sank sensitively. For she was resolved not to tell the Langens that any misfortune had befallen her family, or to make herself in any way indebted to their compassion; and if she were to part with her jewelry to any observable extent, they would interfere by inquiries and remonstrances. The course that held the least risk of intolerable annoyance was to raise money on her necklace early in the morning, tell the Langens that her mother desired her immediate return without giving a reason, and take the train for Brussels that evening. She had no maid with her, and the Langens might make difficulties about her returning home, but her will was peremptory.
Instead of going to bed she made as brilliant a light as she could and began to pack, working diligently, though all the while visited by the scenes that might take place on the coming day﻿—now by the tiresome explanations and farewells, and the whirling journey toward a changed home, now by the alternative of staying just another day and standing again at the roulette-table.

===Chinese===

她钱夹里只剩四个拿破仑金币了，不过她还有些首饰可以变卖：这种事在德国浴场的时髦圈子里司空见惯，用不着害臊；即使没收到母亲的信，她多半也会打定主意把那条伊特鲁里亚项链换钱——恰巧她来到此地后一直没戴过它；不但如此，她甚至可以从中获得一种快意，觉得自己活得有几分刺激，逃脱了平淡无奇的日子。手里有了十个路易，加之昔日手气多半会回来，还有什么比再赌几天更好的呢？即便家里亲友们不赞成她弄钱的这番手段——那是肯定不会赞成的——钱总归是钱，摆在那里。格温多琳的想象力在这条路上流连，编出种种称心的后果，却不是那种不可动摇的自信和步步高涨的笃定——倘若她沾上了赌徒的疯狂，便会是那样了。她上轮盘赌桌并非出于嗜赌的激情，而是去寻激情的：她的头脑依然健全，还能掂量各种可能性的轻重，赢钱的希望在引诱她，输钱的可能也轮番以同样的力量逼到眼前，化成一幅令她的自尊心敏感地畏缩下去的景象。因为她已打定主意，绝不告诉兰根一家自家遭了灾，也绝不受他们怜悯的恩惠；倘若她把首饰变卖得太惹眼，他们就要过问、要劝阻了。最不招烦的做法是：一清早拿项链去换钱，告诉兰根一家说母亲叫她立刻回去却不说明缘由，当晚就搭上去布鲁塞尔（Brussels）的火车。她没带女仆，兰根一家也许会拦着不让她独行，可她的意志是说一不二的。
她没有上床，而是把灯点得雪亮，动手收拾行李，做得勤勤恳恳，只是脑海里始终盘旋着第二天可能出现的种种场面——一会儿是那番恼人的解释和道别，那趟奔向一个变了个样的家的旋风似的旅程；一会儿又换作多留一天的打算，重新站到轮盘赌桌前去。

===Original===

But always in this latter scene there was the presence of that Deronda, watching her with exasperating irony, and﻿—the two keen experiences were inevitably revived together﻿—beholding her again forsaken by luck. This importunate image certainly helped to sway her resolve on the side of immediate departure, and to urge her packing to the point which would make a change of mind inconvenient. It had struck twelve when she came into her room, and by the time she was assuring herself that she had left out only what was necessary, the faint dawn was stealing through the white blinds and dulling her candles. What was the use of going to bed? Her cold bath was refreshment enough, and she saw that a slight trace of fatigue about the eyes only made her look the more interesting. Before six o’clock she was completely equipped in her gray traveling dress even to her felt hat, for she meant to walk out as soon as she could count on seeing other ladies on their way to the springs. And happening to be seated sideways before the long strip of mirror between her two windows she turned to look at herself, leaning her elbow on the back of the chair in an attitude that might have been chosen for her portrait. It is possible to have a strong self-love without any self-satisfaction, rather with a self-discontent which is the more intense because one’s own little core of egoistic sensibility is a supreme care; but Gwendolen knew nothing of such inward strife. She had a naive delight in her fortunate self, which any but the harshest saintliness will have some indulgence for in a girl who had every day seen a pleasant reflection of that self in her friends’ flattery as well as in the looking-glass. And even in this beginning of troubles, while for lack of anything else to do she sat gazing at her image in the growing light, her face gathered a complacency gradual as the cheerfulness of the morning. Her beautiful lips curled into a more and more decided smile, till at last she took off her hat, leaned forward and kissed the cold glass which had looked so warm. How could she believe in sorrow? If it attacked her, she felt the force to crush it, to defy it, or run away from it, as she had done already. Anything seemed more possible than that she could go on bearing miseries, great or small.

===Chinese===

可是在后一种场面里，总有那个德罗达在场，带着令人恼火的讥诮望着她，而且——两段刻骨的体验总是不由分说一并重现——他眼看着她再度被手运抛下。这个拂之不去的形像，确实帮着她把决心压到了立刻动身这一边，也催着她把行李收拾到不容反悔的地步。她回房时已敲过十二点，等她确信留下的都是必需品时，惨白的曙光已经渗过白色的百叶帘，把烛光衬得暗淡了。这时候还上床做什么？冷水浴足以让她恢复精神，况且她看出眼角一丝倦痕反倒使她更显楚楚动人。不到六点，她已一身灰色旅行装束穿戴齐整，连毛毡帽也戴上了，因为她打算一等能指望在去矿泉的路上遇上别家太太，就出门去。她恰好在两扇窗之间那条长镜前侧身坐着，便转过身来端详自己，一只手肘支在椅背上，那姿态简直可以入画。一个人可能怀有强烈的自恋而毫无自我满足，反倒怀着一种更炽烈的自我不满——因为自己那颗小小的自我敏感的核心乃是头等的操心之事；可是格温多琳全然不识这种内心的交战。她对自己这个幸运的造物怀着天真的欣喜，而这，除了最刻薄的圣徒，谁都会对一个姑娘多少宽容些——她天天从朋友们的奉承里，也从镜子里，看到那个自我的可爱倒影。即便在这灾难的开端，她因无事可做而坐在渐亮的晨光里凝望自己的影像，脸上还是渐渐聚起一层自得，像晨光一样缓缓开朗起来。她那美丽的双唇弯成越来越鲜明的笑意，末了她索性摘下帽子，俯身吻了吻那看起来如此温暖的冰冷镜面。她怎么能相信悲伤？悲伤若敢来犯，她自信有力气把它碾碎、把它傲然打退，或者干脆躲开它，就像从前那样。在她看来，天下什么事都比她长年累月地忍受苦难——无论大小——更可能些。

===Original===

Madame von Langen never went out before breakfast, so that Gwendolen could safely end her early walk by taking her way homeward through the Obere Strasse in which was the needed shop, sure to be open after seven. At that hour any observers whom she minded would be either on their walks in the region of the springs, or would be still in their bedrooms; but certainly there was one grand hotel, the Czarina from which eyes might follow her up to Mr. Wiener’s door. This was a chance to be risked: might she not be going in to buy something which had struck her fancy? This implicit falsehood passed through her mind as she remembered that the Czarina was Deronda’s hotel; but she was then already far up the Obere Strasse, and she walked on with her usual floating movement, every line in her figure and drapery falling in gentle curves attractive to all eyes except those which discerned in them too close a resemblance to the serpent, and objected to the revival of serpent-worship. She looked neither to the right hand nor to the left, and transacted her business in the shop with a coolness which gave little Mr. Wiener nothing to remark except her proud grace of manner, and the superior size and quality of the three central turquoises in the necklace she offered him. They had belonged to a chain once her father’s: but she had never known her father; and the necklace was in all respects the ornament she could most conveniently part with. Who supposes that it is an impossible contradiction to be superstitious and rationalizing at the same time? Roulette encourages a romantic superstition as to the chances of the game, and the most prosaic rationalism as to human sentiments which stand in the way of raising needful money. Gwendolen’s dominant regret was that after all she had only nine louis to add to the four in her purse: these Jew dealers were so unscrupulous in taking advantage of Christians unfortunate at play! But she was the Langens’ guest in their hired apartment, and had nothing to pay there: thirteen louis would do more than take her home; even if she determined on risking three, the remaining ten would more than suffice, since she meant to travel right on, day and night.

===Chinese===

冯·兰根太太从不在早饭前出门，因此格温多琳尽可以放心地早早散步，归途取道上街，那家要找的铺子就在街上，七点以后必定开门。在那个时辰，她在意的那些人都或者在矿泉一带散步，或者还在卧室里；不过有一家大旅馆——「女沙皇」——难免有眼睛会跟着她一直盯到维纳先生的店门口。这个险值得一冒：她兴许只是进店去买件看中了的小玩意呢？这个心照不宣的谎从她心头掠过，因为她想起「女沙皇」正是德罗达下榻的旅馆；不过那时她已走上上街好一段了，她依旧带着那种飘然从容的步态往前走，身姿和衣褶的每一条线条都弯成柔美的弧度，引人瞩目——只除了那些看出其中与蛇过于相似、反对恢复拜蛇仪式的眼睛。她目不斜视，在铺子里不动声色地办妥了交易，那份镇定让矮小的维纳先生无话可说，只留意到她高贵优雅的仪态，以及她递上的项链正中三颗绿松石格外大的尺寸和成色。那原是她父亲一条链子上的东西：可她从未见过父亲；这条项链是她在一切首饰里最方便脱手的一件。谁会以为，一个人迷信和精于算计不能并存？轮盘赌助长一种关于赌运的浪漫迷信，也助长一种关于人情的最庸俗的算计——凡挡了凑钱之路的情面，一概精打细算。格温多琳主要的遗憾是，到头来她只换得九个路易，添进钱夹里那四个去：这些犹太商人趁基督徒赌客倒霉，占起便宜来真是无所顾忌！不过她在兰根家租住的公寓里是客，分文不用花：十三个路易送她回家绰绰有余；就算她决心拿三个路易去冒险，剩下的十个也尽够了，因为她打算日夜兼程、一路坐到底。

===Original===

As she turned homeward, nay, entered and seated herself in the salon to await her friends and breakfast, she still wavered as to her immediate departure, or rather she had concluded to tell the Langens simply that she had had a letter from her mamma desiring her return, and to leave it still undecided when she should start. It was already the usual breakfast-time, and hearing someone enter as she was leaning back rather tired and hungry with her eyes shut, she rose expecting to see one or other of the Langens﻿—the words which might determine her lingering at least another day, ready-formed to pass her lips. But it was the servant bringing in a small packet for Miss Harleth, which had at that moment been left at the door. Gwendolen took it in her hand and immediately hurried into her own room. She looked paler and more agitated than when she had first read her mamma’s letter. Something﻿—she never quite knew what﻿—revealed to her before she opened the packet that it contained the necklace she had just parted with. Underneath the paper it was wrapped in a cambric handkerchief, and within this was a scrap of torn-off notepaper, on which was written with a pencil, in clear but rapid handwriting﻿—“A stranger who has found Miss Harleth’s necklace returns it to her with the hope that she will not again risk the loss of it.”
Gwendolen reddened with the vexation of wounded pride. A large corner of the handkerchief seemed to have been recklessly torn off to get rid of a mark; but she at once believed in the first image of “the stranger” that presented itself to her mind. It was Deronda; he must have seen her go into the shop; he must have gone in immediately after and repurchased the necklace. He had taken an unpardonable liberty, and had dared to place her in a thoroughly hateful position. What could she do?﻿—Not, assuredly, act on her conviction that it was he who had sent her the necklace and straightway send it back to him: that would be to face the possibility that she had been mistaken; nay, even if the “stranger” were he and no other, it would be something too gross for her to let him know that she had divined this, and to meet him again with that recognition in their minds. He knew very well that he was entangling her in helpless humiliation: it was another way of smiling at her ironically, and taking the air of a supercilious mentor.

===Chinese===

转身往回走的时候，乃至进了门在客厅里坐下等候朋友们和早饭的时候，她仍在犹豫是否立刻动身，或者说，她已经拿定主意只告诉兰根一家她收到母亲来信叫她回去，而把动身的日期暂且悬着。这时已是平日用早饭的时辰，她正又累又饿地仰靠着闭目养神，听见有人进来，便站起身来，以为是兰根夫妇中的哪一位——那几句也许能定下她多盘桓一天的话，已经到了嘴边。来的却是仆人，捧着一个给哈利思小姐的小包裹，方才有人送到门口的。格温多琳把它拿在手里，立刻匆匆进了自己的房间。她的脸色比初读母亲那封信时还要苍白、还要激动。某种东西——她自己始终说不清是什么——在她拆开包裹之前就告诉她，里面是她刚刚脱手的那条项链。包在纸里的是一条细麻纱手绢，手绢里裹着一小片撕下来的便笺，上面用铅笔写着一行清晰而仓促的字——「一位陌生人拾得哈利思小姐的项链，今奉还之，并望小姐不再将它置于失去之险。」
格温多琳涨红了脸，自尊受创的恼怒涌上心头。那块手绢仿佛被人鲁莽地撕去了一大角，为的是去掉一个标记；可她立刻就相信了脑海中浮现的第一个「陌生人」的形像。那是德罗达；他一定看见她进了铺子；一定紧跟着进去把项链赎了回来。他这是强人所难地冒犯了她，竟敢把她置于一个彻头彻尾可憎的境地。她能怎么办呢？——当然不能凭着一口咬定是他把项链送回来的，就原样退还给他：那就得面对自己也许认错了人的可能；不，纵然那「陌生人」千真万确就是他，让他知道她识破了这一点、再带着这份心照不宣与他重逢，也是她万难容忍的粗鄙之事。他分明知道自己把她缠进了无以自解的羞辱之中：这是换了一种方式讥笑她，摆出一副高高在上的训导者的架子。

===Original===

Gwendolen felt the bitter tears of mortification rising and rolling down her cheeks. No one had ever before dared to treat her with irony and contempt. One thing was clear: she must carry out her resolution to quit this place at once; it was impossible for her to reappear in the public salon, still less stand at the gaming-table with the risk of seeing Deronda. Now came an importunate knock at the door: breakfast was ready. Gwendolen with a passionate movement thrust necklace, cambric, scrap of paper, and all into her *nécessaire*, pressed her handkerchief against her face, and after pausing a minute or two to summon back her proud self-control, went to join her friends. Such signs of tears and fatigue as were left seemed accordant enough with the account she at once gave of her having sat up to do her packing, instead of waiting for help from her friend’s maid. There was much protestation, as she had expected, against her traveling alone, but she persisted in refusing any arrangements for companionship. She would be put into the ladies’ compartment and go right on. She could rest exceedingly well in the train, and was afraid of nothing.
In this way it happened that Gwendolen never reappeared at the roulette-table, but that Thursday evening left Leubronn for Brussels, and on Saturday morning arrived at Offendene, the home to which she and her family were soon to say a last goodbye.

===Chinese===

格温多琳感到屈辱的苦涩泪水涌上来，滚下双颊。从来没有谁敢这样讥诮她、轻慢她。有一件事是明白的：她必须实行立刻离开此地的决心；她再也不能在公共客厅里露面，更不能站到赌桌前，冒着撞见德罗达的风险。这时门上响起一阵急促的敲门声：早饭备好了。格温多琳激愤地把项链、麻纱手绢、纸片一股脑塞进她的针线匣，用手绢按了按脸，停了一两分钟，唤回她那高傲的自制，才出去与朋友们会合。她脸上残留的泪痕倦容，倒与她随口的说法十分相称——她说自己为了收拾行李熬了个通宵，没等朋友的贴身女仆来帮忙。不出所料，众人纷纷反对她独自上路，可她执意谢绝了一切结伴的安排。她会给安置进女士车厢，一路坐到底。她在火车上能歇得很好，什么也不怕。
事情就这样，格温多琳从此没有再在轮盘赌桌前露过面；那个星期四的傍晚，她离开卢布隆去了布鲁塞尔，星期六早晨到了奥芬迪恩——那座她和她的家人不久就要永别的家。

### III / 第三章
===Original===

> “Let no flower of the spring pass by us; let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they be withered.”

Pity that Offendene was not the home of Miss Harleth’s childhood, or endeared to her by family memories! A human life, I think, should be well rooted in some spot of a native land, where it may get the love of tender kinship for the face of earth, for the labors men go forth to, for the sounds and accents that haunt it, for whatever will give that early home a familiar unmistakable difference amid the future widening of knowledge: a spot where the definiteness of early memories may be inwrought with affection, and﻿—kindly acquaintance with all neighbors, even to the dogs and donkeys, may spread not by sentimental effort and reflection, but as a sweet habit of the blood. At five years old, mortals are not prepared to be citizens of the world, to be stimulated by abstract nouns, to soar above preference into impartiality; and that prejudice in favor of milk with which we blindly begin, is a type of the way body and soul must get nourished at least for a time. The best introduction to astronomy is to think of the nightly heavens as a little lot of stars belonging to one’s own homestead.
But this blessed persistence in which affection can take root had been wanting in Gwendolen’s life. It was only a year before her recall from Leubronn that Offendene had been chosen as her mamma’s home, simply for its nearness to Pennicote Rectory, and that Mrs. Davilow, Gwendolen, and her four half-sisters (the governess and the maid following in another vehicle) had been driven along the avenue for the first time, on a late October afternoon when the rooks were crawing loudly above them, and the yellow elm-leaves were whirling.
The season suited the aspect of the old oblong redbrick house, rather too anxiously ornamented with stone at every line, not excepting the double row of narrow windows and the large square portico. The stone encouraged a greenish lichen, the brick a powdery gray, so that though the building was rigidly rectangular there was no harshness in the physiognomy which it turned to the three avenues cut east, west and south in the hundred yards’ breadth of old plantation encircling the immediate grounds.

===Chinese===

> 「莫让春天的花朵从我们身边溜过；趁玫瑰蕾尚未凋萎，让我们以之为冠。」

可惜奥芬迪恩（Offendene）不是哈利思小姐度过童年的家，也没有家族的记忆使她与之亲近！我想，一个人的生命应当牢牢扎根在故土的某个角落，在那里，他可以对大地的容颜、对人们外出从事的劳作、对萦绕其间的声响与口音，生出温柔的亲情；无论日后见识如何拓宽，那个早年的家园始终保有熟悉而无可错认的独特之处——在那里，早年记忆的轮廓可以与深情交织在一起；与四邻的熟稔，甚至与那里的狗和驴子的熟稔，不必靠感伤的努力与思量去延展，而是化作血脉里一种甜蜜的习性。人在五岁上，还没准备好做世界公民，还没准备好被抽象名词激励，还没准备好超越偏好而登临公正无私；我们盲目开始时对乳汁的偏爱，正是身心至少在一段时期内必须如此汲取养分的一个征兆。入门天文学的最佳途径，是把夜空的繁星看作自家宅院的一小片星辰。
可是这种让爱意得以扎根的、可贵的延续性，在格温多琳的生命里却一直缺席。她从卢布隆（Leubronn）被召回的前一年，奥芬迪恩才被选为她母亲的居所，无非因为它离彭尼科特牧师宅近。十月底的一个下午，戴维洛太太、格温多琳和她的四个异姓姐妹（家庭女教师和女仆乘另一辆车跟在后面）第一次驱车驶上林荫道，那时白嘴鸦在头顶喧噪，黄色的榆树叶在打着旋儿。
这个季节正衬着这座老式长方形红砖房的气象——每一道线条都镶着石头，未免过于刻意，连那两排窄窗和方形大柱廊也不例外。石上生出青绿的苔藓，砖上蒙着粉灰，于是尽管房舍轮廓分毫不苟地方正，它朝向东、西、南三条林荫道的那副面孔，却并无一丝冷峻——三条道穿过环绕宅园、百码宽的老树种植园。

===Original===

One would have liked the house to have been lifted on a knoll, so as to look beyond its own little domain to the long thatched roofs of the distant villages, the church towers, the scattered homesteads, the gradual rise of surging woods, and the green breadths of undulating park which made the beautiful face of the earth in that part of Wessex. But though standing thus behind a screen amid flat pastures, it had on one side a glimpse of the wider world in the lofty curves of the chalk downs, grand steadfast forms played over by the changing days.
The house was but just large enough to be called a mansion, and was moderately rented, having no manor attached to it, and being rather difficult to let with its sombre furniture and faded upholstery. But inside and outside it was what no beholder could suppose to be inhabited by retired tradespeople: a certainty which was worth many conveniences to tenants who not only had the taste that shrinks from new finery, but also were in that border-territory of rank where annexation is a burning topic: and to take up her abode in a house which had once sufficed for dowager countesses gave a perceptible tinge to Mrs. Davilow’s satisfaction in having an establishment of her own. This, rather mysteriously to Gwendolen, appeared suddenly possible on the death of her stepfather, Captain Davilow, who had for the last nine years joined his family only in a brief and fitful manner, enough to reconcile them to his long absences; but she cared much more for the fact than for the explanation. All her prospects had become more agreeable in consequence. She had disliked their former way of life, roving from one foreign watering-place or Parisian apartment to another, always feeling new antipathies to new suites of hired furniture, and meeting new people under conditions which made her appear of little importance; and the variation of having passed two years at a showy school, where, on all occasions of display, she had been put foremost, had only deepened her sense that so exceptional a person as herself could hardly remain in ordinary circumstances or in a social position less than advantageous. Any fear of this latter evil was banished now that her mamma was to have an establishment; for on the point of birth Gwendolen was quite easy.

===Chinese===

谁都会希望这房子坐落在一座小丘上，好让它越过自家的小小领地，望见远处村落长长的茅草屋顶、教堂的尖塔、散落的农舍、渐次涌起的林涛，还有那起伏的绿茵牧场——它们构成了威塞克斯那一带大地美丽的容颜。然而它虽这样藏在一带平缓牧场的屏障之后，一侧却可以瞥见更广阔的天地：白垩丘高耸的弧线，那庄严坚定的形骸，任变幻的天光在其上流转。
这房子大小刚刚够得上称作宅邸，租金也不高，不带庄园产业，加上家具暗沉、幔帘褪色，颇难租出。但由内到外，谁都看不出它的住户会是退隐的商贾人家：对房客们来说，这份确凿抵得过许多便利——他们不仅趣味高雅，见不得崭新的华丽，而且身处身份等级的边境地带，那里「兼并」是个烫手的话题；能住进一座曾容得下遇居的伯爵夫人的宅子，给戴维洛太太自置门户的欢喜平添了一抹可辨的色泽。这事在格温多琳看来颇有些神秘：继父戴维洛上尉一死，这事忽然就办得成了——过去九年里，他与其家人团聚的日子短促而断续，倒也让他们习惯了他的长期在外；不过她看重的是这既成的事实，而不是其中的缘由。她的一切前景都随之变得更加称心。她从不喜欢从前那种生活，从一处外国浴场或巴黎公寓辗转到另一处，对每一套租来的家具都生出新的厌倦，而在种种叫她显得无足轻重的境遇下结识一批批新面孔；在一所浮华学校里度过的那两年，也只加深了她的这种感觉——每逢展示的场合她都被推在最前头——像她这样出类拔萃的人，断难安处于平庸的环境或不利的社会地位。如今母亲有了自己的门户，后一种忧患便烟消云散了；因为在出身这一点上，格温多琳是颇为心安的。

===Original===

She had no notion how her maternal grandfather got the fortune inherited by his two daughters; but he had been a West Indian﻿—which seemed to exclude further question; and she knew that her father’s family was so high as to take no notice of her mamma, who nevertheless preserved with much pride the miniature of a Lady Molly in that connection. She would probably have known much more about her father but for a little incident which happened when she was twelve years old. Mrs. Davilow had brought out, as she did only at wide intervals, various memorials of her first husband, and while showing his miniature to Gwendolen recalled with a fervor which seemed to count on a peculiar filial sympathy, the fact that dear papa had died when his little daughter was in long clothes. Gwendolen, immediately thinking of the unlovable stepfather whom she had been acquainted with the greater part of her life while her frocks were short, said,
“Why did you marry again, mamma? It would have been nicer if you had not.”
Mrs. Davilow colored deeply, a slight convulsive movement passed over her face, and straightway shutting up the memorials she said, with a violence quite unusual in her,
“You have no feeling, child!”
Gwendolen, who was fond of her mamma, felt hurt and ashamed, and had never since dared to ask a question about her father.
This was not the only instance in which she had brought on herself the pain of some filial compunction. It was always arranged, when possible, that she should have a small bed in her mamma’s room; for Mrs. Davilow’s motherly tenderness clung chiefly to her eldest girl, who had been born in her happier time. One night under an attack of pain she found that the specific regularly placed by her bedside had been forgotten, and begged Gwendolen to get out of bed and reach it for her. That healthy young lady, snug and warm as a rosy infant in her little couch, objected to step out into the cold, and lying perfectly still, grumbling a refusal. Mrs. Davilow went without the medicine and never reproached her daughter; but the next day Gwendolen was keenly conscious of what must be in her mamma’s mind, and tried to make amends by caresses which cost her no effort.

===Chinese===

她全然不知外祖父那份由两个女儿继承的家产是怎么挣来的；只知道他是个西印度人——这似乎便堵住了一切追问；她还知道自己父家的门第高到不屑理会她母亲，尽管如此，母亲仍颇为自豪地保存着那一门中一位莫莉小姐的袖珍画像。倘若不是她十二岁那年的一件小事，她本可以多知道些父亲的情况。戴维洛太太难得隔上许久才取出亡夫的种种纪念物，这回她把他的袖珍画像拿给格温多琳看，满怀深情地回忆说，亲爱的爸爸去世时，小女儿还在襁褓之中——那语气仿佛指望一份特别的父女之情。格温多琳立刻想起那个并不可爱的继父——在她穿短裙的大半岁月里她所熟悉的唯一父亲——便说：
「妈妈，你为什么要再嫁？不嫁才好呢。」
戴维洛太太深深红了脸，面掣掠过一阵痉挛，随即收起那些纪念物，用她素来没有的激烈口气说：
「你这孩子没有心肝！」
格温多琳本是爱母亲的，觉得又委屈又羞愧，从此再不敢问起父亲的事。
这并不是她唯一一次惹得自己心中愧疚不安。每逢可能，总是安排她睡在母亲房里的一张小床上；因为戴维洛太太的母爱主要系在长女身上——她生于母亲较幸福的年月。一天夜里，母亲疼痛发作，发现照例放在床头的药忘了拿，便求格温多琳下床替她取来。那位健壮的小姐，正像红润的婴儿一样在温暖的小床上舒坦，不肯下地踩冰冷的地板，一动不动地躺着，嘟囔着回绝了。戴维洛太太忍痛没吃药，也从未责备女儿；可第二天格温多琳便敏锐地意识到母亲心里存着什么，便用亲昵来赔补——那对她毫不费力。

===Original===

Having always been the pet and pride of the household, waited on by mother, sisters, governess and maids, as if she had been a princess in exile, she naturally found it difficult to think her own pleasure less important than others made it, and when it was positively thwarted felt an astonished resentment apt, in her cruder days, to vent itself in one of those passionate acts which look like a contradiction of habitual tendencies. Though never even as a child thoughtlessly cruel, nay delighting to rescue drowning insects and watch their recovery, there was a disagreeable silent remembrance of her having strangled her sister’s canary-bird in a final fit of exasperation at its shrill singing which had again and again jarringly interrupted her own. She had taken pains to buy a white mouse for her sister in retribution, and though inwardly excusing herself on the ground of a peculiar sensitiveness which was a mark of her general superiority, the thought of that infelonious murder had always made her wince. Gwendolen’s nature was not remorseless, but she liked to make her penances easy, and now that she was twenty and more, some of her native force had turned into a self-control by which she guarded herself from penitential humiliation. There was more show of fire and will in her than ever, but there was more calculation underneath it.
On this day of arrival at Offendene, which not even Mrs. Davilow had seen before﻿—the place having been taken for her by her brother-in-law, Mr. Gascoigne﻿—when all had got down from the carriage, and were standing under the porch in front of the open door, so that they could have a general view of the place and a glimpse of the stone hall and staircase hung with sombre pictures, but enlivened by a bright wood fire, no one spoke; mamma, the four sisters and the governess all looked at Gwendolen, as if their feelings depended entirely on her decision. Of the girls, from Alice in her sixteenth year to Isabel in her tenth, hardly anything could be said on a first view, but that they were girlish, and that their black dresses were getting shabby. Miss Merry was elderly and altogether neutral in expression. Mrs. Davilow’s worn beauty seemed the more pathetic for the look of entire appeal which she cast at Gwendolen, who was glancing round at the house, the landscape and the entrance hall with an air of rapid judgment.

===Chinese===

她从来是这个家的宠儿和骄傲，母亲、姐妹、家庭教师和女仆们伺候着她，仿佛她是一位流亡中的公主，于是她自然而然觉得，自己的欢愉不会不如别人看重的那么要紧；一旦果真受了阻挠，便生出一种愕然的怨愤——在她年幼粗莽的日子里，这怨愤往往会化作某桩激烈的举动，看上去与她平日的习性截然相反。她虽然从小并无残忍之心，甚至乐于搭救落水的昆虫、看它们缓过气来，却有一段不声不响的不愉快记忆：她曾在金丝雀刺耳的啼叫一而再、再而三地搅了自己的歌声之后，于最后一次恼怒中掐死了姐姐的那只鸟。她费心给姐姐买了一只白鼠作为赔偿；尽管内心以自己特有的敏感为由替自己开脱——那份敏感正是她总体优越的标记——那桩可怜的谋杀总叫她心里发虚。格温多琳的天性并非没有悔恨，只是她喜欢让赎罪变得轻松；如今她已年过二十，天生的一些火气已经化作一种自制，凭它护住自己不受忏悔的羞辱。她的火气与意志比从前更显露，底下却多了算计。
到奥芬迪恩的这一天——连戴维洛太太也未曾先来看过这宅子，是她的姐夫加斯科因先生代为租下的——众人下了车，一齐站在敞开的门前廊下，得以把这座宅子总览一番，并瞥见挂满暗沉画像、却被明亮的柴火映得有了生气的石厅和石阶。谁都不作声；妈妈、四个姐妹和家庭教师都望着格温多琳，仿佛她们的心情全系于她的一句决断。那几个姑娘，从十六岁的爱丽丝到十岁的伊莎贝尔，初看之下几乎无从说起，只能说是些黄毛丫头，黑色的衣裙已见邋遢。梅里小姐上了年纪，神情全然平淡无奇。戴维洛太太那憔悴的美，因为她投向格温多琳的满含仰赖的一瞥而愈发动人；格温多琳正以一副快速评断的神气环顾着宅子、风景和门厅。

===Original===

Imagine a young racehorse in the paddock among untrimmed ponies and patient hacks.
“Well, dear, what do you think of the place,” said Mrs. Davilow at last, in a gentle, deprecatory tone.
“I think it is charming,” said Gwendolen, quickly. “A romantic place; anything delightful may happen in it; it would be a good background for anything. No one need be ashamed of living here.”
“There is certainly nothing common about it.”
“Oh, it would do for fallen royalty or any sort of grand poverty. We ought properly to have been living in splendor, and have come down to this. It would have been as romantic as could be. But I thought my uncle and aunt Gascoigne would be here to meet us, and my cousin Anna,” added Gwendolen, her tone changed to sharp surprise.
“We are early,” said Mrs. Davilow, and entering the hall, she said to the housekeeper who came forward, “You expect Mr. and Mrs. Gascoigne?”
“Yes, madam; they were here yesterday to give particular orders about the fires and the dinner. But as to fires, I’ve had ’em in all the rooms for the last week, and everything is well aired. She was introducing herself anew to relatives who had not seen her since the comparatively unfinished age of sixteen, and she was anxious﻿—no, not anxious, but resolved that they should admire her.
Mrs. Gascoigne bore a family likeness to her sister. But she was darker and slighter, her face was unworn by grief, her movements were less languid, her expression more alert and critical as that of a rector’s wife bound to exert a beneficent authority. Their closest resemblance lay in a nonresistant disposition, inclined to imitation and obedience; but this, owing to the difference in their circumstances, had led them to very different issues. The younger sister had been indiscreet, or at least unfortunate in her marriages; the elder believed herself the most enviable of wives, and her pliancy had ended in her sometimes taking shapes of surprising definiteness. Many of her opinions, such as those on church government and the character of Archbishop Laud, seemed too decided under every alteration to have been arrived at otherwise than by a wifely receptiveness. And there was much to encourage trust in her husband’s authority. He had some agreeable virtues, some striking advantages, and the failings that were imputed to him all leaned toward the side of success.
One of his advantages was a fine person, which perhaps was even more impressive at fifty-seven than it had been earlier in life. There were no distinctively clerical lines in the face, no tricks of starchiness or of affected ease: in his Inverness cape he could not have been identified except as a gentleman with handsome dark features, a nose which began with an intention to be aquiline but suddenly became straight, and iron-gray hair. Perhaps he owed this freedom from the sort of professional makeup which penetrates skin, tones and gestures and defies all drapery, to the fact that he had once been Captain Gaskin, having taken orders and a diphthong but shortly before his engagement to Miss Armyn. If anyone had objected that his preparation for the clerical function was inadequate, his friends might have asked who made a better figure in it, who preached better or had more authority in his parish? He had a native gift for administration, being tolerant both of opinions and conduct, because he felt himself able to overrule them, and was free from the irritations of conscious feebleness.
