两位朋友一同上伦敦去：梅里克回切尔西的小家，同母亲和妹妹们同庆；德龙达去办那件较不易的任务——向雨果爵士敞开自己的心。他多少指望从男爵素来容得下人的怪僻，但他遇到的阻力比预想的少。

===Original===

He was received with even warmer kindness than usual, the failure was passed over lightly, and when he detailed his reasons for wishing to quit the university and go to study abroad, Sir Hugo sat for some time in a silence which was rather meditative than surprised. At last he said, looking at Daniel with examination, “So you don’t want to be an Englishman to the backbone after all?”
“I want to be an Englishman, but I want to understand other points of view. And I want to get rid of a merely English attitude in studies.”
“I see; you don’t want to be turned out in the same mould as every other youngster. And I have nothing to say against your doffing some of our national prejudices. I feel the better myself for having spent a good deal of my time abroad. But, for God’s sake, keep an English cut, and don’t become indifferent to bad tobacco! And, my dear boy, it is good to be unselfish and generous; but don’t carry that too far. It will not do to give yourself to be melted down for the benefit of the tallow-trade; you must know where to find yourself. However, I shall put no veto on your going. Wait until I can get off Committee, and I’ll run over with you.”
So Deronda went according to his will. But not before he had spent some hours with Hans Meyrick, and been introduced to the mother and sisters in the Chelsea home. The shy girls watched and registered every look of their brother’s friend, declared by Hans to have been the salvation of him, a fellow like nobody else, and, in fine, a brick. They so thoroughly accepted Deronda as an ideal, that when he was gone the youngest set to work, under the criticism of the two elder girls, to paint him as Prince Camaralzaman.

===Chinese===

他受到的接待比平日更为温暖，那次失败被轻轻带过；待他细陈想离开大学、出国求学的缘由，雨果爵士沉思般地坐了半晌——与其说是惊讶，不如说是沉思。末了他端详着丹尼尔说：「这么说，你到底还是不想做个彻头彻尾的英国人？」
「我想做英国人，可我也想理解别的视角。而且我想摆脱治学上那种纯然英国式的姿态。」
「我明白；你不想同别的每一个年轻人一样从同一个模子里倒出来。你要脱掉几分我们的国民偏见，我无话可反对。我自己在国外住了那么久，也自觉受益。可是看在上帝份上，保持一副英国式样，别变得连坏烟草都无所谓！还有，亲爱的孩子，无私、慷慨固然好；可别做过头。把自己熔了去贴补蜡烛贸易，那可不行；你得知道自己身在何处。不过，你走，我不否决。等我委员会的事一了，我陪你跑一趟。」
于是德龙达如愿而行。只是行前他先同汉斯·梅里克盘桓了几个钟头，又被引见给切尔西那小家里的母亲和妹妹们。那几个羞怯的姑娘注视着、记下了哥哥这位朋友的每一瞥——据汉斯宣称，此人是他的救星，天下再无第二个，总而言之，是个好汉。她们把德龙达全然奉为理想，乃至他走后，最小的那个便在两个姐姐的批评指正下，动手把他画成卡玛拉尔赞王子。

### XVII / 第十七章
===Original===

> This is truth the poet sings,

That a sorrow’s crown of sorrow is remembering happier things.

===Chinese===

> 诗人所唱乃是真理：
悲伤之悲伤的冠冕，是回忆幸福的时光。

===Original===

On a fine evening near the end of July, Deronda was rowing himself on the Thames. It was already a year or more since he had come back to England, with the understanding that his education was finished, and that he was somehow to take his place in English society; but though, in deference to Sir Hugo’s wish, and to fence off idleness, he had begun to read law, this apparent decision had been without other result than to deepen the roots of indecision. His old love of boating had revived with the more force now that he was in town with the Mallingers, because he could nowhere else get the same still seclusion which the river gave him. He had a boat of his own at Putney, and whenever Sir Hugo did not want him, it was his chief holiday to row till past sunset and come in again with the stars. Not that he was in a sentimental stage; but he was in another sort of contemplative mood perhaps more common in the young men of our day﻿—that of questioning whether it were worth while to take part in the battle of the world: I mean, of course, the young men in whom the unproductive labor of questioning is sustained by three or five percent, on capital which somebody else has battled for. It puzzled Sir Hugo that one who made a splendid contrast with all that was sickly and puling should be hampered with ideas which, since they left an accomplished Whig like himself unobstructed, could be no better than spectral illusions; especially as Deronda set himself against authorship﻿—a vocation which is understood to turn foolish thinking into funds.
Rowing in his dark-blue shirt and skullcap, his curls closely clipped, his mouth beset with abundant soft waves of beard, he bore only disguised traces of the seraphic boy “trailing clouds of glory.” Still, even one who had never seen him since his boyhood might have looked at him with slow recognition, due perhaps to the peculiarity of the gaze which Gwendolen chose to call “dreadful,” though it had really a very mild sort of scrutiny. The voice, sometimes audible in subdued snatches of song, had turned out merely a high baritone; indeed, only to look at his lithe, powerful frame and the firm gravity of his face would have been enough for an experienced guess that he had no rare and ravishing tenor such as nature reluctantly makes at some sacrifice.

===Chinese===

七月末一个晴朗的傍晚，德龙达独自在泰晤士河上划船。他回英国已有一年多，按事先的默契，他的学业已告完成，接下来要设法在英国社交界占一个位置；虽然出于对雨果爵士意愿的尊重、也为了挡开无所事事，他开始攻读法律，但这表面的定夺别无结果，只是把优柔寡断的根扎得更深。他对划船的旧爱，如今随他同马林格一家住在城里而复燃得更旺，因为别处再找不回河流给他的这种静寂的独处。他在帕特尼有一条自己的船；雨果爵士用不着他的时候，他最大的假日便是划到日落之后，再伴着星星归航。倒不是他到了伤感的年纪，而是他正处在另一种沉思的心境里——这种心境如今在青年中或许更普遍——质疑参加世界的战斗究竟值不值得：当然，我指的是那种青年，他们那不产出任何成果的质疑劳动，靠百分之三或五的利息养着——本金是别人替他们战斗挣来的。叫雨果爵士困惑的是：一个同一切孱弱娇气形成鲜明对照的人，竟被一些念头绊住脚；这些念头既然拦不住他这样一位功成名就的辉格党人，至多是些幽灵的幻象罢了；尤其德龙达还偏偏不肯当作家——那可是公认的能把愚蠢的思考转换成资金的行当。

他穿着深蓝色衬衫、戴着便帽划着船，鬈发剪得短短，嘴边蓄着浓密柔软的波浪状胡须，那个「拖曳着荣耀云霞」的小天使，如今只剩改头换面的些许痕迹了。不过，即使一个从少年时代就没见过他的人，看他一眼也会缓缓认出来，多半是因为那目光的特异——格温多琳偏偏管它叫「怕人」，其实那不过是一种非常温和的审视。那嗓音——有时低低的几句歌听得见——最终定型为偏高的男中音；其实，只消看看他柔韧有力的身架和脸上坚定的沉肃，有经验的人便猜得出，他并没有那种造化吝于造就、必得付出牺牲才肯给的希罕而迷人的男高音。

===Original===

Look at his hands: they are not small and dimpled, with tapering fingers that seem to have only a deprecating touch: they are long, flexible, firmly-grasping hands, such as Titian has painted in a picture where he wanted to show the combination of refinement with force. And there is something of a likeness, too, between the faces belonging to the hands﻿—in both the uniform pale-brown skin, the perpendicular brow, the calmly penetrating eyes. Not seraphic any longer: thoroughly terrestrial and manly; but still of a kind to raise belief in a human dignity which can afford to recognize poor relations.
Such types meet us here and there among average conditions; in a workman, for example, whistling over a bit of measurement and lifting his eyes to answer our question about the road. And often the grand meanings of faces as well as of written words may lie chiefly in the impressions that happen just now to be of importance in relation to Deronda, rowing on the Thames in a very ordinary equipment for a young Englishman at leisure, and passing under Kew Bridge with no thought of an adventure in which his appearance was likely to play any part. In fact, he objected very strongly to the notion, which others had not allowed him to escape, that his appearance was of a kind to draw attention; and hints of this, intended to be complimentary, found an angry resonance in him, coming from mingled experiences, to which a clue has already been given. His own face in the glass had during many years associated for him with thoughts of someone whom he must be like﻿—one about whose character and lot he continually wondered, and never dared to ask.
In the neighborhood of Kew Bridge, between six and seven o’clock, the river was no solitude. Several persons were sauntering on the towing-path, and here and there a boat was plying. Deronda had been rowing fast to get over this spot, when, becoming aware of a great barge advancing toward him, he guided his boat aside, and rested on his oar within a couple of yards of the river-brink. He was all the while unconsciously continuing the low-toned chant which had haunted his throat all the way up the river﻿—the gondolier’s song in the *Otello*, where Rossini has worthily set to music the immortal words of Dante,

> “Nessun maggior dolore

Che ricordarsi del tempo felice

Nella miseria:”1

===Chinese===

看他的手：不是小小的、带着酒窝、指尖细削仿佛只会安抚的手；而是修长、灵活、握持有力的手，提香在一幅想表现精致与力量相结合的画里画过的那种。手的主人的脸，也有几分相似——两幅脸上同样是匀净的棕白皮肤、挺直的额头、沉静而通透的眼睛。不再是小天使：彻头彻尾入世而男子气了；但仍旧是那一种脸，叫人相信一种负担得起认穷亲戚的人类尊严。

这样的类型，我们在寻常境遇中处处可遇：比如一个工匠，一边量着活计吹口哨，一边抬眼回答我们问路。而面孔如文字一样，其宏大的含义往往主要系于恰在眼下、与德龙达相关的种种印象——此刻他正划着船，一身英国闲适青年极寻常的装束，从丘桥下经过，做梦也想不到一场他的外貌将担任角色的奇遇。事实上，别人硬塞给他、不许他逃掉的那个说法——说他的外貌属于引人注目的一类——他非常反感；那些存心恭维的暗示，总在他心里激起愤怒的回响，来自种种交杂的经历，线索前文已有所交代。多年来，镜子里他自己的脸，总让他联想到一个他想必相像的人——一个他不断揣度其性情与命运、却从不敢发问的人。

六七点钟之间，丘桥一带的河面并不冷清。纤道上有人闲逛，水上时有小船往来。德龙达为快点划过这段，正加速划着，忽见一艘大驳船迎面驶来，便把船引向一旁，收桨停在离岸边两三码处。一路上他喉咙里始终低回着一支歌，此刻不自觉地还在哼——罗西尼的《奥赛罗》里贡多拉船夫的歌，作曲家在那里面为但丁不朽的诗句谱了相称的音乐：

> 「再没有更大的悲伤，

莫过于在苦难中

回忆幸福的时光。」

===Original===

and, as he rested on his oar, the pianissimo fall of the melodic wail “*nella miseria*” was distinctly audible on the brink of the water. Three or four persons had paused at various spots to watch the barge passing the bridge, and doubtless included in their notice the young gentleman in the boat; but probably it was only to one ear that the low vocal sounds came with more significance than if they had been an insect-murmur amidst the sum of current noises. Deronda, awaiting the barge, now turning his head to the riverside, and saw at a few yards’ distant from him a figure which might have been an impersonation of the misery he was unconsciously giving voice to: a girl hardly more than eighteen, of low slim figure, with most delicate little face, her dark curls pushed behind her ears under a large black hat, a long woolen cloak over her shoulders. Her hands were hanging down clasped before her, and her eyes were fixed on the river with a look of immovable, statue-like despair. This strong arrest of his attention made him cease singing: apparently his voice had entered her inner world without her taking any note of whence it came, for when it suddenly ceased she changed her attitude slightly, and, looking round with a frightened glance, met Deronda’s face. It was but a couple of moments, but that seemed a long while for two people to look straight at each other. Her look was something like that of a fawn or other gentle animal before it turns to run away: no blush, no special alarm, but only some timidity which yet could not hinder her from a long look before she turned. In fact, it seemed to Deronda that she was only half conscious of her surroundings: was she hungry, or was there some other cause of bewilderment? He felt an outleap of interest and compassion toward her; but the next instant she had turned and walked away to a neighboring bench under a tree. He had no right to linger and watch her: poorly-dressed, melancholy women are common sights; it was only the delicate beauty, picturesque lines and color of the image that was exceptional, and these conditions made it more markedly impossible that he should obtrude his interest upon her. He began to row away and was soon far up the river; but no other thoughts were busy enough quite to expel that pale image of unhappy girlhood.

===Chinese===

他停桨的当儿，那旋律的哀叹「*在苦难中*」以最轻的弱音，在岸边清晰可闻。岸上有三四个行人停在各处看驳船过桥，多半也把船里这位年轻先生收在眼里；但那低低的歌声，多半也只对一只耳朵携带了超出虫鸣的意义——在这满河嘈杂的总和里。德龙达等驳船过去，转头朝岸边一望，看见几码外一个身影，简直可以充当他不自觉唱出的那种苦难的化身：一个至多十八岁的姑娘，身量纤瘦，一张极其精致的小脸，深色的鬈发拢在耳后，戴一顶宽大的黑帽，肩上披着长长的呢斗篷。她双手交握垂在身前，眼睛凝望着河面，带着一种纹丝不动的、雕像般的绝望。这强烈的凝定使他中断了歌唱：显然，他的嗓音已进入她的内心世界，她却并未留意它来自何处；因为歌声一停，她便微微变了姿势，惊惶地环顾，正与德龙达的目光相遇。不过两秒钟，可两个人这样直直对望，两秒钟已显得很久。她的眼神像一头小鹿或别的温顺动物在转身逃开之前的那种：没有脸红，没有特别的惊慌，只有几分羞怯，而那羞怯又挡不住她在转身之前久久地看。在德龙达感觉里，她对自己的周遭只有一半的知觉：她是饿了，还是另有令她失魂落魄的缘故？他心里涌起一阵关切与怜惜；可下一瞬她已转身，走到附近树下的一条长椅那儿去了。他没有权利流连注视她：衣衫寒素、神情忧郁的女人随处都见得到；特殊的只是那形象的纤秀之美、如画的线条与颜色；而这些条件，反倒更使他不可能把自己的关切强加于她。他划船走开，不久便到了上游很远的地方；可是再繁忙的念头，也驱不散那不幸少女的苍白形象。

===Original===

He fell again and again to speculating on the probable romance that lay behind that loneliness and look of desolation; then to smile at his own share in the prejudice that interesting faces must have interesting adventures; then to justify himself for feeling that sorrow was the more tragic when it befell delicate, childlike beauty.
“I should not have forgotten the look of misery if she had been ugly and vulgar,” he said to himself. But there was no denying that the attractiveness of the image made it likelier to last. It was clear to him as an onyx cameo; the brown-black drapery, the white face with small, small features and dark, long-lashed eyes. His mind glanced over the girl-tragedies that are going on in the world, hidden, unheeded, as if they were but tragedies of the copse or hedgerow, where the helpless drag wounded wings forsakenly, and streak the shadowed moss with the red moment-hand of their own death. Deronda of late, in his solitary excursions, had been occupied chiefly with uncertainties about his own course; but those uncertainties, being much at their leisure, were wont to have such wide-sweeping connections with all life and history that the new image of helpless sorrow easily blent itself with what seemed to him the strong array of reasons why he should shrink from getting into that routine of the world which makes men apologize for all its wrongdoing, and take opinions as mere professional equipment﻿—why he should not draw strongly at any thread in the hopelessly-entangled scheme of things.
He used his oars little, satisfied to go with the tide and be taken back by it. It was his habit to indulge himself in that solemn passivity which easily comes with the lengthening shadows and mellow light, when thinking and desiring melt together imperceptibly, and what in other hours may have seemed argument takes the quality of passionate vision. By the time he had come back again with the tide past Richmond Bridge the sun was near setting: and the approach of his favorite hour﻿—with its deepening stillness and darkening masses of tree and building between the double glow of the sky and the river﻿—disposed him to linger as if they had been an unfinished strain of music.

===Chinese===

他一次次猜想，那份孤独和凄惶的神色背后藏着怎样的罗曼史；继而又笑自己也沾了那种偏见——以为有趣的脸必有有趣的遭遇；再继而为自己辩护： sorrow 落在纤秀、孩子气的美上，才更显悲剧。

「倘若她生得又丑又俗，我也不会忘记那悲苦的神情，」他对自己说。但无可否认，形象动人，才更难忘。它像一方缟玛瑙浮雕那样清晰：深棕近黑的衣装，白皙的脸，小小的、小小的五官，睫毛深长的黑眼睛。他的心掠过世上正在上演的种种少女的悲剧——隐秘、无人理会，仿佛只是灌木丛和树篱下的悲剧：在那里，无助的生灵拖着受伤的翅膀孤零零地挣扎，用自己死亡的分针，在阴影里的苔藓上抹下血痕。近来，德龙达在独自出游中盘踞心头的主要是自己前程的不确定；但这些不确定闲得发慌，惯于同全部人生与历史牵出四通八达的关联，于是这无助悲苦的新形象，便轻易地汇入了那一整套在他看来强有力的理由——为什么他应当畏避陷入那个让人替世间一切过错道歉、把见解当职业行头的世故轨道——为什么他不该在那张理不清的乱网里用力去拉任何一根线头。

他很少划桨，听凭潮水载他去，再载他回来。他惯于沉溺在那种庄严的消极里——影子渐长、光线渐醇时极易到来的心境：思考与愿望不知不觉融为一体，别的时候也许像论证的东西，此刻带上了炽热幻象的性质。待他乘潮水回来、过里士满桥时，太阳已近落山：他心爱的时辰临近了——四下愈深的寂静，天空与河流的双重辉光之间愈暗的树与楼的团块——叫他流连，仿佛那是一支未完的乐曲。

===Original===

He looked out for a perfectly solitary spot where he could lodge his boat against the bank, and, throwing himself on his back with his head propped on the cushions, could watch out the light of sunset and the opening of that bead-roll which some oriental poet describes as God’s call to the little stars, who each answer, “Here am I.” He chose a spot in the bend of the river just opposite Kew Gardens, where he had a great breadth of water before him reflecting the glory of the sky, while he himself was in shadow. He lay with his hands behind his head, propped on a level with the boat’s edge, so that he could see all round him, but could not be seen by anyone at a few yards’ distance; and for a long while he never turned his eyes from the view right in front of him. He was forgetting everything else in a half-speculative, half-involuntary identification of himself with the objects he was looking at, thinking how far it might be possible habitually to shift his centre till his own personality would be no less outside him than the landscape﻿—when the sense of something moving on the bank opposite him where it was bordered by a line of willow bushes, made him turn his glance thitherward. In the first moment he had a darting presentiment about the moving figure; and now he could see the small face with the strange dying sunlight upon it. He feared to frighten her by a sudden movement, and watched her with motionless attention. She looked round, but seemed only to gather security from the apparent solitude, hid her hat among the willows, and immediately took off her woolen cloak. Presently she seated herself and deliberately dipped the cloak in the water, holding it there a little while, then taking it out with effort, rising from her seat as she did so. By this time Deronda felt sure that she meant to wrap the wet cloak round her as a drowning shroud; there was no longer time to hesitate about frightening her. He rose and seized his oar to ply across; happily her position lay a little below him. The poor thing, overcome with terror at this sign of discovery from the opposite bank, sank down on the brink again, holding her cloak half out of the water. She crouched and covered her face as if she kept a faint hope that she had not been seen, and that the boatman was accidentally coming toward her.

===Chinese===

他寻了一处绝对清静的所在，可以把船泊在岸边，自己仰面躺下，头垫在坐垫上，看落日的余光收尽，看那份星宿的花名册翻开——某位东方诗人把它描述为上帝召唤小星星们，星星们便一颗颗应答：「我在这里。」他选了河湾处正对丘园的一处，面前是宽阔的水面，倒映着天空的辉煌，而他自己在阴影里。他双手垫在脑后，垫得与船舷齐平，看得见四围一切，几码外却谁也看不见他；有很长一段时间，他的目光不曾离开正前方的景色。他正在一种半思辨半不由自主的忘我里，把自己同眼前的景物认成一体，想着若能习惯地把自我的中心挪出去、直到自己的人格像这片风景一样存在于自身之外，该有多可能——忽然，对面岸上一排柳丛边缘有什么在动的感觉，使他把目光转了过去。第一眼，他对那个移动的身影便掠过一道预感；现在他看清了那张小脸，脸上照着奇异的垂死的日光。他怕突然的动作吓着她，一动不动地注视。她四下望了望，似乎只从表面的僻静里添了胆气，把帽子藏进柳丛，随即脱下呢斗篷。不多时她坐下去，从容地把斗篷浸进水里，按住好一阵，再费力地提出来，提时便从座位上站起了身。到这时，德龙达已确信她是要把湿斗篷裹在身上作溺水的裹尸布了；再没有犹豫的余地，哪怕吓着她。他起身抓桨划过去；幸而她的位置略在他下游。那可怜的人儿一见对岸有被发觉的迹象，吓得又瘫倒在岸边，斗篷还半提在水里。她蜷缩着捂住脸，仿佛还存着一线微弱的希望：自己并没有被看见，船夫只是碰巧朝她这边划来。

===Original===

But soon he was within brief space of her, steadying his boat against the bank, and speaking, but very gently,
“Don’t be afraid. You are unhappy. Pray, trust me. Tell me what I can do to help you.”
She raised her head and looked up at him. His face now was toward the light, and she knew it again. But she did not speak for a few moments which were a renewal of their former gaze at each other. At last she said in a low sweet voice, with an accent so distinct that it suggested foreignness and yet was not foreign, “I saw you before,” and then added dreamily, after a like pause, “*nella miseria*.”
Deronda, not understanding the connection of her thoughts, supposed that her mind was weakened by distress and hunger.
“It was you, singing?” she went on, hesitatingly﻿—“*Nessun maggior dolore.*” The mere words themselves uttered in her sweet undertones seemed to give the melody to Deronda’s ear.
“Ah, yes,” he said, understanding now, “I am often singing them. But I fear you will injure yourself staying here. Pray let me take you in my boat to some place of safety. And that wet cloak﻿—let me take it.”
He would not attempt to take it without her leave, dreading lest he should scare her. Even at his words, he fancied that she shrank and clutched the cloak more tenaciously. But her eyes were fixed on him with a question in them as she said, “You look good. Perhaps it is God’s command.”
“Do trust me. Let me help you. I will die before I will let any harm come to you.”
She rose from her sitting posture, first dragging the saturated cloak and then letting it fall on the ground﻿—it was too heavy for her tired arms. Her little woman’s figure as she laid her delicate chilled hands together one over the other against her waist, and went a step backward while she leaned her head forward as if not to lose sight of his face, was unspeakably touching.
“Great God!” the words escaped Deronda in a tone so low and solemn that they seemed like a prayer become unconsciously vocal. The agitating impression this forsaken girl was making on him stirred a fibre that lay close to his deepest interest in the fates of women﻿—“perhaps my mother was like this one.” The old thought had come now with a new impetus of mingled feeling, and urged that exclamation in which both East and West have for ages concentrated their awe in the presence of inexorable calamity.

===Chinese===

可不久他已到她近前，把船稳稳靠住岸边，开了口，声音极轻：

「别怕。您不快活。求您信我。告诉我，我能帮您什么。」

她抬起头，仰望着他。他的脸此刻向着光，她认出了他。可她好一会儿没有说话——那是对先前彼此对望的延续。终于她用低而甜的声音说，那口音独特得让人想到外国人、却又不尽然：「我从前见过您，」随后又同样顿了一顿，梦呓似的补上：「*在苦难中*。」

德龙达不明白她思绪的关联，只当她被愁苦和饥饿折磨得神志衰弱了。

「是您，在唱歌？」她迟疑地接着说——「*再没有更大的悲伤*。」单是这几个字，用她甜甜的低音吐出，仿佛就把旋律送回了德龙达的耳中。

「啊，是的，」他现在懂了，「我常唱这几句。可您待在这儿要伤身体的。求您让我用船送您到一个安全的地方。还有那件湿斗篷——让我来拿。」

没有得到她的许可他不便去拿，生怕惊了她。就连听到这话，他都仿佛觉得她瑟缩了一下，把斗篷抓得更牢。但她的眼睛盯住他，眼里含着一个问题：「您看起来是好人。这也许是上帝的旨意。」

「一定信我。让我帮您。我宁可死，也不让任何伤害落到您身上。」

她从坐姿站起，先拖起那浸透的斗篷，随即任它落在地上——它对她疲乏的手臂太沉了。她那小小的女子身形，把冰凉的纤手一只叠一只按在腰前，退后一步，头却前倾着，仿佛不愿让他的脸离开视线，说不出的动人。

「伟大的上帝！」这几个字从德龙达口中逸出，声音低沉郑重，仿佛一句不知不觉出了声的祈祷。这个被遗弃的姑娘在他心里激起的动荡，触动了一根紧贴着他最深层关切的纤维——他对女性命运的最深关切——「也许我母亲当年就像这一个。」这个老念头此刻带着新涌的复杂情感卷土重来，逼出了那声感叹——面对无可挽回的灾难，东方与西方千百年来的敬畏都凝聚在其中。

===Original===

The low-toned words seemed to have some reassurance in them for the hearer: she stepped forward close to the boat’s side, and Deronda put out his hand, hoping now that she would let him help her in. She had already put her tiny hand into his which closed around it, when some new thought struck her, and drawing back she said,
“I have nowhere to go﻿—nobody belonging to me in all this land.”
“I will take you to a lady who has daughters,” said Deronda, immediately. He felt a sort of relief in gathering that the wretched home and cruel friends he imagined her to be fleeing from were not in the near background. Still she hesitated, and said more timidly than ever,
“Do you belong to the theatre?”
“No; I have nothing to do with the theatre,” said Deronda, in a decided tone. Then beseechingly, “I will put you in perfect safety at once; with a lady, a good woman; I am sure she will be kind. Let us lose no time: you will make yourself ill. Life may still become sweet to you. There are good people﻿—there are good women who will take care of you.”
She drew backward no more, but stepped in easily, as if she were used to such action, and sat down on the cushions.
“You had a covering for your head,” said Deronda.
“My hat?” (She lifted up her hands to her head.) “It is quite hidden in the bush.”
“I will find it,” said Deronda, putting out his hand deprecatingly as she attempted to rise. “The boat is fixed.”
He jumped out, found the hat, and lifted up the saturated cloak, wringing it and throwing it into the bottom of the boat.
“We must carry the cloak away, to prevent anyone who may have noticed you from thinking you have been drowned,” he said, cheerfully, as he got in again and presented the old hat to her. “I wish I had any other garment than my coat to offer you. But shall you mind throwing it over your shoulders while we are on the water? It is quite an ordinary thing to do, when people return late and are not enough provided with wraps.” He held out the coat toward her with a smile, and there came a faint melancholy smile in answer, as she took it and put it on very cleverly.
“I have some biscuits﻿—should you like them?” said Deronda.
“No; I cannot eat. I had still some money left to buy bread.”
He began to ply his oar without further remark, and they went along swiftly for many minutes without speaking.

===Chinese===

这低低的几个字，于听者似乎含着某种安抚：她朝船舷走近一步，德龙达伸出手，指望她肯让他扶她上船了。她已经把她的小手放进他握拢的手里，忽然又起了个什么念头，缩回去说：

「我没有可去的地方——在这片土地上没有一个亲人。」

「我带您去一位有女儿的太太家，」德龙达立刻说。他松了口气似的得知：他想象她逃离的那个悲惨的家和狠心的亲友，并不在近旁。可她仍在迟疑，比先前更怯地说：

「您是戏院里的吗？」

「不是；我与戏院毫无干系，」德龙达断然说。随即恳求道：「我这就把您安置到绝对安全的地方；一位太太，一位好女人；我相信她会善待您。我们不能耽搁：您会把自己弄出病来的。生活对您仍可能变得甜美。世上有好人——有会照料您的好女人。」

她不再后退，轻轻巧巧地跨进船里，仿佛惯于这类动作，在坐垫上坐下了。

「您本来头上有个遮着的，」德龙达说。

「我的帽子？」（她双手摸向头。）「藏在树丛里了。」

「我去找，」德龙达见她要起身，忙伸手拦住。「船拴着呢。」

他跳上岸，找到帽子，又提起那浸透的斗篷，拧了拧，丢进船底。

「斗篷得带走，免得留意到您的人以为您淹死了，」他重新上船，一面把旧帽子递给她，一面轻快地说。「可惜除了我的外套，我没有别的能给您。在水上的时候，披在肩上您不会介意吧？回来晚了、御寒衣物带得不够的人常这么办，再平常不过。」他含笑把外套递过去；回答他的是一丝淡淡的、含愁的微笑，她接过来，很灵巧地披上了。

「我这儿有点饼干——您要吗？」德龙达说。

「不；我吃不下。我还剩了点钱买面包。」

他不再多说，划起桨来；两人顺水疾行了好几分钟，谁也没有说话。

===Original===

She did not look at him, but was watching the oar, leaning forward in an attitude of repose, as if she were beginning to feel the comfort of returning warmth and the prospect of life instead of death. The twilight was deepening; the red flush was all gone and the little stars were giving their answer one after another. The moon was rising, but was still entangled among the trees and buildings. The light was not such that he could distinctly discern the expression of her features or her glance, but they were distinctly before him nevertheless﻿—features and a glance which seemed to have given a fuller meaning for him to the human face. Among his anxieties one was dominant: his first impression about her, that her mind might be disordered, had not been quite dissipated: the project of suicide was unmistakable, and given a deeper color to every other suspicious sign. He longed to begin a conversation, but abstained, wishing to encourage the confidence that might induce her to speak first. At last she did speak.
“I like to listen to the oar.”
“So do I.”
“If you had not come, I should have been dead now.”
“I cannot bear you to speak of that. I hope you will never be sorry that I came.”
“I cannot see how I shall be glad to live. The *maggior dolore* and the *miseria* have lasted longer than the *tempo felice*.” She paused and then went on dreamily﻿—“*Dolore﻿—miseria*﻿—I think those words are alive.”
Deronda was mute: to question her seemed an unwarrantable freedom; he shrank from appearing to claim the authority of a benefactor, or to treat her with the less reverence because she was in distress. She went on musingly,
“I thought it was not wicked. Death and life are one before the Eternal. I know our fathers slew their children and then slew themselves, to keep their souls pure. I meant it so. But now I am commanded to live. I cannot see how I shall live.”
“You will find friends. I will find them for you.”
She shook her head and said mournfully, “Not my mother and brother. I cannot find them.”
“You are English? You must be﻿—speaking English so perfectly.”
She did not answer immediately, but looked at Deronda again, straining to see him in the double light. Until now she had been watching the oar. It seemed as if she were half roused, and wondered which part of her impression was dreaming and which waking.

===Chinese===

她不看他，只望着桨，身子前倾，一副安歇的姿态，仿佛开始觉出回暖的舒适，觉出生之前景而非死。暮色渐深；天边的红晕褪尽了，小星星们一颗接一颗地给出各自的回答。月亮正在升起，却还缠在树木与楼宇之间。这样的光线不足以让他看清她的五官和眼神的表情，可它们仍清晰地在他眼前——那仿佛已为人类的脸赋予了更完满意义的五官与眼神。在种种焦虑中，有一桩占着上风：他对她的第一印象——她的神志也许错乱了——并未完全消散；自尽的心思是确凿无疑的，这给其余一切可疑的迹象都染上了更深的颜色。他渴望开口攀谈，却忍住了，只盼以静默鼓励那可能引她先开口的信任。她终于开口了。

「我爱听桨声。」

「我也爱。」

「若不是您来了，我这会儿已经死了。」

「别提那个，我受不住。愿您永不后悔我来了。」

「我看不出我怎么会乐于活着。*更大的悲伤*和*苦难*，比*幸福的时光*更长。」她顿了顿，又梦呓似的说下去——「悲伤——苦难——我觉得这几个词是活的。」

德龙达默然：向她发问似乎是一种越礼；他不愿显得以恩人自居，也不愿因她落难就以较少的敬意待她。她若有所思地继续说：

「我原以为那不是罪。死与生在永恒者面前本为一体。我知道我们的先人为保全灵魂的洁净，曾杀掉自己的孩子，然后自尽。我本就是这个意思。可现在我奉命要活。我看不出我怎么活。」

「您会找到朋友的。我替您找。」

她摇摇头，悲戚地说：「不是我的母亲和哥哥。我找不到他们。」

「您是英国人？您准是——英语说得这么地道。」

她没有立刻回答，又看了看德龙达，在两重光里竭力看他。直到方才，她一直望着桨。她像是被唤醒了一半，纳闷自己的印象哪一半是梦、哪一半是醒。

===Original===

Sorrowful isolation had benumbed her sense of reality, and the power of distinguishing outward and inward was continually slipping away from her. Her look was full of wondering timidity such as the forsaken one in the desert might have lifted to the angelic vision before she knew whether his message was in anger or in pity.
“You want to know if I am English?” she said at last, while Deronda was reddening nervously under a gaze which he felt more fully than he saw.
“I want to know nothing except what you like to tell me,” he said, still uneasy in the fear that her mind was wandering. “Perhaps it is not good for you to talk.”
“Yes, I will tell you. I am English-born. But I am a Jewess.”
Deronda was silent, inwardly wondering that he had not said this to himself before, though anyone who had seen delicate-faced Spanish girls might simply have guessed her to be Spanish.
“Do you despise me for it?” she said presently in low tones, which had a sadness that pierced like a cry from a small dumb creature in fear.
“Why should I?” said Deronda. “I am not so foolish.”
“I know many Jews are bad.”
“So are many Christians. But I should not think it fair for you to despise me because of that.”
“My mother and brother were good. But I shall never find them. I am come a long way﻿—from abroad. I ran away; but I cannot tell you﻿—I cannot speak of it. I thought I might find my mother again﻿—God would guide me. But then I despaired. This morning when the light came, I felt as if one word kept sounding within me﻿—Never! never! But now﻿—I begin﻿—to think﻿—” her words were broken by rising sobs﻿—“I am commanded to live﻿—perhaps we are going to her.”
With an outburst of weeping she buried her head on her knees. He hoped that this passionate weeping might relieve her excitement. Meanwhile he was inwardly picturing in much embarrassment how he should present himself with her in Park Lane﻿—the course which he had at first unreflectingly determined on. No one kinder and more gentle than Lady Mallinger; but it was hardly probable that she would be at home; and he had a shuddering sense of a lackey staring at this delicate, sorrowful image of womanhood﻿—of glaring lights and fine staircases, and perhaps chilling suspicious manners from lady’s maid and housekeeper, that might scare the mind already in a state of dangerous susceptibility.

===Chinese===

愁苦的孤绝已使她对现实的知觉麻木了，区分内与外的能力不断从她身上溜走。她的目光里满是诧怯，像荒漠中被弃者抬眼望见天使的幻影时那样——还不知道那信息是出于震怒还是怜悯。

「您想知道我是不是英国人？」她终于说；德龙达正被这道目光看得发窘——他感到它，胜于看见它。

「除了您愿意告诉我的，我什么也不想知道，」他说，仍担心她的神志在游走。「谈话对您也许不好。」

「不，我告诉您。我生在英国。可我是犹太人。」

德龙达沉默了，心里诧异自己先前竟没有想到——虽然，见过西班牙姑娘那种精致面孔的人，本可以干脆猜她是西班牙人。

「您因此看不起我吗？」她片刻后低声说，那声音里的悲哀，像小兽恐惧中一声喑哑的哀鸣，直扎进人心里。

「我为什么要？」德龙达说。「我没那么蠢。」

「我知道许多犹太人是坏的。」

「许多基督徒也坏。可您若因此就看不起我，我也觉得不公平。」

「我的母亲和哥哥是好人。可我永远找不到他们了。我走了好远——从国外。我逃出来的；可我不能告诉您——我说不出口。我想我也许能再找到母亲——上帝会引路。可后来我绝望了。今早天亮的时候，我觉得有一个词一直在心里响——永远！永远！可是现在——我开始——觉得——」她的话被涌上来的抽噎打断——「我奉命要活——也许我们正走向她。」

她放声痛哭，把头埋进膝间。他盼望这场痛哭能缓解她的亢奋。与此同时，他心里正尴尬地盘算着，如何带着她出现在帕克巷——那是他起初不假思索定下的去处。再没有比马林格夫人更仁厚温柔的人了；可她多半不在家；他一想到一个男仆盯着这纤秀愁苦的女性形象——白晃晃的灯火、华美的楼梯，也许还有女管家和贴身女仆冷冷的、带疑忌的态度，可能惊吓这颗已处在危险易感状态的心——便不寒而栗。

===Original===

But to take her to any other shelter than a home already known to him was not to be contemplated: he was full of fears about the issue of the adventure which had brought on him a responsibility all the heavier for the strong and agitating impression this childlike creature had made on him. But another resource came to mind: he could venture to take her to Mrs. Meyrick’s﻿—to the small house at Chelsea﻿—where he had been often enough since his return from abroad to feel sure that he could appeal there to generous hearts, which had a romantic readiness to believe in innocent need and to help it. Hans Meyrick was safe away in Italy, and Deronda felt the comfort of presenting himself with his charge at a house where he would be met by a motherly figure of quakerish neatness, and three girls who hardly knew of any evil closer to them than what lay in history-books, and dramas, and would at once associate a lovely Jewess with Rebecca in *Ivanhoe*, besides thinking that everything they did at Deronda’s request would be done for their idol, Hans. The vision of the Chelsea home once raised, Deronda no longer hesitated.
The rumbling thither in the cab after the stillness of the water seemed long. Happily his charge had been quiet since her fit of weeping, and submitted like a tired child. When they were in the cab, she laid down her hat and tried to rest her head, but the jolting movement would not let it rest. Still she dozed, and her sweet head hung helpless, first on one side, then on the other.
“They are too good to have any fear about taking her in,” thought Deronda. Her person, her voice, her exquisite utterance, were one strong appeal to belief and tenderness. Yet what had been the history which had brought her to this desolation? He was going on a strange errand﻿—to ask shelter for this waif. Then there occurred to him the beautiful story Plutarch somewhere tells of the Delphic women: how when the Maenads, outworn with their torch-lit wanderings, lay down to sleep in the marketplace, the matrons came and stood silently round them to keep guard over their slumbers; then, when they waked, ministered to them tenderly and saw them safely to their own borders. He could trust the women he was going to for having hearts as good.

===Chinese===

可是，把她带到任何一个他不熟识的栖身之处，则想都不用想：这场奇遇已把一副责任压到他身上，而这孩子般的人儿给他的印象那样强烈、那样激荡，责任便愈发沉重；他满心都是对后果的忧惧。好在他想起了另一条路：他可以带她去梅里克太太家——切尔西那座小宅——回国后他去得够多，确知在那里可以求助到慷慨的心肠，它们对无辜的困厄怀有罗曼蒂克式的轻信与相助的热忱。汉斯·梅里克（Hans Meyrick）稳稳当当地远在意大利；德龙达想到自己将带着受托之人叩响的门里，迎接他的将是一位公谊会式整洁的母亲形象和三个姑娘——她们对邪恶的最近距离的认识，不过是史书和戏剧里的那些——而且一见面就会把可爱的犹太姑娘同《艾凡赫》里的丽贝卡联想到一起，还会觉得为德龙达做的每一件事都是为她们的偶像汉斯做的，便觉宽慰。切尔西那座小宅的图景一经升起，德龙达不再迟疑。

水面静寂之后，马车一路轰隆着驶往切尔西，显得漫长。幸好他受托的人自那阵痛哭后一直安静，像个疲乏的孩子般顺从。上了车，她摘下帽子想把头靠一靠，可颠簸不容她靠稳。她还是打起了盹，那可爱的脑袋无助地垂着，一会儿歪向这边，一会儿歪向那边。

「他们心肠太好，收留她不会有半点犹豫，」德龙达想。她的人、她的声音、她精妙的谈吐，本身就是对信任与温柔的有力呼吁。然而，把她带到这步荒凉境地的，究竟是一段怎样的历史？他正去办一件奇怪的差事——为这个漂泊者求一席庇护。这时他想起普鲁塔克某处讲的德尔斐妇女的美丽故事：酒神的女祭司们举着火把游荡得精疲力竭、躺在集市上睡去时，妇人们走来，默默围立守护她们的酣眠；待她们醒来，又温柔地照料她们，平安送她们回到自己的地界。他去求助的这几位女人，他信得过她们有同样好的心。

===Original===

Deronda felt himself growing older this evening and entering on a new phase in finding a life to which his own had come﻿—perhaps as a rescue; but how to make sure that snatching from death was rescue? The moment of finding a fellow-creature is often as full of mingled doubt and exultation as the moment of finding an idea.

===Chinese===

这个傍晚，德龙达觉得自己老成了几分，进入了人生的一个新阶段——他的人生撞上了另一条生命，也许是一场拯救；可是，怎样保证从死亡手里抢下来的就是拯救呢？发现一个同类的时刻，往往像发现一个观念的时刻一样，满盛着疑虑与狂喜的交织。

### XVIII / 第十八章
===Original===

> Life is a various mother: now she dons

Her plumes and brilliants, climbs the marble stairs

With head aloft, nor ever turns her eyes

On lackeys who attend her; now she dwells

Grim-clad, up darksome alleys, breathes hot gin,

And screams in pauper riot.

But to these

She came a frugal matron, neat and deft,

With cheerful morning thoughts and quick device

To find the much in little.

===Chinese===

> 人生是位多变的母亲：忽而她插上

羽翎、佩上钻石，昂首登上大理石阶，

目不斜视，不看一眼侍立的仆役；忽而她又

一身褴褛，栖身幽暗的陋巷，喷着杜松子酒的热气，

在穷人的骚乱里尖叫。

而对这些人，

她来时是一位节俭的主妇，干净利落，

怀着清晨的愉快念头，善于

从少许里取出丰足。

===Original===

Mrs. Meyrick’s house was not noisy: the front parlor looked on the river, and the back on gardens, so that though she was reading aloud to her daughters, the window could be left open to freshen the air of the small double room where a lamp and two candles were burning. The candles were on a table apart for Kate, who was drawing illustrations for a publisher; the lamp was not only for the reader but for Amy and Mab, who were embroidering satin cushions for “the great world.”
Outside, the house looked very narrow and shabby, the bright light through the holland blind showing the heavy old-fashioned window-frame; but it is pleasant to know that many such grim-walled slices of space in our foggy London have been and still are the homes of a culture the more spotlessly free from vulgarity, because poverty has rendered everything like display an impersonal question, and all the grand shows of the world simply a spectacle which rouses petty rivalry or vain effort after possession.
The Meyricks’ was a home of that kind: and they all clung to this particular house in a row because its interior was filled with objects always in the same places, which, for the mother held memories of her marriage time, and for the young ones seemed as necessary and uncriticised a part of their world as the stars of the Great Bear seen from the back windows. Mrs. Meyrick had borne much stint of other matters that she might be able to keep some engravings specially cherished by her husband; and the narrow spaces of wall held a world history in scenes and heads which the children had early learned by heart. The chairs and tables were also old friends preferred to new. But in these two little parlors with no furniture that a broker would have cared to cheapen except the prints and piano, there was space and apparatus for a wide-glancing, nicely-select life, opened to the highest things in music, painting and poetry. I am not sure that in the times of greatest scarcity, before Kate could get paid-work, these ladies had always had a servant to light their fires and sweep their rooms; yet they were fastidious in some points, and could not believe that the manners of ladies in the fashionable world were so full of coarse selfishness, petty quarreling, and slang as they are represented to be in what are called literary photographs.

===Chinese===

梅里克太太的宅子不吵：前客厅临河，后窗对花园，所以虽然她正给女儿们朗读，窗子仍开着，给这前后两间的小屋换换空气——屋里点着一盏油灯、两支蜡烛。蜡烛单搁在一张桌上，是给凯特照明用的，她正给一家出版社画插图；油灯则既照着朗读者，也照着艾米和梅布，她们在给「大世界」绣缎子靠垫。

宅子外观看上去又窄又寒酸，荷兰布帘里透出的亮光，照出那沉重的老式窗框；但知道这一点是令人愉快的：在雾气弥漫的伦敦，许多这样墙面灰暗的窄窄一条空间，曾经是、如今仍是一种教养的家——这种教养格外一尘不染地免于俗气，因为贫穷已使一切铺张成为一个与己无关的问题，使世上一切盛大的排场，只余一场景观，激起的不过是小小的攀比或徒然的占有欲。

梅里克家正是这样一处家宅；一家人死守着排屋里的这一座，因为屋内的物件永远在原处：对母亲，它们存着她新婚岁月的记忆；对孩子们，它们如同从后窗望见的大熊星，是自己世界里必要而无可非议的一部分。梅里克太太在其他一切上缩衣节食，为的是保住丈夫生前特别珍爱的几幅版画；于是窄窄的墙面挂着一部以场景与头像写成的世界史，孩子们早已烂熟于心。椅子和桌子也是不肯换新的旧友。而在这样两间小客厅里——除了版画和钢琴，再没有一件旧货商看得上眼的家什——却容纳着一种眼观四路、精于取舍的生活的余地与装备，向音乐、绘画与诗歌中至高的东西敞开。我不敢说，在凯特还没接到有酬活计之前、手头最拮据的那段日子，这几位太太小姐屋里是否总雇得起一个生火扫屋的女仆；可她们在某些点上极其讲究，而且怎么也不肯相信上流社会淑女们的举止，当真像所谓「文学照相」里描写的那样，满是粗俗的自私、琐碎的口角和行话黑话。

===Original===

The Meyricks had their little oddities, streaks of eccentricity from the mother’s blood as well as the father’s, their minds being like medieval houses with unexpected recesses and openings from this into that, flights of steps and sudden outlooks.
But mother and daughters were all united by a triple bond﻿—family love; admiration for the finest work, the best action; and habitual industry. Hans’ desire to spend some of his money in making their lives more luxurious had been resisted by all of them, and both they and he had been thus saved from regrets at the threatened triumphs of his yearning for art over the attractions of secured income﻿—a triumph that would by-and-by oblige him to give up his fellowship. They could all afford to laugh at his Gavarni-caricatures and to hold him blameless in following a natural bent which their unselfishness and independence had left without obstacle. It was enough for them to go on in their old way, only having a grand treat of opera-going (to the gallery) when Hans came home on a visit.
Seeing the group they made this evening, one could hardly wish them to change their way of life. They were all alike small, and so in due proportion to their miniature rooms. Mrs. Meyrick was reading aloud from a French book; she was a lively little woman, half French, half Scotch, with a pretty articulateness of speech that seemed to make daylight in her hearer’s understanding. Though she was not yet fifty, her rippling hair, covered by a quakerish net cap, was chiefly gray, but her eyebrows were brown as the bright eyes below them; her black dress, almost like a priest’s cassock with its rows of buttons, suited a neat figure hardly five feet high. The daughters were to match the mother, except that Mab had Hans’ light hair and complexion, with a bossy, irregular brow, and other quaintnesses that reminded one of him. Everything about them was compact, from the firm coils of their hair, fastened back *à la Chinoise*, to their gray skirts in Puritan nonconformity with the fashion, which at that time would have demanded that four feminine circumferences should fill all the free space in the front parlor. All four, if they had been waxwork, might have been packed easily in a fashionable lady’s traveling trunk.

===Chinese===

梅里克一家人各有小小的怪癖，血里带着来自父母双方的逸气；他们的头脑像中世纪的宅子，有意想不到的凹室，从这间通到那间的开口，一层层台阶和蓦然出现的眺望。

但母女们由一条三股的绳索拧在一起——天伦之爱；对最好的作品、最好的行为的敬仰；和习以为惯的勤勉。汉斯想拿出一部分钱让她们过得宽裕些，遭到了全体的一致抵制；于是无论他们还是他，都因此免于遗憾——他那艺术之恋压倒稳定收入的诱惑、眼看要取得的胜利，本会迫使他迟早放弃研究员的位置。他们尽可以拿他的加瓦尔尼式漫画取笑，也可以认为他顺应天性无可指摘——是她们的无私与自立让这条天性之路畅通无阻。她们只要照老样子过下去就够，只等汉斯回家探亲时，来一场坐（顶层楼座的）歌剧院的盛筵。

看看他们今晚组成的这一圈人，谁也不会愿意他们换一种活法。他们个个都小，恰好配得上他们袖珍的房间。梅里克太太正朗读一本法文书；她是个活泼的小妇人，半法国半苏格兰血统，谈吐伶俐清晰，仿佛能在听者的心里照出白昼。她还不到五十岁，罩着公谊会式网帽的波浪头发已大半灰白，可她的眉毛还同眉下明亮的眼睛一样是棕色的；黑裙子几乎像教士的袍子，缀着一排排纽扣，衬着一副还不到五英尺高的干净身量。女儿们同母亲相配，只是梅布生了汉斯那样的浅色头发和肤色，额前一个疙疙瘩瘩、不规整的凸脑门，还有别的几分古怪，处处教人想起他。她们身上的一切都是紧凑的：从挽起盘紧、*中国式*拢在脑后的发髻，到清教徒式地不肯苟同时尚的灰裙子——那个年头，时尚本会要求四条女性的圆周占满前客厅的全部空地。她们四个若是蜡人，轻轻松松就能装进一位时髦太太的旅行衣箱。

===Original===

Their faces seemed full of speech, as if their minds had been shelled, after the manner of horse-chestnuts, and become brightly visible. The only large thing of its kind in the room was Hafiz, the Persian cat, comfortably poised on the brown leather back of a chair, and opening his large eyes now and then to see that the lower animals were not in any mischief.
The book Mrs. Meyrick had before her was Erckmann-Chatrian’s *Historie d’un Conscrit*. She had just finished reading it aloud, and Mab, who had let her work fall on the ground while she stretched her head forward and fixed her eyes on the reader, exclaimed,
“I think that is the finest story in the world.”
“Of course, Mab!” said Amy, “it is the last you have heard. Everything that pleases you is the best in its turn.”
“It is hardly to be called a story,” said Kate. “It is a bit of history brought near us with a strong telescope. We can see the soldiers’ faces: no, it is more than that﻿—we can hear everything﻿—we can almost hear their hearts beat.”
“I don’t care what you call it,” said Mab, flirting away her thimble. “Call it a chapter in Revelations. It makes me want to do something good, something grand. It makes me so sorry for everybody. It makes me like Schiller﻿—I want to take the world in my arms and kiss it. I must kiss you instead, little mother!” She threw her arms round her mother’s neck.
“Whenever you are in that mood, Mab, down goes your work,” said Amy. “It would be doing something good to finish your cushion without soiling it.”
“Oh﻿—oh﻿—oh!” groaned Mab, as she stooped to pick up her work and thimble. “I wish I had three wounded conscripts to take care of.”
“You would spill their beef tea while you were talking,” said Amy.
“Poor Mab! don’t be hard on her,” said the mother. “Give me the embroidery now, child. You go on with your enthusiasm, and I will go on with the pink and white poppy.”
“Well, ma, I think you are more caustic than Amy,” said Kate, while she drew her head back to look at her drawing.
“Oh﻿—oh﻿—oh!” cried Mab again, rising and stretching her arms. “I wish something wonderful would happen. I feel like the deluge. The waters of the great deep are broken up, and the windows of heaven are opened. I must sit down and play the scales.”

===Chinese===

她们脸上仿佛满是言语，仿佛心智像马栗一样褪了壳，变得明亮可见。屋里唯一称得上庞大的同类，是那只波斯猫哈菲兹：它舒舒服服地蹲在椅子的棕色皮背上，时不时睁开大眼睛，看看这些低等动物有没有捣乱。

梅里克太太面前摊着的是埃尔克曼-夏特里安的《一个应征兵的故事》。她刚念完，梅布早把活计掉在地上，伸着脖子、眼睛盯住朗读的人，此刻喊道：

「我看这是世上最好的故事。」

「那当然，梅布！」艾米说，「这是你最新听完的一个。凡叫你高兴的，轮到它都是天下第一。」

「这 hardly 算得上故事，」凯特说。「这是把一段历史用高倍望远镜拉近给我们看。我们看得见士兵们的脸：不，还不止——我们什么都听得见——几乎听得见他们的心跳。」

「我才不管你们管它叫什么，」梅布说，把顶针一甩。「叫它《启示录》里的一章也行。它叫我想做点好事，做点了不起的事。它叫我替每一个人难过。它叫我像席勒——我想把整个世界搂在怀里亲一亲。只好亲亲你啦，小妈妈！」她张开双臂搂住母亲的脖子。

「梅布，你每回一到这个劲儿，活计准完蛋，」艾米说。「把靠垫绣完还别弄脏，才算做了件好事呢。」

「哦——哦——哦！」梅布一面弯腰去拾活计和顶针，一面呻吟。「真希望我有三个受伤的新兵好照料。」

「你准会一边说话一边把牛肉汤泼在他们身上，」艾米说。

「可怜的梅布！别对她太凶，」母亲说。「孩子，把绣活给我吧。你接着去热情，我接着绣这朵粉红带白的罂粟花。」

「唷，妈妈，我看您比艾米还尖刻，」凯特说着，仰头端详自己的画稿。

「哦——哦——哦！」梅布又喊起来，站起身伸展双臂。「真盼望有点什么奇事发生。我觉得自己像大洪水。大渊的泉源裂开了，天上的窗户也敞开了。我得坐下练音阶了。」

===Original===

Mab was opening the piano while the others were laughing at this climax, when a cab stopped before the house, and there forthwith came a quick rap of the knocker.
“Dear me!” said Mrs. Meyrick, starting up, “it is after ten, and Phoebe is gone to bed.” She hastened out, leaving the parlor door open.
“Mr. Deronda!” The girls could hear this exclamation from their mamma. Mab clasped her hands, saying in a loud whisper, “There now! something *is* going to happen.” Kate and Amy gave up their work in amazement. But Deronda’s tone in reply was so low that they could not hear his words, and Mrs. Meyrick immediately closed the parlor door.
“I know I am trusting to your goodness in a most extraordinary way,” Deronda went on, after giving his brief narrative; “but you can imagine how helpless I feel with a young creature like this on my hands. I could not go with her among strangers, and in her nervous state I should dread taking her into a house full of servants. I have trusted to your mercy. I hope you will not think my act unwarrantable.”
“On the contrary. You have honored me by trusting me. I see your difficulty. Pray bring her in. I will go and prepare the girls.”
While Deronda went back to the cab, Mrs. Meyrick turned into the parlor again and said: “Here is somebody to take care of instead of your wounded conscripts, Mab: a poor girl who was going to drown herself in despair. Mr. Deronda found her only just in time to save her. He brought her along in his boat, and did not know what else it would be safe to do with her, so he has trusted us and brought her here. It seems she is a Jewess, but quite refined, he says﻿—knowing Italian and music.”
The three girls, wondering and expectant, came forward and stood near each other in mute confidence that they were all feeling alike under this appeal to their compassion. Mab looked rather awestricken, as if this answer to her wish were something preternatural.
Meanwhile Deronda going to the door of the cab where the pale face was now gazing out with roused observation, said, “I have brought you to some of the kindest people in the world: there are daughters like you. It is a happy home. Will you let me take you to them?”

===Chinese===

梅布正掀琴盖，众人笑这最高潮的话，忽有一辆马车在门前停下，门环随即被急促地叩响。

「哎呀！」梅里克太太跳起来，「十点多了，菲比已经睡了。」她匆匆出去，客厅门敞着。

「德龙达先生！」姑娘们听见母亲这一声惊呼。梅布双手一合，大声耳语道：「看吧！*果然*要出事了。」凯特和艾米惊讶地撂下活计。可德龙达回话的声音太低，听不清字句，梅里克太太随即关上了客厅门。

「我知道，我这是用一种极不寻常的方式信赖你们的善良，」德龙达简要讲完经过后接着说，「可您想得到，这样一位年轻的人儿在我手里，我多么无措。我不能带她到陌生人中间去；以她那神经过敏的状态，我又怕带她进一幢满是仆人的宅子。我信了您的仁心。望您不要觉得我的做法唐突。」

「恰恰相反。您信得过我，是抬举我。您的难处我明白。快请她进来。我去跟姑娘们打个招呼。」

德龙达回马车去时，梅里克太太转回客厅说：「梅布，给你一个照料的对象，不用你那些受伤的新兵了：一个绝望得要投河的可怜姑娘。德龙达先生抢救得正是时候。他用船把她带上岸，不知此外还有什么稳妥的办法，就信了我们，把她带到这儿来了。据说是个犹太姑娘，人很文雅，他说——懂意大利语，懂音乐。」

三个姑娘又惊又盼地迎上前来，彼此挨近站着，默默地相信这一对怜悯的呼吁，她们心里的感受完全一样。梅布看起来近乎敬畏，仿佛对她愿望的这一应答带着超自然的色彩。

这时德龙达走到车门口——那张苍白的脸正睁着观察的眼睛向外望——说：「我把您带到了世上最好心的人中间：这里有和您一样的女儿们。这是个幸福的家。您愿意让我带您去见她们吗？」

===Original===

She stepped out obediently, putting her hand in his and forgetting her hat; and when Deronda led her into the full light of the parlor where the four little women stood awaiting her, she made a picture that would have stirred much duller sensibilities than theirs. At first she was a little dazed by the sudden light, and before she had concentrated her glance he had put her hand into the mother’s. He was inwardly rejoicing that the Meyricks were so small: the dark-curled head was the highest among them. The poor wanderer could not be afraid of these gentle faces so near hers: and now she was looking at each of them in turn while the mother said, “You must be weary, poor child.”
“We will take care of you﻿—we will comfort you﻿—we will love you,” cried Mab, no longer able to restrain herself, and taking the small right hand caressingly between both her own. This gentle welcoming warmth was penetrating the bewildered one: she hung back just enough to see better the four faces in front of her, whose good will was being reflected in hers, not in any smile, but in that undefinable change which tells us that anxiety is passing in contentment. For an instant she looked up at Deronda, as if she were referring all this mercy to him, and then again turning to Mrs. Meyrick, said with more collectedness in her sweet tones than he had heard before,
“I am a stranger. I am a Jewess. You might have thought I was wicked.”
“No, we are sure you are good,” burst out Mab.
“We think no evil of you, poor child. You shall be safe with us,” said Mrs. Meyrick. “Come now and sit down. You must have some food, and then you must go to rest.”
The stranger looked up again at Deronda, who said,
“You will have no more fears with these friends? You will rest tonight?”
“Oh, I should not fear. I should rest. I think these are the ministering angels.”
Mrs. Meyrick wanted to lead her to seat, but again hanging back gently, the poor weary thing spoke as if with a scruple at being received without a further account of herself.
“My name is Mirah Lapidoth. I am come a long way, all the way from Prague by myself. I made my escape. I ran away from dreadful things. I came to find my mother and brother in London. I had been taken from my mother when I was little, but I thought I could find her again. I had trouble﻿—the houses were all gone﻿—I could not find her.

===Chinese===

她顺从地下车来，把手放进他手里，忘了拿帽子；当德龙达把她领进灯火通明的客厅、四位小妇人立着等她时，她构成的那幅画，比她们迟钝得多的人也会为之动容。起先她被骤亮的灯光照得有点发怔，还没定下神来看，他已把她的手交到那位母亲手里。他心里暗喜梅里克一家都生得娇小：这颗深色鬈发的头在她们中间是最高的。可怜的漂泊者不会怕这些离她这么近的温柔面孔：此刻她正逐一端详她们，那位母亲说着：「您一定累了，可怜的孩子。」

「我们会照料您——我们会安慰您——我们会爱您，」梅布再也忍不住，喊了出来，双手把那只小右手爱怜地握在自己两手里。这温柔的、迎候的暖意正渗进那个神志迷乱的人：她微微后仰，恰好把面前四张脸看得更清楚，她们的善意映在她脸上——不是以微笑，而是以那种说不出名目的变化，告诉我们焦虑正化为安宁。有一瞬她抬眼看了看德龙达，仿佛把这一切恩慈都归到他名下；随后又转向梅里克太太，用她那甜甜的声音说，比他先前听过的任何时候都更镇定：

「我是个外乡人。我是个犹太姑娘。你们本可能当我是坏人的。」

「不，我们肯定您是好人，」梅布脱口而出。

「我们不会把您往坏处想的，可怜的孩子。您在我们这里很安全，」梅里克太太说。「来，坐下吧。您得吃点东西，然后好好休息。」

那外乡的姑娘又抬眼望德龙达，他说：

「有这些朋友在，您不再害怕了吧？今晚能安睡了？」

「哦，我不会怕了。我能睡了。我想这些就是侍奉的天使。」

梅里克太太想引她就座，可这疲乏的可怜人又轻轻后仰，仿佛对未曾再多交代自己就被收留，心有所不安，说：

「我的名字是米拉·拉皮多思（Mirah Lapidoth）。我走了好远，一个人从布拉格一路走来。我是逃出来的。我从可怕的事情里逃出来。我来伦敦找我的母亲和哥哥。我很小的时候就被从母亲身边带走了，可我想我还能找到她。我找了又找——原来的房子都没了——我找不到她。

===Original===

It has been a long while, and I had not much money. That is why I am in distress.”
“Our mother will be good to you,” cried Mab. “See what a nice little mother she is!”
“Do sit down now,” said Kate, moving a chair forward, while Amy ran to get some tea.
Mirah resisted no longer, but seated herself with perfect grace, crossing her little feet, laying her hands one over the other on her lap, and looking at her friends with placid reverence; whereupon Hafiz, who had been watching the scene restlessly came forward with tail erect and rubbed himself against her ankles. Deronda felt it time to go.
“Will you allow me to come again and inquire﻿—perhaps at five tomorrow?” he said to Mrs. Meyrick.
“Yes, pray; we shall have had time to make acquaintance then.”
“Goodbye,” said Deronda, looking down at Mirah, and putting out his hand. She rose as she took it, and the moment brought back to them both strongly the other moment when she had first taken that outstretched hand. She lifted her eyes to his and said with reverential fervor, “The God of our fathers bless you and deliver you from all evil as you have delivered me. I did not believe there was any man so good. None before have thought me worthy of the best. You found me poor and miserable, yet you have given me the best.”
Deronda could not speak, but with silent adieux to the Meyricks, hurried away.

===Chinese===

隔了好久了，我身边的钱也不多。所以我落到这步田地。」

「我们的妈妈会好好待你的，」梅布喊道。「瞧她是个多好的小妈妈！」

「快坐下吧，」凯特说着往前挪了张椅子，艾米跑去端茶。

米拉不再推却，姿态完美优雅地坐下，小小的双脚交叠，双手一只叠一只搁在膝上，安详而虔敬地望着她的朋友们；这时哈菲兹一直不安地观望着这一幕，走上前来，尾巴竖得笔直，在她脚踝上蹭来蹭去。德龙达觉得该走了。

「请允许我明天再来问问——五点钟左右行吗？」他对梅里克太太说。

「行，一定来；那时我们也混熟了。」

「再见，」德龙达低头看着米拉，伸出手说。她握住手时站起身来；这一刻把先前那一幕清晰地带回两人心里——她第一次握住那只伸出的手的时刻。她抬眼望着他，带着虔敬的炽热说：「愿我们先祖的上帝赐福您，救您脱离一切灾殃，正如您救了我。我原不信世上有这么好的人。从前从没有人认为我配得上最好的。您见我又穷又苦，却把最好的给了我。」

德龙达说不出话，只默默向梅里克一家道了别，匆匆离去。

## Book / 第三卷 抉择中的少女
===Original===

III Maidens Choosing

===Chinese===

第三卷 抉择中的少女

### XIX / 第十九章
===Original===

> I pity the man who can travel from Dan to Beersheba, and say, “ ’Tis all barren”: and so it is: and so is all the world to him who will not cultivate the fruits it offers.

===Chinese===

> 我怜悯那种人：他能从但走到别是巴，一路却说「这一路尽是荒瘠」；在他确实如此——对那不肯耕种大地所出果实的人，全世界也都是荒瘠。

===Original===

To say that Deronda was romantic would be to misrepresent him; but under his calm and somewhat self-repressed exterior there was a fervor which made him easily find poetry and romance among the events of everyday life. And perhaps poetry and romance are as plentiful as ever in the world except for those phlegmatic natures who I suspect would in any age have regarded them as a dull form of erroneous thinking. They exist very easily in the same room with the microscope and even in railway carriages: what banishes them is the vacuum in gentlemen and lady passengers. How should all the apparatus of heaven and earth, from the farthest firmament to the tender bosom of the mother who nourished us, make poetry for a mind that had no movements of awe and tenderness, no sense of fellowship which thrills from the near to the distant, and back again from the distant to the near?
To Deronda this event of finding Mirah was as heart-stirring as anything that befell Orestes or Rinaldo. He sat up half the night, living again through the moments since he had first discerned Mirah on the river-brink, with the fresh and fresh vividness which belongs to emotive memory. When he took up a book to try and dull this urgency of inward vision, the printed words were no more than a network through which he saw and heard everything as clearly as before﻿—saw not only the actual events of two hours, but possibilities of what had been and what might be which those events were enough to feed with the warm blood of passionate hope and fear. Something in his own experience caused Mirah’s search after her mother to lay hold with peculiar force on his imagination. The first prompting of sympathy was to aid her in her search: if given persons were extant in London there were ways of finding them, as subtle as scientific experiment, the right machinery being set at work. But here the mixed feelings which belonged to Deronda’s kindred experience naturally transfused themselves into his anxiety on behalf of Mirah.
The desire to know his own mother, or to know about her, was constantly haunted with dread; and in imagining what might befall Mirah it quickly occurred to him that finding the mother and brother from whom she had been parted when she was a little one might turn out to be a calamity.

===Chinese===

说德龙达是个罗曼蒂克的人，是错描了他；但在他那沉静而略加自抑的外表之下，有一团火焰，使他在日常生活的种种事件里轻易便寻见诗与传奇。而诗与传奇，在这个世界上或许一如既往地丰盈，只除了那些黏液质的天性——我疑心那种人无论生在哪个时代，都会把它们看作沉闷的、想岔了的念头。诗与传奇同显微镜共处一室毫不为难，甚至在火车车厢里也活得自在：把它们驱逐出境的，是男女乘客心里的真空。天地间的全部造化——从最远的苍穹到哺育过我们的母亲的温柔胸怀——对一个心里没有敬畏与温情的悸动、没有那种由近及远、又由远返近地震颤着的同胞之感的心灵，又怎能成其为诗呢？

对德龙达来说，遇见米拉这件事，其动人心魄不亚于俄瑞斯忒斯或里纳尔多遭遇的任何一桩。他半宿没睡，把自初见米拉在河岸上起的每时每刻重温了一遍，带着情感的记忆所特有的、一遍新似一遍的鲜明。他拿起一册书，想压下这内心视象的催逼，印着的文字却不过是一层网，隔着它，一切照旧看得见听得清——不但看见那两个钟头里实际发生的一切，还看见种种可能的曾经与将来，那些事件足以用炽热的希望与恐惧的暖血去喂养它们。他自己经历中的某种东西，使米拉寻母这件事以特殊的力量攫住了他的想象。同情的第一个冲动是帮助她寻找：只要人还在伦敦，总有办法找到，可以精微得像科学实验，只要开动恰当的机器。但在这里，属于德龙达同类经历的复杂情感，自然而然地渗入了他为米拉的焦虑之中。

想认识自己的母亲、或想了解她的愿望，始终萦绕着恐惧；在想象米拉可能遭遇什么时，他很快便想到：找到她幼年离散的母亲和哥哥，结果也许是一场灾祸。

===Original===

When she was in the boat she said that her mother and brother were good; but the goodness might have been chiefly in her own ignorant innocence and yearning memory, and the ten or twelve years since the parting had been time enough for much worsening. Spite of his strong tendency to side with the objects of prejudice, and in general with those who got the worst of it, his interest had never been practically drawn toward existing Jews, and the facts he knew about them, whether they walked conspicuous in fine apparel or lurked in by-streets, were chiefly of a sort most repugnant to him. Of learned and accomplished Jews he took it for granted that they had dropped their religion, and wished to be merged in the people of their native lands. Scorn flung at a Jew as such would have roused all his sympathy in griefs of inheritance; but the indiscriminate scorn of a race will often strike a specimen who has well earned it on his own account, and might fairly be gibbeted as a rascally son of Adam. It appears that the Caribs, who know little of theology, regard thieving as a practice peculiarly connected with Christian tenets, and probably they could allege experimental grounds for this opinion. Deronda could not escape (who can?) knowing ugly stories of Jewish characteristics and occupations; and though one of his favorite protests was against the severance of past and present history, he was like others who shared his protest, in never having cared to reach any more special conclusions about actual Jews than that they retained the virtues and vices of a long-oppressed race. But now that Mirah’s longing roused his mind to a closer survey of details, very disagreeable images urged themselves of what it might be to find out this middle-aged Jewess and her son. To be sure, there was the exquisite refinement and charm of the creature herself to make a presumption in favor of her immediate kindred, but﻿—he must wait to know more: perhaps through Mrs. Meyrick he might gather some guiding hints from Mirah’s own lips. Her voice, her accent, her looks﻿—all the sweet purity that clothed her as with a consecrating garment made him shrink the more from giving her, either ideally or practically, an association with what was hateful or contaminating. But these fine words with which we fumigate and becloud unpleasant facts are not the language in which we think.

===Chinese===

她在船上时说过，母亲和哥哥是好人；可那份好，也许大半在她自己无知的纯真和渴念的记忆里；别后十来年，足够让很多东西变坏。尽管他有一种强烈的倾向，站在偏见所针对的人们一边，一般地说站在吃了亏的人们一边，他的关切此前从未实际投向现实中的犹太人；他所知道的关于他们的事实——无论他们衣着鲜亮招摇过市，还是潜身僻街陋巷——多半属于他最反感的那一类。至于博学而有造诣的犹太人，他想当然地认为他们早已抛掉了自己的宗教，但愿融入各自出生地的民族。见人以犹太人的身份掷去轻蔑，会激起他对遗传之殇的全部同情；可是对一个种族不加分辨的轻蔑，往往偏偏砸中一个凭自己就活该被砸的人，把他吊上绞架当亚当的流氓儿子也名正言顺。据说加勒比人对神学所知甚少，却把偷窃看作与基督教教义特别相联的行当，而且他们多半拿得出经验上的根据。德龙达也逃脱不掉（谁逃得掉？）一些关于犹太人特性与营生的丑陋故事；虽然他心爱的抗议之一，是反对把过去的历史同现在割裂，可他也同持这份抗议的人们一样，从未费心对现实中的犹太人得出任何更具体的结论，只知道一句：他们保留着一个久受压迫种族的美德与恶行。可如今米拉的渴望唤醒他的心思去做一番更贴近的细节检视，种种极不愉快的图景便不请自来：找到这位中年的犹太妇人和她的儿子，可能会是怎样一副光景。当然，米拉本人那精致入骨的秀气与魅力，可以构成一个有利于她至亲的推定；可是——他必须等知道得更多再说：也许通过梅里克太太，他能从来拉自己嘴里得到一些指引性的线索。她的声音、她的口音、她的容貌——那把她像一件圣衣一样裹着的全部甜美纯贞——使他越发畏于让她在想象里或实际上，同一个可憎的、玷污性的东西发生关联。可是，我们用来给不愉快的事实熏香、遮雾的这些漂亮字眼，并不是我们思考时所用的语言。

德龙达的思考以飞快的画面进行着种种可能：他看见自己被某个官家的眼线引进一条灰暗的街；他穿过幽暗的门洞，看见一个鹰眼的女人，头发蓬乱、不曾梳洗，正同饥饿的姑娘压价，买她最后一件像样的衣饰；或者，在某个只因更时髦而愈发丑恶的地段，他听见一个年轻的犹太人在耳边絮叨而狎昵，乐于显示自己熟悉绅士们的口味，而且只要绅士们肯赏脸，什么交易他都不嫌脏——如此等等，他在这类经验上的短短一章便翻完了。请原谅他：他的头脑并不惯于自发地跑进侮辱性的念头里，也不惯于玩那种把摩西同广告附页认作一家的机智；只是他此刻被恐惧主宰着；倘若米拉的父母是基督徒，唯一的不同是他的预感会有更广的见识来喂养。把恐惧同未知的出身联系在一起，本是他心智的习惯；而这一桩同他自己那一桩一样，都足以让这联系合乎情理。

可是，米拉怎么办？她需要最完全意义上的庇护与保护；他的全部侠士心肠都奋起坚持：他能越早、越充分地为她争取到除他之外旁人的关切，就越好地偿清她对他的权利。他无权把她整个供养起来，尽管他也许供养得起；她给他的印象愈深，他愈希望她明白自己在经济上完全独立于他。对未来种种他试图当作妄想驱散的模糊幻象，仍留下了一点影响——一种比任何说得出的动机都强烈的焦虑：凡贴近看到他行动的人，应当从一开始就了解他同米拉关系的来历。他已学会憎恨对他人生大纽带、大义务的保密——愈发憎恨，因为一股由种种敏感交织成的强韧符咒，碍着他去捅破这层保密。德龙达对自己立过誓——既然使凡人蒙羞的种种真相，并不全由他们自己铸成——那么，真相决不可因为他的行为，变成另一个人的耻辱。

===Original===

Deronda’s thinking went on in rapid images of what might be: he saw himself guided by some official scout into a dingy street; he entered through a dim doorway, and saw a hawk-eyed woman, rough-headed, and unwashed, cheapening a hungry girl’s last bit of finery; or in some quarter only the more hideous for being smarter, he found himself under the breath of a young Jew talkative and familiar, willing to show his acquaintance with gentlemen’s tastes, and not fastidious in any transactions with which they would favor him﻿—and so on through the brief chapter of his experience in this kind. Excuse him: his mind was not apt to run spontaneously into insulting ideas, or to practice a form of wit which identifies Moses with the advertisement sheet; but he was just now governed by dread, and if Mirah’s parents had been Christian, the chief difference would have been that his forebodings would have been fed with wider knowledge. It was the habit of his mind to connect dread with unknown parentage, and in this case as well as his own there was enough to make the connection reasonable.
But what was to be done with Mirah? She needed shelter and protection in the fullest sense, and all his chivalrous sentiment roused itself to insist that the sooner and the more fully he could engage for her the interest of others besides himself, the better he should fulfill her claims on him. He had no right to provide for her entirely, though he might be able to do so; the very depth of the impression she had produced made him desire that she should understand herself to be entirely independent of him; and vague visions of the future which he tried to dispel as fantastic left their influence in an anxiety stronger than any motive he could give for it, that those who saw his actions closely should be acquainted from the first with the history of his relation to Mirah. He had learned to hate secrecy about the grand ties and obligations of his life﻿—to hate it the more because a strong spell of interwoven sensibilities hindered him from breaking such secrecy. Deronda had made a vow to himself that﻿—since the truths which disgrace mortals are not all of their own making﻿—the truth should never be made a disgrace to another by his act.
