===Original===

He was not without terror lest he should break this vow, and fall into the apologetic philosophy which explains the world into containing nothing better than one’s own conduct.
At one moment he resolved to tell the whole of his adventure to Sir Hugo and Lady Mallinger the next morning at breakfast, but the possibility that something quite new might reveal itself on his next visit to Mrs. Meyrick’s checked this impulse, and he finally went to sleep on the conclusion that he would wait until that visit had been made.

===Chinese===

他并非没有恐惧，怕自己有朝一日破了这个誓，堕入那套辩解的哲学——把世界解释得再好也不过同自己的行止一样。

有一刻他决意第二天早餐时，把全部奇遇原原本本告诉雨果爵士和马林格夫人；可是想到下次去梅里克家也许会显露出什么全然新鲜的情况，这股冲动便被拦住了；他最后是带着这样的结论入睡的：等那趟拜访做过再说。

### XX / 第二十章
===Original===

> It will hardly be denied that even in this frail and corrupted world, we sometimes meet persons who, in their very mien and aspect, as well as in the whole habit of life, manifest such a signature and stamp of virtue, as to make our judgment of them a matter of intuition rather than the result of continued examination.

Mirah said that she had slept well that night; and when she came down in Mab’s black dress, her dark hair curling in fresh fibrils as it gradually dried from its plenteous bath, she looked like one who was beginning to take comfort after the long sorrow and watching which had paled her cheek and made blue semicircles under her eyes. It was Mab who carried her breakfast and ushered her down﻿—with some pride in the effect produced by a pair of tiny felt slippers which she had rushed out to buy because there were no shoes in the house small enough for Mirah, whose borrowed dress ceased about her ankles and displayed the cheap clothing that, moulding itself on her feet, seemed an adornment as choice as the sheaths of buds. The farthing buckles were bijoux.
“Oh, if you please, mamma?” cried Mab, clasping her hands and stooping toward Mirah’s feet, as she entered the parlor; “look at the slippers, how beautiful they fit! I declare she is like the Queen Budoor﻿—‘two delicate feet, the work of the protecting and all-recompensing Creator, support her; and I wonder how they can sustain what is above them.’ ”
Mirah looked down at her own feet in a childlike way and then smiled at Mrs. Meyrick, who was saying inwardly, “One could hardly imagine this creature having an evil thought. But wise people would tell me to be cautious.” She returned Mirah’s smile and said, “I fear the feet have had to sustain their burden a little too often lately. But today she will rest and be my companion.”
“And she will tell you so many things and I shall not hear them,” grumbled Mab, who felt herself in the first volume of a delightful romance and obliged to miss some chapters because she had to go to pupils.
Kate was already gone to make sketches along the river, and Amy was away on business errands. It was what the mother wished, to be alone with this stranger, whose story must be a sorrowful one, yet was needful to be told.
The small front parlor was as good as a temple that morning.

===Chinese===

> 恐怕不会有人否认：即使在这个脆弱而败坏的人世，我们也偶或遇见这样的人——他们的容止气度、乃至全部生活习性，都带着那样一种德性的印记与鈐记，使我们对他们的评断成了一种直觉，而无须长期考察。
米拉说，那夜她睡得很好；她穿着梅布的黑裙下楼来，深色的头发淋漓洗过之后，新卷的发丝渐渐干透，看上去像一个长久的悲恸与守夜之后开始得着安慰的人——那悲恸熬白了她的双颊，眼下熬出了青色的半环。端早饭、领她下楼的是梅布——颇以一双小毡拖鞋的功效自豪：家里找不出一双够小的鞋给米拉穿，她那身借来的裙子到脚踝便止了，露出裹在脚上那双廉价的袜子，倒像蓓蕾的包皮一样，成了一种精选的装饰。几枚法寻的鞋扣更是珍宝。
「哦，妈妈，请看！」梅布拍着手、朝着米拉的脚俯下身去喊道，她们进了客厅；「看这双拖鞋，多合脚！我说她真像布杜尔王后——『一双纤足，那是庇护万物、补偿一切的主的杰作，支撑着她；我奇怪它们怎么担得起上面的一切。』」
米拉孩子气地低头看看自己的脚，然后朝梅里克太太笑了；太太心里正想着：「简直想象不出这孩子会有恶念。可聪明人定会劝我小心。」她回以一笑，说：「只怕这双脚近来担它的担子，担得太勤了些。不过今天她要歇着，给我作伴。」
「她要讲好多好多事给您听，我可听不成了，」梅布嘟囔道；她觉得自己正处在一部迷人传奇的第一卷里，却因为要去给学生上课，偏偏错过其中几章。
凯特已去河边写生，艾米出门办事。这正是母亲所愿：同这陌生人单独在一起——她的故事必是悲苦的，却不能不叫她讲。
那天早晨，那间小小的前客厅不啻一座神殿。

===Original===

The sunlight was on the river and soft air came in through the open window; the walls showed a glorious silent cloud of witnesses﻿—the Virgin soaring amid her cherubic escort; grand Melancholia with her solemn universe; the Prophets and Sibyls; the School of Athens; the Last Supper; mystic groups where far-off ages made one moment; grave Holbein and Rembrandt heads; the Tragic Muse; last-century children at their musings or their play; Italian poets﻿—all were there through the medium of a little black and white. The neat mother who had weathered her troubles, and come out of them with a face still cheerful, was sorting colored wools for her embroidery. Hafiz purred on the window-ledge, the clock on the mantelpiece ticked without hurry, and the occasional sound of wheels seemed to lie outside the more massive central quiet. Mrs. Meyrick thought that this quiet might be the best invitation to speech on the part of her companion, and chose not to disturb it by remark. Mirah sat opposite in her former attitude, her hands clasped on her lap, her ankles crossed, her eyes at first traveling slowly over the objects around her, but finally resting with a sort of placid reverence on Mrs. Meyrick. At length she began to speak softly.
“I remember my mother’s face better than anything; yet I was not seven when I was taken away, and I am nineteen now.”
“I can understand that,” said Mrs. Meyrick. “There are some earliest things that last the longest.”
“Oh, yes, it was the earliest. I think my life began with waking up and loving my mother’s face: it was so near to me, and her arms were round me, and she sang to me. One hymn she sang so often, so often: and then she taught me to sing it with her: it was the first I ever sang. They were always Hebrew hymns she sang; and because I never knew the meaning of the words they seemed full of nothing but our love and happiness. When I lay in my little bed and it was all white above me, she used to bend over me, between me and the white, and sing in a sweet, low voice. I can dream myself back into that time when I am awake, and it often comes back to me in my sleep﻿—my hand is very little, I put it up to her face and she kisses it. Sometimes in my dreams I begin to tremble and think that we are both dead; but then I wake up and my hand lies like this, and for a moment I hardly know myself.

===Chinese===

阳光落在河上，柔软的空气从敞开的窗子里进来；四壁展现出一大片无声的荣耀见证——在天使簇拥中升天的圣母；伴着她庄严宇宙的伟大的《忧郁》；众先知与众女巫；雅典学院；最后的晚餐；把迢递的世代凝成一瞬的神秘群像；凝重的霍尔拜因与伦勃朗的头像；悲剧缪斯；上世纪沉思或游戏的孩童；意大利的诗人们——都借着一点黑白印在了那里。这位饱经忧患、出来时脸上依然开朗的整洁的母亲，正在为刺绣分拣彩线。哈菲兹在窗台上打着呼噜，壁炉上的钟不慌不忙地滴答，偶尔的车轮声仿佛只躺在更庞大的中央寂静之外。梅里克太太想，这份寂静也许正是对同伴开口的最好邀请，便不去用言语搅扰它。米拉坐在对面，还是先前那副姿势，双手交叠在膝上，脚踝相搭，目光起初缓缓巡过四周的物件，末了带着一种恬静的敬意落在梅里克太太身上。终于，她低低开口了。
「别的我都记不清，母亲的脸却记得最清；可我被带走时还不满七岁，如今已经十九了。」
「这我明白，」梅里克太太说。「有些最早的东西，反而延续得最久。」
「哦，是，那是最早的。我想我的生命是从醒来、爱上母亲的脸开始的：它离我那么近，她的手臂环着我，她唱歌给我听。有一支圣歌她唱得那么多、那么多；后来她教我同她一起唱：那是我唱过的第一支歌。她唱的总是希伯来圣歌；因为我不懂那些字句的意思，它们便仿佛只装满了我们的爱与幸福。我躺在小床上，头顶一片雪白，她常俯下身来，隔着我和那片白，用甜美的低声唱。醒着的时候我能梦回那段时光，睡着时它也常回来——我的手那么小，我举起来摸她的脸，她吻它。梦里有时我会发抖，想我们两个都死了；可随后我醒来，我的手就像这样放着，一时竟认不得自己。

===Original===

But if I could see my mother again I should know her.”
“You must expect some change after twelve years,” said Mrs. Meyrick, gently. “See my grey hair: ten years ago it was bright brown. The days and months pace over us like restless little birds, and leave the marks of their feet backward and forward; especially when they are like birds with heavy hearts﻿—then they tread heavily.”
“Ah, I am sure her heart has been heavy for want of me. But to feel her joy if we could meet again, and I could make her know I love her and give her deep comfort after all her mourning! If that could be, I should mind nothing; I should be glad that I have lived through my trouble. I did despair. The world seemed miserable and wicked; none helped me so that I could bear their looks and words; I felt that my mother was dead, and death was the only way to her. But then in the last moment﻿—yesterday, when I longed for the water to close over me﻿—and I thought that death was the best image of mercy﻿—then goodness came to me living, and I felt trust in the living. And﻿—it is strange﻿—but I began to hope that she was living too. And now I with you﻿—here﻿—this morning, peace and hope have come into me like a flood. I want nothing; I can wait; because I hope and believe and am grateful﻿—oh, so grateful! You have not thought evil of me﻿—you have not despised me.”
Mirah spoke with low-toned fervor, and sat as still as a picture all the while.
“Many others would have felt as we do, my dear,” said Mrs. Meyrick, feeling a mist come over her eyes as she looked at her work.
“But I did not meet them﻿—they did not come to me.”
“How was it that you were taken from your mother?”
“Ah, I am a long while coming to that. It is dreadful to speak of, yet I must tell you﻿—I must tell you everything. My father﻿—it was he that took me away. I thought we were only going on a little journey; and I was pleased. There was a box with all my little things in. But we went on board a ship, and got farther and farther away from the land. Then I was ill; and I thought it would never end﻿—it was the first misery, and it seemed endless. But at last we landed. I knew nothing then, and believed what my father said. He comforted me, and told me I should go back to my mother. But it was America we had reached, and it was long years before we came back to Europe.

===Chinese===

可只要能再见母亲一面，我一定认得她。」
「十二年了，你总得料到有些变化，」梅里克太太温存地说。「看看我的白发：十年前还是亮褐色呢。日子和月份像不安分的小鸟在我们身上踏过，来来回回留下爪痕；尤其当它们是心情沉重的小鸟时——便踏得格外重。」
「啊，我确信她的心一定因思念我而沉重。可要是我们能重逢，让她知道我爱她，让她在一切哀伤之后从我这里得到深深的安慰——想想她的欢喜！若能那样，我就什么都不在乎了；我会庆幸自己活过了这场苦难。我确实绝望过。世界显得凄惨而邪恶；没有一个人帮了我、而我又受得住他们的眼色和言语；我以为母亲死了，而死亡是通往她唯一的路。可就在最后一刻——昨天，我盼着水合拢到我头上的时候——我想死亡是慈悲最好的形象——那时善活生生地来到我面前，我对活着的生命有了信任。而且——说来奇怪——我开始希望她也活着。如今我同你们在一起——在这里——今天早晨，平安和希望像洪水一样涌进我心里。我什么都不缺了；我能等；因为我怀着希望、怀着信念、怀着感激——哦，多么感激！你们没有把我想坏——你们没有轻看我。」
米拉声音低而炽热，说话时始终端坐如画。
「许多别人也会像我们这样的，亲爱的，」梅里克太太说，看着手里的活计，眼里蒙上一层雾。
「可我没有遇上他们——他们没有来到我身边。」
「你是怎么从你母亲身边被带走的？」
「啊，我讲了这么半天才到这一桩。说起来可怕，可我必须告诉您——我必须把一切都告诉您。是我父亲——是他把我带走的。我只当我们要出一趟小远门；我还挺高兴。有一只箱子，装着我全部的小东西。可我们上了船，离陆地越来越远。随后我晕起船来；我以为这罪永远受不到头——那是头一桩苦，而它像是没有底的。可我们终于上了岸。我那时什么都不懂，父亲说什么我信什么。他安慰我，说我就会回母亲那里去。可我们到的是美洲，过了好多年才回欧洲。」

===Original===

At first I often asked my father when we were going back; and I tried to learn writing fast, because I wanted to write to my mother; but one day when he found me trying to write a letter, he took me on his knee and told me that my mother and brother were dead; that was why we did not go back. I remember my brother a little; he carried me once; but he was not always at home. I believed my father when he said that they were dead. I saw them under the earth when he said they were there, with their eyes forever closed. I never thought of its not being true; and I used to cry every night in my bed for a long while. Then when she came so often to me, in my sleep, I thought she must be living about me though I could not always see her, and that comforted me. I was never afraid in the dark, because of that; and very often in the day I used to shut my eyes and bury my face and try to see her and to hear her singing. I came to do that at last without shutting my eyes.”
Mirah paused with a sweet content in her face, as if she were having her happy vision, while she looked out toward the river.
“Still your father was not unkind to you, I hope,” said Mrs. Meyrick, after a minute, anxious to recall her.
“No; he petted me, and took pains to teach me. He was an actor; and I found out, after, that the ‘Coburg’ I used to hear of his going to at home was a theatre. But he had more to do with the theatre than acting. He had not always been an actor; he had been a teacher, and knew many languages. His acting was not very good; I think, but he managed the stage, and wrote and translated plays. An Italian lady, a singer, lived with us a long time. They both taught me, and I had a master besides, who made me learn by heart and recite. I worked quite hard, though I was so little; and I was not nine when I first went on the stage. I could easily learn things, and I was not afraid. But then and ever since I hated our way of life. My father had money, and we had finery about us in a disorderly way; always there were men and women coming and going; there was loud laughing and disputing, strutting, snapping of fingers, jeering, faces I did not like to look at﻿—though many petted and caressed me. But then I remembered my mother.

===Chinese===

起初我常问父亲我们什么时候回去；我拼命快学写字，因为想给母亲写信；可有一天他撞见我在学写信，把我抱到膝上，告诉我母亲和哥哥都死了；所以我们不回去。哥哥我还记得一点；他抱过我一次；可他不大在家。父亲说他们死了，我就信了。他说他们在地下，我便看见他们在地下，眼睛永远闭着。我从没想到这会不是真的；有好长一段日子，我夜夜在床上哭。后来她常常到梦里来，我想她想必就在我身边活着，只是我不能常见到她，这念头安慰了我。因为这个，我在黑暗里从不害怕；白天我也常闭上眼、埋下脸，想看见她、听见她唱歌。到后来，不闭眼也能做到了。」
米拉停下来，脸上带着甜甜的满足，仿佛正怀着她的幸福幻象，眼睛望向河那边。
「不过你父亲待你总不算苛刻吧，我希望，」过了一分钟，梅里克太太说，急着把她唤回来。
「不；他宠我，也肯费心教我。他是演戏的；后来我才弄明白，我常听他说起的那个『科堡』是一家戏院。可他同戏院的关系不止于演戏。他并不是一向做演员；他做过教师，懂好多种语言。他的戏演得并不怎么好，我想；可他管着舞台，还编写和翻译剧本。有位意大利太太、唱歌的，同我们一起住了很久。他们两个都教我，另外还给我请了位教师，教我背诵。我很用功，虽然年纪那么小；不满九岁我头一回登台。东西我学得快，人也不怯场。可打那时起、也一直到现在，我恨透了我们的那种生活。父亲有钱，我们身边乱糟糟地围着许多华丽东西；总有男男女女来来往往；大声的哄笑和争吵、昂首阔步、捻着响指、讥诮、我不爱看的嘴脸——尽管许多人也宠爱我、抚爱我。可我心里总记着母亲。

===Original===

Even at first when I understood nothing, I shrank away from all those things outside me into companionship with thoughts that were not like them; and I gathered thoughts very fast, because I read many things﻿—plays and poetry, Shakespeare and Schiller, and learned evil and good. My father began to believe that I might be a great singer: my voice was considered wonderful for a child; and he had the best teaching for me. But it was painful that he boasted of me, and set me to sing for show at any minute, as if I had been a musical box. Once when I was nine years old, I played the part of a little girl who had been forsaken and did not know it, and sat singing to herself while she played with flowers. I did it without any trouble; but the clapping and all the sounds of the theatre were hateful to me; and I never liked the praise I had, because it all seemed very hard and unloving: I missed the love and trust I had been born into. I made a life in my own thoughts quite different from everything about me: I chose what seemed to me beautiful out of the plays and everything, and made my world out of it; and it was like a sharp knife always grazing me that we had two sorts of life which jarred so with each other﻿—women looking good and gentle on the stage, and saying good things as if they felt them, and directly after I saw them with coarse, ugly manners. My father sometimes noticed my shrinking ways; and Signora said one day, when I had been rehearsing, ‘She will never be an artist: she has no notion of being anybody but herself. That does very well now, but by-and-by you will see﻿—she will have no more face and action than a singing-bird.’ My father was angry, and they quarreled. I sat alone and cried, because what she had said was like a long unhappy future unrolled before me. I did not want to be an artist; but this was what my father expected of me. After a while Signora left us, and a governess used to come and give me lessons in different things, because my father began to be afraid of my singing too much; but I still acted from time to time. Rebellious feelings grew stronger in me, and I wished to get away from this life; but I could not tell where to go, and I dreaded the world.

===Chinese===

从最初什么都不懂的时候起，我就从外面这一切里退缩出来，躲进同它们不一样的念想做伴；我攒念头攒得很快，因为我读了许多东西——剧本和诗，莎士比亚和席勒，学会了恶与善。父亲渐渐相信我或许能成为大歌唱家：我童年的嗓子被视为奇迹；他给我请了最好的教习。可叫人难受的是他拿我夸口，随时叫我出来唱给人看，好像我是一只八音盒。九岁那年，我演过一个被遗弃而不自知的小女孩，坐在那里一面玩花一面自顾自唱歌。我演来毫不费力；可剧场里的掌声和一切声响都叫我憎厌；得了称赞我也从不喜欢，因为那一切显得生硬而没有爱：我想念我生来便有的爱与信。我在自己的思想里造了一个同周围一切全然不同的生活：我从剧本和一切里面拣出我认为美的，拿来造我的世界；而最刺我的是，我们竟有两套如此相磨相磕的生活——女人在台上一副良善温柔的面孔，说着动听的话仿佛出于真心，转眼我又看见她们举止粗俗丑陋。父亲有时注意到我畏缩的样子；那位意大利太太有一天、在我排练之后说：『她永远成不了艺术家：她除了做她自己，没有扮演旁人的念头。眼下还使得，往后你瞧吧——她会连一只鸣禽的脸色和身段都不剩。』父亲发了火，他们吵了一场。我独自坐着哭，因为她那话像一幅展开在我面前的、漫长而不幸的未来。我不想做艺术家；可这正是父亲指望于我的。过了些时那位太太离开了我们，来了位女教师，教我各门功课，因为父亲开始怕我唱歌唱得太累；可我还是时时演戏。反抗的情绪在我心里越长越壮，我想逃离这种生活；可我不知道往哪儿去，我又怕这个世界。

===Original===

Besides, I felt it would be wrong to leave my father: I dreaded doing wrong, for I thought I might get wicked and hateful to myself, in the same way that many others seemed hateful to me. For so long, so long I had never felt my outside world happy; and if I got wicked I should lose my world of happy thoughts where my mother lived with me. That was my childish notion all through those years. Oh how long they were!”
Mirah fell to musing again.
“Had you no teaching about what was your duty?” said Mrs. Meyrick. She did not like to say “religion”﻿—finding herself on inspection rather dim as to what the Hebrew religion might have turned into at this date.
“No﻿—only that I ought to do what my father wished. He did not follow our religion at New York, and I think he wanted me not to know much about it. But because my mother used to take me to the synagogue, and I remembered sitting on her knee and looking through the railing and hearing the chanting and singing, I longed to go. One day when I was quite small I slipped out and tried to find the synagogue, but I lost myself a long while till a peddler questioned me and took me home. My father, missing me, had been much in fear, and was very angry. I too had been so frightened at losing myself that it was long before I thought of venturing out again. But after Signora left us we went to rooms where our landlady was a Jewess and observed her religion. I asked her to take me with her to the synagogue; and I read in her prayer-books and Bible, and when I had money enough I asked her to buy me books of my own, for these books seemed a closer companionship with my mother: I knew that she must have looked at the very words and said them. In that way I have come to know a little of our religion, and the history of our people, besides piecing together what I read in plays and other books about Jews and Jewesses; because I was sure my mother obeyed her religion. I had left off asking my father about her. It is very dreadful to say it, but I began to disbelieve him. I had found that he did not always tell the truth, and made promises without meaning to keep them; and that raised my suspicion that my mother and brother were still alive though he had told me they were dead.

===Chinese===

再说，我觉得离开父亲是错的：我怕做错事，因为我怕自己也会变坏、变得连自己都憎厌，就像旁人那些人在我眼里可憎一样。那么久、那么久，我从不曾觉得我外面的世界是快乐的；倘若我变坏了，我就会失去我那片母亲同我住在一起的幸福念头的小天地。那些年里，我孩子气的想法一直是这样。哦，那些日子多么长啊！」
米拉又陷入了沉思。
「没有人教过你什么是你的本分吗？」梅里克太太说。她不愿说出「宗教」二字——她发现自己盘算起来，实在说不准希伯来人的宗教到了今日会变成了什么样子。
「没有——只教我该顺从父亲的愿望。在纽约，父亲并不遵行我们的教，我想他还巴不得我少知道些。可因为母亲从前常带我去犹太会堂（synagogue），我记得坐在她膝上，隔着栏杆张望，听着诵唱和歌声，我就一心想去。有一天，我还很小，偷偷溜出去找犹太会堂，可迷了路，转了好久，一个货郎盘问我，把我送回了家。父亲发现我不见了，吓得要命，也发了好大的火。我走失得那样害怕，好长时间不敢再冒险出门。可那位太太走后，我们搬了住处，房东太太是位犹太女人，遵行她的教。我求她带我去犹太会堂；我在她的祈祷书和《圣经》里念书，攒够了钱便请她替我买我自己的书——因为这些书像是同母亲更近的作伴：我知道她必定亲眼看过这些字句、亲口念过它们。这样我才对我们的教、对我们民族的历史略知一二，此外还把剧本和别的书里写到犹太男女的零碎拼凑起来；因为我确信母亲是遵行她的教的。我早已不再向父亲问起她。说出来很可怕，可我开始不信他了。我发现他并不总说真话，许下诺言又不打算践约；这便叫我起了疑：母亲和哥哥也许还活着，尽管他说他们死了。

===Original===

For in going over the past again as I got older and knew more, I felt sure that my mother had been deceived, and had expected to see us back again after a very little while; and my father taking me on his knee and telling me that my mother and brother were both dead seemed to me now but a bit of acting, to set my mind at rest. The cruelty of that falsehood sank into me, and I hated all untruth because of it. I wrote to my mother secretly: I knew the street, Colman Street, where we lived, and that it was not Blackfriars Bridge and the Coburg, and that our name was Cohen then, though my father called us Lapidoth, because, he said, it was a name of his forefathers in Poland. I sent my letter secretly; but no answer came, and I thought there was no hope for me. Our life in America did not last much longer. My father suddenly told me we were to pack up and go to Hamburg, and I was rather glad. I hoped we might get among a different sort of people, and I knew German quite well﻿—some German plays almost all by heart. My father spoke it better than he spoke English. I was thirteen then, and I seemed to myself quite old﻿—I knew so much, and yet so little. I think other children cannot feel as I did. I had often wished that I had been drowned when I was going away from my mother. But I set myself to obey and suffer: what else could I do? One day when we were on our voyage, a new thought came into my mind. I was not very ill that time, and I kept on deck a good deal. My father acted and sang and joked to amuse people on board, and I used often to hear remarks about him. One day, when I was looking at the sea and nobody took notice of me, I overheard a gentleman say, ‘Oh, he is one of those clever Jews﻿—a rascal, I shouldn’t wonder. There’s no race like them for cunning in the men and beauty in the women. I wonder what market he means that daughter for.’ When I heard this it darted into my mind that the unhappiness in my life came from my being a Jewess, and that always to the end the world would think slightly of me and that I must bear it, for I should be judged by that name; and it comforted me to believe that my suffering was part of the affliction of my people, my part in the long song of mourning that has been going on through ages and ages.

===Chinese===

因为随着长大、懂的事多了，我把过去一遍遍重理，我确信母亲是受了欺瞒的，她只当我们很快就会回去；而父亲把我抱到膝上、说我母亲和哥哥都死了，如今在我看来不过是一段做戏，好让我安心。那谎言的残忍渗进了我心里，因了它我恨一切不真。我偷偷给母亲写信：我记得我们住的那条街——科尔曼街，记得家不在黑修士桥和科堡那一带，也记得我们那时姓科恩，虽然父亲管我们叫拉皮多特，说是他祖上在波兰的姓。我把信偷偷寄了出去；可没有回音来，我以为再没有指望了。我们在美洲的日子没有再过多久。父亲忽然告诉我，收拾行装去汉堡，我倒有点高兴。我盼着能换到另一类人中间去；我的德文相当好——有几部德国剧本几乎全文能背。父亲的德文说得比英文还好。那年我十三岁，自觉已经很老成了——懂得那么多，却又懂得那么少。我想别的孩子不会像我那样。我常常巴不得当初离开母亲时就淹死在水里。可我打定主意顺从、受苦：不这样又能怎样呢？航行途中有一天，一个新念头进了我心里。那一回我晕得不厉害，多半时候待在甲板上。父亲又演又唱又打趣，逗船上的人开心，我常听见人家议论他。有一天，我望着海，谁也不理我，偶然听见一位先生说：『哦，他是那种机灵的犹太人——弄不好还是个骗子。论心机之深、论女人之美，天下没有哪个种族比得上他们。不知道他打算把那女儿卖到哪个市场去。』我听了这话，心里忽然一亮：我生命里的不幸，原是因我是个犹太女子；这世界到末了都会看轻我，我只能忍受，因为我将顶着这个名字受审判；而相信我的苦难是我整个民族苦难的一部分、是我的一份、汇入那世世代代唱个不停的哀歌——这信念反倒安慰了我。

===Original===

For if many of our race were wicked and made merry in their wickedness﻿—what was that but part of the affliction borne by the just among them, who were despised for the sins of their brethren?﻿—But you have not rejected me.”
Mirah had changed her tone in this last sentence, having suddenly reflected that at this moment she had reason not for complaint but for gratitude.
“And we will try to save you from being judged unjustly by others, my poor child,” said Mrs. Meyrick, who had now given up all attempt at going on with her work, and sat listening with folded hands and a face hardly less eager than Mab’s would have been. “Go on, go on: tell me all.”
“After that we lived in different towns﻿—Hamburg and Vienna, the longest. I began to study singing again: and my father always got money about the theatres. I think he brought a good deal of money from America, I never knew why we left. For some time he was in great spirits about my singing, and he made me rehearse parts and act continually. He looked forward to my coming out in the opera. But by-and-by it seemed that my voice would never be strong enough﻿—it did not fulfill its promise. My master at Vienna said, ‘Don’t strain it further: it will never do for the public:﻿—it is gold, but a thread of gold dust.’ My father was bitterly disappointed: we were not so well off at that time. I think I have not quite told you what I felt about my father. I knew he was fond of me and meant to indulge me, and that made me afraid of hurting him; but he always mistook what would please me and give me happiness. It was his nature to take everything lightly; and I soon left off asking him any questions about things that I cared for much, because he always turned them off with a joke. He would even ridicule our own people; and once when he had been imitating their movements and their tones in praying, only to make others laugh, I could not restrain myself﻿—for I always had an anger in my heart about my mother﻿—and when we were alone, I said, ‘Father, you ought not to mimic our own people before Christians who mock them: would it not be bad if I mimicked you, that they might mock you?’ But he only shrugged his shoulders and laughed and pinched my chin, and said, ‘You couldn’t do it, my dear.’

===Chinese===

因为倘若我们族里也有许多人作恶、还在恶里作乐——那岂不也是他们中间的义人所受苦难的一部分？义人岂不正因为同胞的罪而受人白眼？——可你们并没有弃绝我。」
说到末一句，米拉的语气变了——她忽然想到，此刻她该感恩，而不是抱怨。
「我们也要设法叫你不再受人不公道的评断，我可怜的孩子，」梅里克太太说。她早已丢下手里的活计，交叠着双手坐在那里听，脸上的急切不亚于梅布。「讲下去，讲下去：全都告诉我。」
「那以后我们住在不同的城市——汉堡和维也纳，维也纳住得最久。我重新开始学唱；父亲总在戏院周围弄到钱。我想他从美洲带回不少钱，我们为什么离开，我始终不知道。有一阵他对我的唱歌兴致极高，叫我不断排练角色、不断登台。他指望我进歌剧界出头。可渐渐地，看我的嗓子终究壮不起来——它没有兑现童年的指望。我在维也纳的老师说：『别再勉强它了：它上不得台面——是金子，可只是一缕金粉。』父亲失望透了：那时我们的境况也不宽裕。我还没有完全告诉您我对父亲的感情。我知道他疼我、想娇惯我，这叫我怕伤了他；可他总猜错什么能叫我欢喜、给我幸福。凡事看得轻浮是他的天性；不久，凡是我很在乎的事，我便不再问他，因为他总拿玩笑岔开。他甚至讥笑我们自己民族的人；有一回他学他们祈祷时的举动和腔调，只为逗旁人笑，我再也忍不住——我心里对母亲的事总存着一股怒气——等只剩我们两个时，我说：『父亲，你不该在基督徒面前学我们自己人的样子，他们会笑话他们的；倘若我学你的样子、好叫他们笑话你，岂不也是坏事？』可他只耸耸肩，笑笑，捏捏我的下巴，说：『你学不来，亲爱的。』

===Original===

It was this way of turning off everything, that made a great wall between me and my father, and whatever I felt most I took the most care to hide from him. For there were some things﻿—when they were laughed at I could not bear it: the world seemed like a hell to me. Is this world and all the life upon it only like a farce or a vaudeville, where you find no great meanings? Why then are there tragedies and grand operas, where men do difficult things and choose to suffer? I think it is silly to speak of all things as a joke. And I saw that his wishing me to sing the greatest music, and parts in grand operas, was only wishing for what would fetch the greatest price. That hemmed in my gratitude for his affectionateness, and the tenderest feeling I had toward him was pity. Yes, I did sometimes pity him. He had aged and changed. Now he was no longer so lively. I thought he seemed worse﻿—less good to others than to me. Every now and then in the latter years his gaiety went away suddenly, and he would sit at home silent and gloomy; or he would come in and fling himself down and sob, just as I have done myself when I have been in trouble. If I put my hand on his knee and say, ‘What is the matter, father?’ he would make no answer, but would draw my arm round his neck and put his arm round me and go on crying. There never came any confidence between us; but oh, I was sorry for him. At those moments I knew he must feel his life bitter, and I pressed my cheek against his head and prayed. Those moments were what most bound me to him; and I used to think how much my mother once loved him, else she would not have married him.
“But soon there came the dreadful time. We had been at Pest and we came back to Vienna. In spite of what my master Leo had said, my father got me an engagement, not at the opera, but to take singing parts at a suburb theatre in Vienna. He had nothing to do with the theatre then; I did not understand what he did, but I think he was continually at a gambling house, though he was careful always about taking me to the theatre. I was very miserable. The plays I acted in were detestable to me. Men came about us and wanted to talk to me: women and men seemed to look at me with a sneering smile; it was no better than a fiery furnace.

===Chinese===

正是这种把什么都岔开的做法，在我和父亲之间砌起了一堵高墙；我心里最深的感情，最要小心瞒他。因为有些东西——被人取笑，我便受不了：世界便像一座地狱。难道这个世界和世上的一切生活，只是一出滑稽戏或歌舞杂剧，找不出重大的意义？那又为什么有悲剧、有大歌剧，人们做艰难的事、甘愿受苦？我看把一切都当成玩笑，才是愚蠢。我也看明白了：他要我唱最伟大的音乐、演大歌剧的角色，无非是要那卖得出最大价钱的东西。这就把他那点亲爱之情圈在了墙里；我对他最温柔的感情，是怜悯。是的，我有时真怜悯他。他见老、变了。如今不再那么爱热闹了。我看他变得坏了些——待旁人不如待我好。后来那些年里，他的兴致隔三差五忽然没了，会闷坐在家里，一言不发、阴沉沉的；或者一头闯进来，扑倒就哭，正像我烦恼时那样。我把手放在他膝上说：『怎么了，父亲？』他总不回答，只把我的胳膊拉过去环住他的脖子，一只胳膊搂着我，哭个不停。我们之间从没有过什么知心话；可是，哦，我可怜他。那些时刻我知道他必定觉得自己的日子苦，我便把脸颊贴住他的头，为他祈祷。把我同他拴得最紧的，正是那些时刻；我常想，母亲当初该多爱他，不然不会嫁给他。
「可是可怕的日子不久就来了。我们原在佩斯，回到了维也纳。我的老师莱奥虽那样告诫过，父亲还是替我攥了一门营生——不在歌剧院，是在维也纳一家郊区戏院唱戏中的歌段。他那时同戏院没有关系了；他做些什么我不明白，可我想他成天泡在赌场里，虽然送我去戏院倒是从来小心的。我苦恼极了。演的那些戏我看不上眼。男人们凑上来想同我搭话；那些女人男人看我时仿佛都带着讥笑；那日子同火炉没有两样。

===Original===

Perhaps I make it worse than it was﻿—you don’t know that life: but the glare and the faces, and my having to go on and act and sing what I hated, and then see people who came to stare at me behind the scenes﻿—it was all so much worse than when I was a little girl. I went through with it; I did it; I had set my mind to obey my father and work, for I saw nothing better that I could do. But I felt that my voice was getting weaker, and I knew that my acting was not good except when it was not really acting, but the part was one that I could be myself in, and some feeling within me carried me along. That was seldom.
“Then, in the midst of all this, the news came to me one morning that my father had been taken to prison, and he had sent for me. He did not tell me the reason why he was there, but he ordered me to go to an address he gave me, to see a Count who would be able to get him released. The address was to some public rooms where I was to ask for the Count, and beg him to come to my father. I found him, and recognized him as a gentleman whom I had seen the other night for the first time behind the scenes. That agitated me, for I remembered his way of looking at me and kissing my hand﻿—I thought it was in mockery. But I delivered my errand, and he promised to go immediately to my father, who came home again that very evening, bringing the Count with him. I now began to feel a horrible dread of this man, for he worried me with his attentions, his eyes were always on me: I felt sure that whatever else there might be in his mind toward me, below it all there was scorn for the Jewess and the actress. And when he came to me the next day in the theatre and would put my shawl around me, a terror took hold of me; I saw that my father wanted me to look pleased. The Count was neither very young nor very old; his hair and eyes were pale; he was tall and walked heavily, and his face was heavy and grave except when he looked at me. He smiled at me, and his smile went through me with horror: I could not tell why he was so much worse to me than other men. Some feelings are like our hearing: they come as sounds do, before we know their reason. My father talked to me about him when we were alone, and praised him﻿—said what a good friend he had been. I said nothing, because I supposed he had got my father out of prison. When the Count came again, my father left the room.

===Chinese===

也许我把它说得比实情更糟——你们不认识那种生活：可那刺眼的灯光和那些嘴脸，逼着我上台去演、去唱我所恨的东西，下来还得见那些专到后台来盯着我看的人——这一切，比我做小女孩时糟了不知多少。我熬过来了；我演了；我拿定主意顺从父亲、干活，因为我看不出还有什么更好的路。可我觉得嗓子越来越弱，我也知道自己的戏并不好——除非那算不得演戏，而是角色恰好容得下我自己，心里某种感情把我带了过去。那样的时候很少。
「就在这一切中间，一天早晨消息传来，说父亲被抓进监狱了，要我去。他不说自己为什么在那里，只吩咐我按他给的地址去找一位伯爵——那位伯爵有办法把他保出来。那地址是几间公共娱乐室，我要到那里找伯爵，求他到我父亲那里去。我找到了他，认出正是前几晚头一回在后台见到的那位先生。这叫我心慌，因为我记得他看我的样子、他吻我手的样子——我原以为是讥笑。可我把口信带到了，他答应立刻去看我父亲；当晚父亲就回来了，把伯爵也带回了家。我开始对这个人起了可怕的畏惧：他的殷勤缠得我不安生，他的眼睛总盯着我；我确信，他心里不论还有别的什么，底下总归是对犹太女子、对戏子的轻蔑。第二天他到戏院来，要亲手替我围披肩，一阵恐怖攫住了我；我看出父亲要我显出高兴的样子。伯爵不算很年轻也不算很老；头发和眼睛都是浅色的；个子高，脚步沉重，脸也沉重、板正——除非是在看我的时候。他朝我笑，那笑叫我通体恐怖：我说不清为什么他比别的男人更叫我害怕。有些感觉像我们的听觉：先来了声音，理由随后才到。我们单独在一起时，父亲同我谈起他，夸他——说他是多好的朋友。我什么也没说，因为想是他把父亲从监狱里捞出来的。伯爵再来的时候，父亲退出了房间。

===Original===

He asked me if I liked being on the stage. I said No, I only acted in obedience to my father. He always spoke French, and called me *petite ange* and such things, which I felt insulting. I knew he meant to make love to me, and I had it firmly in my mind that a nobleman and one who was not a Jew could have no love for me that was not half contempt. But then he told me that I need not act any longer; he wished me to visit him at his beautiful place, where I might be queen of everything. It was difficult to me to speak, I felt so shaken with anger: I could only say, ‘I would rather stay on the stage forever,’ and I left him there. Hurrying out of the room I saw my father sauntering in the passage. My heart was crushed. I went past him and locked myself up. It had sunk into me that my father was in a conspiracy with that man against me. But the next day he persuaded me to come out: he said that I had mistaken everything, and he would explain: if I did not come out and act and fulfill my engagement, we should be ruined and he must starve. So I went on acting, and for a week or more the Count never came near me. My father changed our lodgings, and kept at home except when he went to the theatre with me. He began one day to speak discouragingly of my acting, and say, I could never go on singing in public﻿—I should lose my voice﻿—I ought to think of my future, and not put my nonsensical feelings between me and my fortune. He said, ‘What will you do? You will be brought down to sing and beg at people’s doors. You have had a splendid offer and ought to accept it.’ I could not speak: a horror took possession of me when I thought of my mother and of him. I felt for the first time that I should not do wrong to leave him. But the next day he told me that he had put an end to my engagement at the theatre, and that we were to go to Prague. I was getting suspicious of everything, and my will was hardening to act against him. It took us two days to pack and get ready; and I had it in my mind that I might be obliged to run away from my father, and then I would come to London and try if it were possible to find my mother. I had a little money, and I sold some things to get more. I packed a few clothes in a little bag that I could carry with me, and I kept my mind on the watch.

===Chinese===

他问我喜欢不喜欢舞台。我说不喜欢，我演戏只为顺从父亲。他总说法语，管我叫『小天使』什么的，我觉得是侮辱。我知道他存心向我求爱，而我心里拿得很死：一位贵族、一个非犹太人，对我的爱里不会没有一半的轻蔑。可随后他说，我不必再演戏了；他要我去他美丽的宅第做客，在那里我什么都是女王。我气得发抖，话都难出口：只说得出一句『我宁可一辈子留在舞台上』，便擬下他走了。匆忙出屋时，我看见父亲在过道里踱着。我的心碎了。我从他身边走过，把自己锁进房里。我心里透了亮：父亲同那人串通好了算计我。可第二天他又劝我出来：说我什么都误会了，他会解释；我若不出来演戏、履行合同，我们就完了，他就要挨饿。于是我接着演，有一个多礼拜伯爵没有露面。父亲换了住处，除了陪我上戏院从不出门。有一天他开始数落我的演艺，说我反正唱不长——嗓子要没了——该想想前程，别让那些糊涂感情挡了自己的财运。他说：『你能怎么办？到头来在人家门口卖唱讨饭。人家给你开了那样好的条件，就该接受。』我说不出话：一想到母亲、一想到他，一阵恐怖便攫住我。我头一回觉得，离开他不算错。可第二天他告诉我，戏院的合同他已经替我退了，我们要去布拉格。我对一切都起了疑，主意也越拿越硬，要同他对着干。收拾准备花了两天；我心里打定：必要时就从父亲身边逃走，然后去伦敦，试试能不能找到母亲。我有一点钱，又变卖了几件东西凑钱。我把几件衣裳装进一只随身提得动的小提包，时时提着神。

===Original===

My father’s silence﻿—his letting drop that subject of the Count’s offer﻿—made me feel sure that there was a plan against me. I felt as if it had been a plan to take me to a madhouse. I once saw a picture of a madhouse, that I could never forget; it seemed to me very much like some of the life I had seen﻿—the people strutting, quarreling, leering﻿—the faces with cunning and malice in them. It was my will to keep myself from wickedness; and I prayed for help. I had seen what despised women were: and my heart turned against my father, for I saw always behind him that man who made me shudder. You will think I had not enough reason for my suspicions, and perhaps I had not, outside my own feeling; but it seemed to me that my mind had been lit up, and all that might be stood out clear and sharp. If I slept, it was only to see the same sort of things, and I could hardly sleep at all. Through our journey I was everywhere on the watch. I don’t know why, but it came before me like a real event, that my father would suddenly leave me and I should find myself with the Count where I could not get away from him. I thought God was warning me: my mother’s voice was in my soul. It was dark when we reached Prague, and though the strange bunches of lamps were lit it was difficult to distinguish faces as we drove along the street. My father chose to sit outside﻿—he was always smoking now﻿—and I watched everything in spite of the darkness. I do believe I could see better then than I ever did before: the strange clearness within seemed to have got outside me. It was not my habit to notice faces and figures much in the street; but this night I saw everyone; and when we passed before a great hotel I caught sight only of a back that was passing in﻿—the light of the great bunch of lamps a good way off fell on it. I knew it﻿—before the face was turned, as it fell into shadow, I knew who it was. Help came to me. I feel sure help came. I did not sleep that night. I put on my plainest things﻿—the cloak and hat I have worn ever since; and I sat watching for the light and the sound of the doors being unbarred. Someone rose early﻿—at four o’clock, to go to the railway. That gave me courage. I slipped out, with my little bag under my cloak, and none noticed me.

===Chinese===

父亲的沉默——他把伯爵那桩事撂下再不提——叫我确信对我有一个圈套。我觉得那像是要把我送进疯人院的圈套。我从前见过一幅疯人院的画，永远忘不掉；它同我见过的某种生活像极了——人们昂首阔步、吵吵嚷嚷、挤眉弄眼——一张张脸里藏着奸恶。我的意志是守住自己不做恶事；我祈求帮助。我见过被人贱看的女人是什么样：我的心转而背离父亲，因为我总看见他背后站着那个叫我发抖的男人。你们会想，我的疑心没有足够的根由；或许吧——在旁人看来；可我觉得自己的心智被点亮了，一切可能的事都又清楚又尖利地立着。睡着了，也净见同样的事，几乎睡不成。一路之上我处处提防。不知为什么，一个念头总像真事一样来到我面前：父亲会忽然把我丢下，我会发现自己落到伯爵手里，脱不了身。我想是上帝在警诫我：母亲的声音在我灵魂里。我们到布拉格时天已黑了，街上虽然点起了一簇簇陌生的灯，行车之间还是难辨面目。父亲偏要坐在车外——他如今总抽烟——我不顾天黑，什么都要看。我真信那一刻我看得比平生任何时候都清楚：内心的那种异常的明亮仿佛挪到了我身外。在街上留意行人的脸和身形本不是我的习惯；可这一夜我个个都看见；经过一家大旅馆门前时，我瞥见一个正走进去的背影——远处一大簇灯光正落在那背上。我认出了它——脸还没转过来、没落进暗处，我就认出那是谁。援助来到了我身边。我深信援助来到了。那一夜我没有睡。我穿上最素净的衣裳——就是后来一直穿的这件斗篷和帽子；我守着，等天亮，等门闩卸下的声响。有人起得早——四点钟，赶火车。这给了我胆量。我夹着斗篷下的小提包溜了出去，没有人看见我。

===Original===

I had been a long while attending to the railway guide that I might learn the way to England; and before the sun had risen I was in the train for Dresden. Then I cried for joy. I did not know whether my money would last out, but I trusted. I could sell the things in my bag, and the little rings in my ears, and I could live on bread only. My only terror was lest my father should follow me. But I never paused. I came on, and on, and on, only eating bread now and then. When I got to Brussels I saw that I should not have enough money, and I sold all that I could sell; but here a strange thing happened. Putting my hand into the pocket of my cloak, I found a half-napoleon. Wondering and wondering how it came there, I remembered that on the way from Cologne there was a young workman sitting against me. I was frightened at everyone, and did not like to be spoken to. At first he tried to talk, but when he saw that I did not like it, he left off. It was a long journey; I ate nothing but a bit of bread, and he once offered me some of the food he brought in, but I refused it. I do believe it was he who put that bit of gold in my pocket. Without it I could hardly have got to Dover, and I did walk a good deal of the way from Dover to London. I knew I should look like a miserable beggar-girl. I wanted not to look very miserable, because if I found my mother it would grieve her to see me so. But oh, how vain my hope was that she would be there to see me come! As soon as I set foot in London, I began to ask for Lambeth and Blackfriars Bridge, but they were a long way off, and I went wrong. At last I got to Blackfriars Bridge and asked for Colman Street. People shook their heads. None knew it. I saw it in my mind﻿—our doorsteps, and the white tiles hung in the windows, and the large brick building opposite with wide doors. But there was nothing like it. At last when I asked a tradesman where the Coburg Theatre and Colman Street were, he said, ‘Oh, my little woman, that’s all done away with. The old streets have been pulled down; everything is new.’ I turned away and felt as if death had laid a hand on me. He said: ‘Stop, stop! young woman; what is it you’re wanting with Colman Street, eh?’ meaning well, perhaps. But his tone was what I could not bear; and how could I tell him what I wanted? I felt blinded and bewildered with a sudden shock.

===Chinese===

我早留意铁路指南很久了，为的是认得去英国的路；太阳还没升起，我已坐上去德累斯顿的火车。那时我为欢喜哭了。我不知道钱够不够，可我信得过。提包里的东西可以卖，耳朵上的小耳环可以卖，光吃面包也活得下去。我唯一的恐惧是父亲追来。可我一步没有停。我走啊，走啊，走啊，只偶尔吃口面包。到了布鲁塞尔（Brussels），我看出来钱不够了，把能卖的都卖了；可这里出了一件怪事。我把手伸进斗篷口袋，摸出半个拿破仑金币。我纳闷又纳闷它怎么来的，才记起从科隆来的路上，有个年轻工人挨着我坐。我那时见谁都怕，不喜欢同人搭话。起先他试着说话，见我不喜欢，也就算了。路很长；我只吃过一小块面包，他有一回把手里的吃食让给我，我谢绝了。我深信那一点金子就是他放进我口袋的。没有它我几乎到不了多佛尔；从多佛尔到伦敦，好一段路也是一步步走的。我知道自己看上去像个可怜的讨饭丫头。我不想显得太可怜，因为倘若找到母亲，叫她看见我这副样子，她要伤心的。可是，我盼着她在那里看我到来的指望，多么落空啊！一踏上伦敦，我就打听兰贝斯和黑修士桥，可路远得很，又走岔了。好容易到了黑修士桥，打听科尔曼街。人们摇头。谁都不知道。那条街在我心里清清楚楚——我们的门阶，窗里挂的白瓷砖，对门那座大门宽敞的大砖楼。可再没有一处像它。末了我问一位店家，科堡戏院和科尔曼街在哪儿，他说：『哦，小姑娘，那些全拆掉啦。老街道都扒了；一切全是新的。』我转过身去，只觉死亡伸手按在了我身上。他又说：『站住，站住！姑娘；你找科尔曼街做什么，嗯？』——也许是好意。可他那口气我受不了；我又怎么能对他说出我要找什么？我只觉眼前一黑，天旋地转。

===Original===

I suddenly felt that I was very weak and weary, and yet where could I go? for I looked so poor and dusty, and had nothing with me﻿—I looked like a street-beggar. And I was afraid of all places where I could enter. I lost my trust. I thought I was forsaken. It seemed that I had been in a fever of hope﻿—delirious﻿—all the way from Prague: I thought that I was helped, and I did nothing but strain my mind forward and think of finding my mother; and now﻿—there I stood in a strange world. All who saw me would think ill of me, and I must herd with beggars. I stood on the bridge and looked along the river. People were going on to a steamboat. Many of them seemed poor, and I felt as if it would be a refuge to get away from the streets; perhaps the boat would take me where I could soon get into a solitude. I had still some pence left, and I bought a loaf when I went on the boat. I wanted to have a little time and strength to think of life and death. How could I live? And now again it seemed that if ever I were to find my mother again, death was the way to her. I ate, that I might have strength to think. The boat set me down at a place along the river﻿—I don’t know where﻿—and it was late in the evening. I found some large trees apart from the road, and I sat down under them that I might rest through the night. Sleep must have soon come to me, and when I awoke it was morning. The birds were singing, and the dew was white about me, I felt chill and oh, so lonely! I got up and walked and followed the river a long way and then turned back again. There was no reason why I should go anywhere. The world about me seemed like a vision that was hurrying by while I stood still with my pain. My thoughts were stronger than I was; they rushed in and forced me to see all my life from the beginning; ever since I was carried away from my mother I had felt myself a lost child taken up and used by strangers, who did not care what my life was to me, but only what I could do for them. It seemed all a weary wandering and heart-loneliness﻿—as if I had been forced to go to merrymakings without the expectation of joy. And now it was worse. I was lost again, and I dreaded lest any stranger should notice me and speak to me. I had a terror of the world. None knew me; all would mistake me. I had seen so many in my life who made themselves glad with scorning, and laughed at another’s shame.

===Chinese===

我忽然觉得自己又虚弱又疲惫，可又能上哪儿去呢？我这样一副寒尘相，身上一无所有——活像个街头的乞丐。我怕一切进得去的门。我失了信靠。我以为自己被弃绝了。原来从布拉格一路之上，我一直在发着希望的高热——说着胡话——我以为自己有神相助，只顾把心朝前赶，一心想着找到母亲；而如今——我站在一个陌生的世界里。看见我的人都会想坏我，我只得同乞丐为伍。我站到桥上，顺着河望。人们正陆续上一艘汽船。许多像是穷人，我觉得离开街道、上那船去像个避难；也许船会把我载到一个很快便能独处的地方。我还剩几个便士，上船时买了一条面包。我想得有点时间、有点力气，把生与死想一想。我怎么活呢？而此刻又觉得：若还想再见到母亲，死亡又是那条路了。我吃了，好吃有力气想。船在河上一处地方把我放下来——不知是什么地方——已是深夜。我寻到几棵离大路远远的大树，在树下坐定，预备这样过夜。睡意想必很快来了，醒来已是清晨。鸟在唱，四围一片白露，我冷，哦，那么孤单！我起身走了走，顺着河走了好远，又折回来。我已没有理由去任何地方。身边的世界像一幅匆匆掠过的幻象，而我带着我的疼痛站在原地。我的念头比我自己有力；它们涌进来，逼我把一生从头看遍：自从被从母亲身边带走，我始终觉得自己是个迷路的孩子，被陌生人捡去使用，他们不管我的生命于我自己是什么，只管我能为他们做什么。一切显得是疲惫的流离和心底的孤单——像被人硬拽去赴一场不指望欢乐的喜宴。而如今更糟了。我又迷了路，生怕任何陌生人留意我、同我说话。我怕这个世界。谁也不认识我；人人都会错看我。我一生见惯了太多以刻薄为乐、笑人耻辱的人。

===Original===

What could I do? This life seemed to be closing in upon me with a wall of fire﻿—everywhere there was scorching that made me shrink. The high sunlight made me shrink. And I began to think that my despair was the voice of God telling me to die. But it would take me long to die of hunger. Then I thought of my people, how they had been driven from land to land and been afflicted, and multitudes had died of misery in their wandering﻿—was I the first? And in the wars and troubles when Christians were cruelest, our fathers had sometimes slain their children and afterward themselves: it was to save them from being false apostates. That seemed to make it right for me to put an end to my life; for calamity had closed me in too, and I saw no pathway but to evil. But my mind got into war with itself, for there were contrary things in it. I knew that some had held it wrong to hasten their own death, though they were in the midst of flames; and while I had some strength left it was a longing to bear if I ought to bear﻿—else where was the good of all my life? It had not been happy since the first years: when the light came every morning I used to think, ‘I will bear it.’ But always before I had some hope; now it was gone. With these thoughts I wandered and wandered, inwardly crying to the Most High, from whom I should not flee in death more than in life﻿—though I had no strong faith that He cared for me. The strength seemed departing from my soul; deep below all my cries was the feeling that I was alone and forsaken. The more I thought the wearier I got, till it seemed I was not thinking at all, but only the sky and the river and the Eternal God were in my soul. And what was it whether I died or lived? If I lay down to die in the river, was it more than lying down to sleep?﻿—for there too I committed my soul﻿—I gave myself up. I could not bear memories any more; I could only feel what was present in me﻿—it was all one longing to cease from my weary life, which seemed only a pain outside the great peace that I might enter into. That was how it was. When the evening came and the sun was gone, it seemed as if that was all I had to wait for. And a new strength came into me to will what I would do. You know what I did. I was going to die. You know what happened﻿—did he not tell you? Faith came to me again; I was not forsaken. He told you how he found me?”
Mrs.

===Chinese===

我还能怎样呢？这种生活像四面燃起一道火墙朝我围拢——处处是叫我退缩的灼烤。高照的太阳也叫我退缩。我开始想，我的绝望就是上帝叫我死的声音。可饿死要死很久。于是我想到我的民族，他们怎样被从一地驱赶到另一地、受尽苦难，流亡途中成千上万地死于困厄——难道我是头一个？而在基督徒最残酷的那些战乱年代里，我们的先人有时先杀死自己的孩子、再结束自己：那是为了救他们不做背教的叛徒。这么一想，仿佛我便也可以结束自己的生命了；因为灾祸也把我围住了，我眼前除了通向恶的路，再没有路。可我的心自己同自己打起仗来，因为心里有相抗的东西。我知道有人在烈火之中也认定自行速死是罪；只要还剩一分力气，我便渴望该受的苦就受下去——不然我这一生的好处又在哪里？自最初几年之后，它就不曾快乐过：每天早晨光亮来时我总想：『我受着。』可从前多少还有指望；如今指望没有了。怀着这些念头，我走来走去，向至高者哀告——死也逃不开他，生也逃不开他——虽说我也并没有坚信他在乎我。力气仿佛正从我灵魂里退去；在我一切呼喊的底下，深深的，是孤单元告之感。越想越疲，到后来仿佛什么都不想了，只有天空、河流和永生的神在我灵魂里。那我死了还是活着，又有什么分别？我若躺进河里死去，岂不胜过躺下睡去？——在那里我也把灵魂交托——我把自己交出去。回忆我再也担不起了；我只感觉得到此刻在我里面的东西——那全是对结束这疲惫生命的一个渴望，这生命仿佛只是我可以进去的那大平安之外的一点疼痛。事情就是这样。傍晚来临、太阳落尽时，仿佛那就是我唯一要等的了。一股新的力气进到我里面，去定我要做的。你们知道我做了什么。我是要去死的。你们知道后来怎样——他没有告诉你们吗？信心又回到我这里；我没有被弃绝。他告诉你们他怎样找到我的了？」

===Original===

Meyrick gave no audible answer, but pressed her lips against Mirah’s forehead.
---
“She’s just a pearl; the mud has only washed her,” was the fervid little woman’s closing commentary when, tête-à-tête with Deronda in the back parlor that evening, she had conveyed Mirah’s story to him with much vividness.
“What is your feeling about a search for this mother?” said Deronda. “Have you no fears? I have, I confess.”
“Oh, I believe the mother’s good,” said Mrs. Meyrick, with rapid decisiveness; “or *was* good. She may be dead﻿—that’s my fear. A good woman, you may depend: you may know it by the scoundrel the father is. Where did the child get her goodness from? Wheaten flour has to be accounted for.”
Deronda was rather disappointed at this answer; he had wanted a confirmation of his own judgment, and he began to put in demurrers. The argument about the mother would not apply to the brother; and Mrs. Meyrick admitted that the brother might be an ugly likeness of the father. Then, as to advertising, if the name was Cohen, you might as well advertise for two undescribed terriers; and here Mrs. Meyrick helped him, for the idea of an advertisement, already mentioned to Mirah, had roused the poor child’s terror; she was convinced that her father would see it﻿—he saw everything in the papers. Certainly there were safer means than advertising; men might be set to work whose business it was to find missing persons; but Deronda wished Mrs. Meyrick to feel with him that it would be wiser to wait, before seeking a dubious﻿—perhaps a deplorable result; especially as he was engaged to go abroad the next week for a couple of months. If a search were made, he would like to be at hand, so that Mrs. Meyrick might not be unaided in meeting any consequences﻿—supposing that she would generously continue to watch over Mirah.
“We should be very jealous of anyone who took the task from us,” said Mrs. Meyrick. “She will stay under my roof; there is Hans’s old room for her.”
“Will she be content to wait?” said Deronda, anxiously.
“No trouble there. It is not her nature to run into planning and devising: only to submit. See how she submitted to that father! It was a wonder to herself how she found the will and contrivance to run away from him.

梅里克太太没有出声，只把嘴唇贴在米拉的额头上。

「她分明是一颗珍珠；泥污只不过把她洗得更亮了。」当晚，这位热肠的小妇人在后客厅同德龙达单独相对、把米拉的故事绘声绘色转述给他之后，用这句话作了收束。
「关于寻找这位母亲，你意下如何？」德龙达说。「你不担心吗？我承认我担心。」
「哦，我相信那母亲是好的，」梅里克太太斩钉截铁地说；「或者说曾经是好的。她也许死了——这才是我担心的。一个良善的女人，你只管放心：看父亲是何等恶棍就知道了。孩子的这份好，从哪儿来的？麦子总得有个来处。」
德龙达对这回答颇觉失望；他要的是对自己判断的印证，便开始提出异议。母亲那套论证套不到哥哥身上；梅里克太太也承认，那哥哥也许是父亲的丑版翻刻。至于登报寻人，倘若姓的是科恩，登启事同寻两条不加描述的小猎犬没有两样；这一点上梅里克太太帮了他——登启事的主意，先前已对米拉提过，把那可怜的孩子吓得不轻；她认定父亲准会看见——报纸上的事他什么都看得见。当然，比登报稳妥的法子也有：可以雇些以寻人为业的人去办；可德龙达希望梅里克太太同他一样感到：与其求一个可疑的——也许是可悲的——结果，不如先等一等；何况他已定于下周出国两个月。真要寻访，他也愿意在近旁，好叫梅里克太太万一有什么后果时不是孤身应付——这话自然设想着她会慨然继续照看米拉。
「谁要把这担子从我们手里抢去，我们还不依呢，」梅里克太太说。「她就住在我家屋檐下；汉斯那间旧屋子给她住。」
「她肯安心等吗？」德龙达不放心地问。
「这个不愁。她的天性不是谋划盘算的那一路：只会顺服。想想她是怎样顺服那个父亲的！能拿定主意、想出法子从他手里逃出来，连她自己都觉着是桩奇迹。

===Original===

About finding her mother, her only notion now is to trust; since you were sent to save her and we are good to her, she trusts that her mother will be found in the same unsought way. And when she is talking I catch her feeling like a child.”
Mrs. Meyrick hoped that the sum Deronda put into her hands as a provision for Mirah’s wants was more than would be needed; after a little while Mirah would perhaps like to occupy herself as the other girls did, and make herself independent. Deronda pleaded that she must need a long rest. “Oh, yes; we will hurry nothing,” said Mrs. Meyrick.
“Rely upon it, she shall be taken tender care of. If you like to give me your address abroad, I will write to let you know how we get on. It is not fair that we should have all the pleasure of her salvation to ourselves. And besides, I want to make believe that I am doing something for you as well as for Mirah.”
“That is no make-believe. What should I have done without you last night? Everything would have gone wrong. I shall tell Hans that the best of having him for a friend is, knowing his mother.”
After that they joined the girls in the other room, where Mirah was seated placidly, while the others were telling her what they knew about Mr. Deronda﻿—his goodness to Hans, and all the virtues that Hans had reported of him.
“Kate burns a pastille before his portrait every day,” said Mab. “And I carry his signature in a little black-silk bag round my neck to keep off the cramp. And Amy says the multiplication-table in his name. We must all do something extra in honor of him, now he has brought you to us.”
“I suppose he is too great a person to want anything,” said Mirah, smiling at Mab, and appealing to the graver Amy. “He is perhaps very high in the world?”
“He is very much above us in rank,” said Amy. “He is related to grand people. I dare say he leans on some of the satin cushions we prick our fingers over.”
“I am glad he is of high rank,” said Mirah, with her usual quietness.
“Now, why are you glad of that?” said Amy, rather suspicious of this sentiment, and on the watch for Jewish peculiarities which had not appeared.
“Because I have always disliked men of high rank before.”
“Oh, Mr. Deronda is not so very high,” said Kate. “He need not hinder us from thinking ill of the whole peerage and baronetage if we like.”

===Chinese===

说到找母亲，她如今唯一的念头就是信靠：既然上天差你去救了她、我们又待她好，她便信母亲也会这样不求而至地被寻见。她说话的时候，我常捕捉到她孩子似的这种心情。」
梅里克太太巴望德龙达交到她手里、作为米拉需用之资的那笔钱，用不完；过些时候米拉或许愿意像别的姑娘一样做点事，自己养活自己。德龙达则说她必定需要长长地休养一阵。「哦，是；我们什么都不催，」梅里克太太说。
「放心，她会被温柔照看的。你若肯把国外的地址留给我，我会写信告诉你我们的近况。救她的这份快乐不能叫我们一家独享。再说，我也想装作自己除了米拉、也为你做了点什么呢。」
「那不是装作。昨晚没有你们，我可怎么办？什么事都要砸的。我要对汉斯说，交到他这样一个朋友，最大的好处就是认识了他母亲。」
随后他们到另一间屋同姑娘们会合；米拉安静地坐在那里，众人正把她们知道的德龙达先生的一切讲给她听——他对汉斯的好，以及汉斯转述的他的一应美德。
「凯特每天在他的画像前点一炷香，」梅布说。「我把他的签名装在黑丝小袋里挂在脖子上，防止抽筋。艾米用他的名字念乘法表。如今他把你带来了，我们人人都得为他做点格外的事。」
「我想他是太高的人物，什么都不缺了，」米拉笑着对梅布说，又向持重的艾米求证。「他在世上想必地位很高吧？」
「论门第他在我们之上很远，」艾米说。「他同显贵人家沾亲。说不定他正靠着某匹缎面软垫，我们扎破手指地绣的就是它呢。」
「他门第高，我倒高兴，」米拉用她惯常的平静说。
「咦，这有什么可高兴的？」艾米说，对这话颇有戒心，提防着至今没有显形的犹太人的特别心性。
「因为我一向不喜欢门第高的男人。」
「哦，德龙达先生也没有那么高，」凯特说。「我们若高兴，照样可以把整个贵族从男爵爵册往坏里想，他拦不住。」

===Original===

When he entered, Mirah rose with the same look of grateful reverence that she had lifted to him the evening before: impossible to see a creature freer at once from embarrassment and boldness. Her theatrical training had left no recognizable trace; probably her manners had not much changed since she played the forsaken child at nine years of age; and she had grown up in her simplicity and truthfulness like a little flower-seed that absorbs the chance confusion of its surrounding into its own definite mould of beauty. Deronda felt that he was making acquaintance with something quite new to him in the form of womanhood. For Mirah was not childlike from ignorance: her experience of evil and trouble was deeper and stranger than his own. He felt inclined to watch her and listen to her as if she had come from a far off shore inhabited by a race different from our own.
But for that very reason he made his visit brief with his usual activity of imagination as to how his conduct might affect others, he shrank from what might seem like curiosity or the assumption of a right to know as much as he pleased of one to whom he had done a service. For example, he would have liked to hear her sing, but he would have felt the expression of such a wish to be rudeness in him﻿—since she could not refuse, and he would all the while have a sense that she was being treated like one whose accomplishments were to be ready on demand. And whatever reverence could be shown to woman, he was bent on showing to this girl. Why? He gave himself several good reasons; but whatever one does with a strong unhesitating outflow of will has a store of motive that it would be hard to put into words. Some deeds seem little more than interjections which give vent to the long passion of a life.
So Deronda soon took his farewell for the two months during which he expected to be absent from London, and in a few days he was on his way with Sir Hugo and Lady Mallinger to Leubronn.
He had fulfilled his intention of telling them about Mirah. The baronet was decidedly of opinion that the search for the mother and brother had better be let alone.

===Chinese===

他进来时，米拉站起身，脸上是前一晚向他仰起过的那种感激的敬意：再也找不出一个生灵比她更全然地不尴尬、也不放肆。戏剧训练没有在她身上留下可辨的痕迹；她那副仪态，恐怕同九岁演弃儿时没有多大分别；她就在这份单纯与真实里长大，像一粒花籽，把周遭杂乱的际遇都吸进自己那副确定的美的模子里。德龙达觉得自己正结识一种全然陌生的女性形态。因为米拉的孩子气并非出于无知：她对恶与忧患的经验，比他自己更深、更奇。他不免想注视她、听她说话，仿佛她来自一片远方的海岸，那里住着与我们不同的种族。
但正因如此，他的拜访简短——他惯常活跃地想象着自己的举动会如何影响旁人；他畏避任何看似好奇、或自命有权对一位受过他恩惠的人想知多少便知多少的嫌疑。譬如，他想听她唱歌，可他觉得表露这个愿望于他是粗鲁——因为她无从拒绝，而他又会始终自觉这等于把她当作一个才艺须随叫随到的人。而凡是人对女子所能表示的敬意，他都决意对这位姑娘尽到。为什么？他给自己举出好几条理由；可凡是出于一股坚定不疑的意志之流的事，底下总蓄着难以言宣的动机。有些行为，仿佛不过是感叹词，道出的是一生的长情。
于是德龙达很快道了别——他预计离开伦敦两个月——几天之后，他已随雨果爵士和马林格爵士夫人踏上去卢布隆（Leubronn）的旅途。
他已把米拉的事对他们讲了。从男爵明确主张，寻访母亲和哥哥的事还是搁下为好。

===Original===

Lady Mallinger was much interested in the poor girl, observing that there was a society for the conversion of the Jews, and that it was to be hoped Mirah would embrace Christianity; but perceiving that Sir Hugo looked at her with amusement, she concluded that she had said something foolish. Lady Mallinger felt apologetically about herself as a woman who had produced nothing but daughters in a case where sons were required, and hence regarded the apparent contradictions of the world as probably due to the weakness of her own understanding. But when she was much puzzled, it was her habit to say to herself, “I will ask Daniel.” Deronda was altogether a convenience in the family; and Sir Hugo too, after intending to do the best for him, had begun to feel that the pleasantest result would be to have this substitute for a son always ready at his elbow.
This was the history of Deronda, so far as he knew it, up to the time of that visit to Leubronn in which he saw Gwendolen Harleth at the gaming-table.

===Chinese===

马林格爵士夫人对这可怜的姑娘很关切，说如今有个向犹太人传教的团体，但愿米拉能皈依基督教；可她察觉雨果爵士含笑望着自己，便断定自己说了蠢话。马林格爵士夫人一向自愧身为女人，在需要儿子的地方却只生了一串女儿，因而把世上种种看似矛盾之处，多半归于自己见识的薄弱。可每逢大惑不解，她的习惯是自语一句：「我问丹尼尔去。」德龙达在这家里处处是件便利；雨果爵士也是，在有心为他作最好的打算之后，也开始觉得最惬意的结局莫过于让这个代子永远近在手边。
这便是德龙达的历史——就他自己所知而言——直到那次去卢布隆、在赌桌旁望见格温多琳·哈利斯（Gwendolen Harleth）的时候。

### XXI / 第二十一章
===Original===

> It is a common sentence that Knowledge is power; but who hath duly considered or set forth the power of Ignorance? Knowledge slowly builds up what Ignorance in an hour pulls down. Knowledge, through patient and frugal centuries, enlarges discovery and makes record of it; Ignorance, wanting its day’s dinner, lights a fire with the record, and gives a flavor to its one roast with the burned souls of many generations. Knowledge, instructing the sense, refining and multiplying needs, transforms itself into skill and makes life various with a new six days’ work; comes Ignorance drunk on the seventh, with a firkin of oil and a match and an easy “Let there not be,” and the many-colored creation is shriveled up in blackness. Of a truth, Knowledge is power, but it is a power reined by scruple, having a conscience of what must be and what may be; whereas Ignorance is a blind giant who, let him but wax unbound, would make it a sport to seize the pillars that hold up the long-wrought fabric of human good, and turn all the places of joy dark as a buried Babylon. And looking at life parcel-wise, in the growth of a single lot, who having a practiced vision may not see that ignorance of the true bond between events, and false conceit of means whereby sequences may be compelled﻿—like that falsity of eyesight which overlooks the gradations of distance, seeing that which is afar off as if it were within a step or a grasp﻿—precipitates the mistaken soul on destruction?

===Chinese===

> 知识就是力量，这是一句常言；可谁曾好好掂量、谁曾摆明过无知的力量？知识缓缓建起的，无知一个时辰便拆倒。知识，以坚忍而节俭的世纪，扩大发现并为之立档；无知，等不及当日的一餐，点一把火焚了档案，拿许多世代的焦魂给一顿烤肉添味。知识，教导感官、提炼并繁衍需求，化身为技艺，以新的六日之功使生活多彩；到了第七日，无知醉醺醺地赶来，提一小桶油、一根火柴，轻轻松松一句「不要有」——那五彩的造化便蜷缩成一团漆黑。诚然，知识是力量，可它是一种被顾忌勒住的缰绳下的力量，对何者必为、何者可为自有良知；而无知却是个瞎眼的巨人，一旦放任它挣脱束缚，它会拿拔起支撑人类福祉这座久营大厦的柱子取乐，把一切欢愉之所变成一座埋入地下的巴比伦那般黑暗。再就单个生命的成长逐段来看，凡有历练的眼力者，谁看不出：对事件之间真实纽结的无知，加上对「强制因果之法」的妄信——正如那种无视距离层次、把远在天边看作一步一握之内的视错觉——正在把迷误的灵魂急坠向毁灭？

===Original===

It was half-past ten in the morning when Gwendolen Harleth, after her gloomy journey from Leubronn, arrived at the station from which she must drive to Offendene. No carriage or friend was awaiting her, for in the telegram she had sent from Dover she had mentioned a later train, and in her impatience of lingering at a London station she had set off without picturing what it would be to arrive unannounced at half an hour’s drive from home﻿—at one of those stations which have been fixed on not as near anywhere, but as equidistant from everywhere. Deposited as a *femme sole* with her large trunks, and having to wait while a vehicle was being got from the large-sized lantern called the Railway Inn, Gwendolen felt that the dirty paint in the waiting-room, the dusty decanter of flat water, and the texts in large letters calling on her to repent and be converted, were part of the dreary prospect opened by her family troubles; and she hurried away to the outer door looking toward the lane and fields. But here the very gleams of sunshine seemed melancholy, for the autumnal leaves and grass were shivering, and the wind was turning up the feathers of a cock and two croaking hens which had doubtless parted with their grown-up offspring and did not know what to do with themselves. The railway official also seemed without resources, and his innocent demeanor in observing Gwendolen and her trunks was rendered intolerable by the cast in his eye; especially since, being a new man, he did not know her, and must conclude that she was not very high in the world. The vehicle﻿—a dirty old barouche﻿—was within sight, and was being slowly prepared by an elderly laborer. Contemptible details these, to make part of a history; yet the turn of most lives is hardly to be accounted for without them. They are continually entering with cumulative force into a mood until it gets the mass and momentum of a theory or a motive. Even philosophy is not quite free from such determining influences; and to be dropped solitary at an ugly, irrelevant-looking spot, with a sense of no income on the mind, might well prompt a man to discouraging speculation on the origin of things and the reason of a world where a subtle thinker found himself so badly off.

===Chinese===

上午十点半，格温多琳·哈利斯结束了从卢布隆出发的阴郁旅程，抵达须乘车前往奥芬迪恩的那个车站。没有马车、没有朋友等她：她从多佛拍去的电报里报的是更晚一班车，而她厌倦在伦敦车站里消磨，便提前动身，全然没有设想一声不响地回到家门口三十分钟车程之外——落在一个「不挨着任何地方、只对一切地方等距」的车站上——会是怎样一番滋味。作为一个孤零零的单身女子（femme sole），同她的一大堆箱子一道被卸下，又得等那家名叫「铁路客栈」的大号灯笼里去张罗车辆，格温多琳只觉得候车室里的脏漆皮、积灰细颈瓶里的走味清水、还有大字书写的劝她悔改归信的经文，统统是她家变故展开的凄凉前景的一部分；她赶紧逃到朝着小径和田野的外门。可在这里，连阳光的闪烁也显得愁惨：秋叶秋草在寒颤，风掀着一只公鸡和两只咯咯叫的母鸡的羽毛——它们多半已送走了长成的儿女，正不知道拿自己怎么办。铁路上的职员也显得没了主意，他打量格温多琳和她的箱子时那副无辜的神态，因他斜视的眼珠而变得难以忍受；尤其他还是个新来的，不认得她，必定断定她在世上混得不怎么样。车子——一辆肮脏的旧四轮马车——已经望得见了，正由一个上了年纪的劳工慢慢收拾。这些细节都寒碜，不配进历史；然而大多数人一生的转折，缺了它们反倒说不清。它们不断带着累积的力量涌进某种心境，直到它获得一种理论或动机的体量与动量。连哲学也难全然免于这类决定性的影响；孤身被抛在一个丑陋而 seemingly 无关紧要的地点，心头压着没有收入之感，这尽可以促人作灰心的玄想：想万物之起源，想这样一个世界的理由——一个精微的思想者在这里竟如此潦倒。

===Original===

How much more might such trifles tell on a young lady equipped for society with a fastidious taste, an Indian shawl over her arm, some twenty cubic feet of trunks by her side, and a mortal dislike to the new consciousness of poverty which was stimulating her imagination of disagreeables? At any rate they told heavily on poor Gwendolen, and helped to quell her resistant spirit. What was the good of living in the midst of hardships, ugliness, and humiliation? This was the beginning of being at home again, and it was a sample of what she had to expect.
Here was the theme on which her discontent rung its sad changes during her slow drive in the uneasy barouche, with one great trunk squeezing the meek driver, and the other fastened with a rope on the seat in front of her. Her ruling vision all the way from Leubronn had been that the family would go abroad again; for of course there must be some little income left﻿—her mamma did not mean that they would have literally nothing. To go to a dull place abroad and live poorly, was the dismal future that threatened her: she had seen plenty of poor English people abroad and imagined herself plunged in the despised dullness of their ill-plenished lives, with Alice, Bertha, Fanny and Isabel all growing up in tediousness around her, while she advanced toward thirty and her mamma got more and more melancholy. But she did not mean to submit, and let misfortune do what it would with her: she had not yet quite believed in the misfortune; but weariness and disgust with this wretched arrival had begun to affect her like an uncomfortable waking, worse than the uneasy dreams which had gone before. The self-delight with which she had kissed her image in the glass had faded before the sense of futility in being anything whatever﻿—charming, clever, resolute﻿—what was the good of it all? Events might turn out anyhow, and men were hateful. Yes, men were hateful. But in these last hours, a certain change had come over their meaning. It is one thing to hate stolen goods, and another thing to hate them the more because their being stolen hinders us from making use of them. Gwendolen had begun to be angry with Grandcourt for being what had hindered her from marrying him, angry with him as the cause of her present dreary lot.

这样的小事，对一个为社交界装备齐全、品味挑剔、臂上搭着印度披肩、身旁堆着约二十立方英尺的行李、又对贫穷的新意识——它正刺激着她对种种不快的想象——怀着死命厌恶的年轻小姐，作用该大多少倍？总之，它们沉沉压在可怜的格温多琳身上，压服了她那股倨傲的反抗精神。活在艰辛、丑陋和屈辱中间，还有什么好？这就是重新到家的开端，也是她今后日子的样本。

Gwendolen felt every word of that speech. 「恕我直言，妈妈。家庭女教师走到哪儿都受苦。我看不出在主教家里被人看低，就比在别家更舒服。何况您很清楚我恨教书。想想把我同三个笨手笨脚的姑娘——有点像艾丽斯那样的——关在一起！我宁可移民，也不当家庭教师。」

移民究竟是怎么一回事，格温多琳没有被要求解释。戴维洛太太哑口无言，看不到出路，只忧心地想着格温多琳同舅父舅母见面时可能爆发的冲突。格温多琳那倨傲抗拒的话里带着一种讳而不宣的神气，暗示她手里另有一项明确的计划；她那不断显形的一窍不通，也抹不掉母亲的信念——她信那股统治过自己的强硬意志与胆气的效力。

「我还有一些首饰，妈妈，可以卖掉，」格温多琳说。「能凑一笔钱：我要一小笔钱——好接着周转。万彻斯特的马歇尔多半肯收：我知道他有一次给我看过几只镯子，说是从一位太太手里买的。乔科莎可以替我去问。乔科莎当然要走了。可她可以先把这事办了。」

「只要办得到，她什么都肯，可怜的亲人。我还有一件事没告诉你——她要把她全部积蓄都给我——她的三百镑。我劝她去开一所小学校。她跟我们这么久了，如今再进新人家，难为她了。」

「哦，就把她推荐给主教家那三个女儿吧，」格温多琳说，脸上忽然闪过一线笑。

===Original===

“I am sure she will do better than I should.”
“Do take care not to say such things to your uncle,” said Mrs. Davilow. “He will be hurt at your despising what he has exerted himself about. But I dare say you have something else in your mind that he might not disapprove, if you consulted him.”
“There is someone else I want to consult first. Are the Arrowpoints at Quetcham still, and is Herr Klesmer there? But I daresay you know nothing about it, poor, dear mamma. Can Jeffries go on horseback with a note?”
“Oh, my dear, Jeffries is not here, and the dealer has taken the horses. But someone could go for us from Leek’s farm. The Arrowpoints are at Quetcham, I know. Miss Arrowpoint left her card the other day: I could not see her. But I don’t know about Herr Klesmer. Do you want to send before tomorrow?”
“Yes, as soon as possible. I will write a note,” said Gwendolen, rising.
“What can you be thinking of, Gwen?” said Mrs. Davilow, relieved in the midst of her wonderment by signs of alacrity and better humor.
“Don’t mind what, there’s a dear, good mamma,” said Gwendolen, reseating herself a moment to give atoning caresses. “I mean to do something. Never mind what until it is all settled. And then you shall be comforted. The dear face!﻿—it is ten years older in these three weeks. Now, now, now! don’t cry”﻿—Gwendolen, holding her mamma’s head with both hands, kissed the trembling eyelids. “But mind you don’t contradict me or put hindrances in my way. I must decide for myself. I cannot be dictated to by my uncle or anyone else. My life is my own affair. And I think”﻿—here her tone took an edge of scorn﻿—“I think I can do better for you than let you live in Sawyer’s Cottage.”
In uttering this last sentence Gwendolen again rose, and went to a desk where she wrote the following note to Klesmer:

> Miss Harleth presents her compliments to Herr Klesmer, and ventures to request of him the very great favor that he will call upon her, if possible, tomorrow. Her reason for presuming so far on his kindness is of a very serious nature. Unfortunate family circumstances have obliged her to take a course in which she can only turn for advice to the great knowledge and judgment of Herr Klesmer.
