I can travel night and day till we get there.”
Rex and Anna hurried away through the sunshine which was suddenly solemn to them, without uttering a word to each other: she chiefly possessed by solicitude about any reopening of his wound, he struggling with a tumultuary crowd of thoughts that were an offence against his better will. The tumult being undiminished when they were at the rectory gate, he said,
“Nannie, I will leave you to say everything to my father. If he wants me immediately, let me know. I shall stay in the shrubbery for ten minutes﻿—only ten minutes.”
Who has been quite free from egoistic escapes of the imagination, picturing desirable consequences on his own future in the presence of another’s misfortune, sorrow, or death? The expected promotion or legacy is the common type of a temptation which makes speech and even prayer a severe avoidance of the most insistent thoughts, and sometimes raises an inward shame, a self-distaste that is worse than any other form of unpleasant companionship. In Rex’s nature the shame was immediate, and overspread like an ugly light all the hurrying images of what might come, which thrust themselves in with the idea that Gwendolen was again free﻿—overspread them, perhaps, the more persistently because every phantasm of a hope was quickly nullified by a more substantial obstacle. Before the vision of “Gwendolen free” rose the impassable vision of “Gwendolen rich, exalted, courted;” and if in the former time, when both their lives were fresh, she had turned from his love with repugnance, what ground was there for supposing that her heart would be more open to him in the future?
These thoughts, which he wanted to master and suspend, were like a tumultuary ringing of opposing chimes that he could not escape from by running. During the last year he had brought himself into a state of calm resolve, and now it seemed that three words had been enough to undo all that difficult work, and cast him back into the wretched fluctuations of a longing which he recognized as simply perturbing and hopeless. And at this moment the activity of such longing had an untimeliness that made it repulsive to his better self. Excuse poor Rex; it was not much more than eighteen months since he had been laid low by an archer who sometimes touches his arrow with a subtle, lingering poison.

The disappointment of a youthful passion has effects as incalculable as those of smallpox which may make one person plain and a genius, another less plain and more foolish, another plain without detriment to his folly, and leave perhaps the majority without obvious change. Everything depends﻿—not on the mere fact of disappointment, but﻿—on the nature affected and the force that stirs it. In Rex’s well-endowed nature, brief as the hope had been, the passionate stirring had gone deep, and the effect of disappointment was revolutionary, though fraught with a beneficent new order which retained most of the old virtues; in certain respects he believed that it had finally determined the bias and color of his life. Now, however, it seemed that his inward peace was hardly more than that of republican Florence, and his heart no better than the alarm-bell that made work slack and tumult busy.
Rex’s love had been of that sudden, penetrating, clinging sort which the ancients knew and sung, and in singing made a fashion of talk for many moderns whose experience has by no means a fiery, demonic character. To have the consciousness suddenly steeped with another’s personality, to have the strongest inclinations possessed by an image which retains its dominance in spite of change and apart from worthiness﻿—nay, to feel a passion which clings faster for the tragic pangs inflicted by a cruel, reorganized unworthiness﻿—is a phase of love which in the feeble and common-minded has a repulsive likeness to his blind animalism insensible to the higher sway of moral affinity or heaven-lit admiration. But when this attaching force is present in a nature not of brutish unmodifiableness, but of a human dignity that can risk itself safely, it may even result in a devotedness not unfit to be called divine in a higher sense than the ancient. Phlegmatic rationality stares and shakes its head at these unaccountable prepossessions, but they exist as undeniably as the winds and waves, determining here a wreck and there a triumphant voyage.
This sort of passion had nested in the sweet-natured, strong Rex, and he had made up his mind to its companionship, as if it had been an object supremely dear, stricken dumb and helpless, and turning all the future of tenderness into a shadow of the past.

少年激情的失意，后果之不可测，好比天花：它可以让这个人变得丑陋而成为天才，让那个变得不那么丑陋却更愚蠢，让另一个丑陋而无损于他的痴愚，也许还给大多数人留下的是不见显明的变化。一切都不单系于失意这个事实，而系于被触动天性的质地，与搅动它的力量。在雷克斯禀赋丰厚的天性里，希望尽管短暂，那场激情的搅动却扎得深，失意的效果是革命性的——尽管携来一种有益的新秩序，还保留着旧日美德的大半；在某些方面他相信，它已最终决定了他一生的偏向与色泽。可现在看来，他内心的太平，也不过相当于共和制的佛罗伦萨；他的心，也不比那口叫工作停顿、骚乱忙碌的警钟更好。
雷克斯的爱属于那种突发的、钻入的、缠附的爱，古人懂得它、歌咛它，并在歌咛中替许多现代人造就了一种谈资——那些人的经历，实在没有一点火烈的、魔性的品质。意识忽然被另一个人的人格浸透；最强的意向被一个形象占据，那形象不顾变迁、无关价值地保住它的统治；不宁唯是，还感到一种激情，因残忍的、重加组织的无价值所加的惨痛而缠附得更紧——这是爱的一个阶段，在孱弱与庸俗的心里，它有令人憎恶的相像：像人盲目的兽性，感不到道德亲合力或上天点亮的倾慕有更高的统辖。可当这种附着力存在于一种并非冥顽难改、而具有敢于冒险的人格尊严的天性里，它甚至可以结出一种奉献，称作神圣也不为过——在比古人更高的意义上。冷静的理性暲着眼、摇着头，看这些无从解释的先入之见；可它们的存在，同风与浪一样无可否认——在这里注定一场沉船，在那里注定一次凯旋的航行。
这样的激情，已在性情温厚、筋骨强健的雷克斯身上筑了巢；他已打定主意与它相伴，仿佛它是一件至亲至爱的东西，遭了殃，哑了，无助了，把日后一切温情的未来，都变成了过去的影子。

But he had also made up his mind that his life was not to be pauperized because he had had to renounce one sort of joy; rather, he had begun life again with a new counting-up of the treasures that remained to him, and he had even felt a release of power such as may come from ceasing to be afraid of your own neck.
And now, here he was pacing the shrubbery, angry with himself that the sense of irrevocableness in his lot, which ought in reason to have been as strong as ever, had been shaken by a change of circumstances that could make no change in relation to him. He told himself the truth quite roughly,

I am exactly of no consequence at all, and am not likely to be of much consequence till my head is turning gray. But what has that to do with it? She would not have me on any terms, and I would not ask her. It is a meanness to be thinking about it now﻿—no better than lurking about the battlefield to strip the dead; but there never was more gratuitous sinning. I have nothing to gain there﻿—absolutely nothing. Then why can’t I face the facts, and behave as they demand, instead of leaving my father to suppose that there are matters he can’t speak to me about, though I might be useful in them?”
The last thought made one wave with the impulse that sent Rex walking firmly into the house and through the open door of the study, where he saw his father packing a traveling-desk.
“Can I be of any use, sir?” said Rex, with rallied courage, as his father looked up at him.

But no doubt the arrangements of the will lately made are satisfactory, and there may possibly be an heir yet to be born. In any case, I feel confident that Gwendolen will be liberally﻿—I should expect, splendidly﻿—provided for.”
“It must have been a great shock for her,” said Rex, getting more resolute after the first twinge had been borne. “I suppose he was a devoted husband.”
“No doubt of it,” said the rector, in his most decided manner. “Few men of his position would have come forward as he did under the circumstances.”
Rex had never seen Grandcourt, had never been spoken to about him by anyone of the family, and knew nothing of Gwendolen’s flight from her suitor to Leubronn. He only knew that Grandcourt, being very much in love with her, had made her an offer in the first weeks of her sudden poverty, and had behaved very handsomely in providing for her mother and sisters. That was all very natural and what Rex himself would have liked to do. Grandcourt had been a lucky fellow, and had had some happiness before he got drowned. Yet Rex wondered much whether Gwendolen had been in love with the successful suitor, or had only forborne to tell him that she hated being made love to.

===Chinese===

不过，新立的那份遗嘱的安排，想必是妥帖的，说不定还会有一位尚待出世的继承人。无论如何，我确信格温多琳会得到慷慨的——我该说，极尽豪奢的——供养。」
「这对她一定是个巨大的打击，」雷克斯说；熬过最初的刺痛之后，他话音更坚定了。「我想，他该是个深情尽职的丈夫吧。」
「毫无疑问，」牧师以他最断然的口气说。「处在他那种地位的人，肯像他那样在那种情形下挺身而出的，没有几个。」
雷克斯从未见过格兰考特，家里人从没有谁同他谈起过此人，也不知道格温多琳当年为躲避求婚者逃往卢布隆的事。他只知道：格兰考特深爱着她，在她骤然落难的头几个星期里向她求婚，并且慷慨周到地供养她的母亲和姐妹。这一切都很自然，也正是雷克斯自己愿意做的。格兰考特是个有福气的人，溺水之前也享过几分幸福。只是雷克斯很纳闷：格温多琳究竟爱没爱过这位得胜的求婚者，还是仅仅忍着没告诉他——她讨厌被人追求。

### LIX / 第五十九章
===Original===

> I count myself in nothing else so happy

As in a soul remembering my good friends.

===Chinese===

> 我自认在别的事上都不曾这样幸福，

如同在一个灵魂里记挂着我各位好友。

===Original===

Sir Hugo Mallinger was not so prompt in starting for Genoa as Mr. Gascoigne had been, and Deronda on all accounts would not take his departure until he had seen the baronet. There was not only Grandcourt’s death, but also the late crisis in his own life to make reasons why his oldest friend would desire to have the unrestrained communication of speech with him, for in writing he had not felt able to give any details concerning the mother who had come and gone like an apparition. It was not till the fifth evening that Deronda, according to telegram, waited for Sir Hugo at the station, where he was to arrive between eight and nine; and while he was looking forward to the sight of the kind, familiar face, which was part of his earliest memories, something like a smile, in spite of his late tragic experience, might have been detected in his eyes and the curve of his lips at the idea of Sir Hugo’s pleasure in being now master of his estates, able to leave them to his daughters, or at least﻿—according to a view of inheritance which had just been strongly impressed on Deronda’s imagination﻿—to take makeshift feminine offspring as intermediate to a satisfactory heir in a grandson. We should be churlish creatures if we could have no joy in our fellow-mortals’ joy, unless it were in agreement with our theory of righteous distribution and our highest ideal of human good: what sour corners our mouths would get﻿—our eyes, what frozen glances! and all the while our own possessions and desires would not exactly adjust themselves to our ideal. We must have some comradeship with imperfection; and it is, happily, possible to feel gratitude even where we discern a mistake that may have been injurious, the vehicle of the mistake being an affectionate intention prosecuted through a lifetime of kindly offices. Deronda’s feeling and judgment were strongly against the action of Sir Hugo in making himself the agent of a falsity﻿—yes, a falsity: he could give no milder name to the concealment under which he had been reared. But the baronet had probably had no clear knowledge concerning the mother’s breach of trust, and with his light, easy way of taking life, had held it a reasonable preference in her that her son should be made an English gentleman, seeing that she had the eccentricity of not caring to part from her child, and be to him as if she were not.

===Chinese===

雨果·马林格爵士（Sir Hugo Mallinger）动身来热那亚（Genoa），不像加斯科因先生那样迅捷；而德龙达无论如何也要见过从男爵才肯离开。不单是格兰考特之死，还有他自己近来那场人生的剧变，都足以叫这位最老的朋友想要同他毫无拘束地面谈；因为写信时，关于那位来去如幽灵一般的母亲，他觉得无法细说。直到第五天晚上，德龙达才按电报约定到车站去等雨果爵士——火车八点到九点之间到；他盼着见到那张和善的、他最早记忆里便有的熟面孔；尽管新近经历了悲剧，想到爵士此刻那份得意——终于做了自己领地的主人，可以把领地传给女儿们了，或者至少——按一种刚在德龙达想象里烙下深印的继承观——先拿将就的女性后裔垫一垫，等孙子辈再得个满意的继承人——他的眼睛里、唇角的弧线里，还是看得出一点近乎微笑的东西。倘若我们不能因同胞的快乐而快乐，除非那快乐恰好合乎我们关于正义分配的理论、合乎我们的人类至善理想，那我们可就成了刻薄鬼了：否则我们的嘴角会撇出多少酸相——我们的眼睛会射出多少冰冷的光！而与此同时，我们自己的财产与欲望，也未必就恰恰摆得合乎我们的理想。我们总得同不完美有点情谊；所幸，即使看出一个也许害过人的错处，也仍可能心怀感激——只要那错处的载体，是一片经由一生仁厚的照拂而贯彻下来的慈爱之心。德龙达的情感与判断都强烈反对雨果爵士的做法——他使自己成为一桩虚假的经办人；是的，一桩虚假：对于自己从小被养育在其中的那桩隐瞒，他想不出更轻的名称。可从男爵多半并不清楚那位母亲背弃信托的内情；而以他那轻快随和的处世之道，他觉得她的偏爱也算合情合理：既然她古怪到不肯同孩子分开、却又要做一个形同不在的母亲，那把儿子造成一个英国绅士，也算是好办法。

===Original===

Daniel’s affectionate gratitude toward Sir Hugo made him wish to find grounds of excuse rather than blame; for it is as possible to be rigid in principle and tender in blame, as it is to suffer from the sight of things hung awry, and yet to be patient with the hanger who sees amiss. If Sir Hugo in his bachelorhood had been beguiled into regarding children chiefly as a product intended to make life more agreeable to the full-grown, whose convenience alone was to be consulted in the disposal of them﻿—why, he had shared an assumption which, if not formally avowed, was massively acted on at that date of the world’s history; and Deronda, with all his keen memory of the painful inward struggle he had gone through in his boyhood, was able also to remember the many signs that his experience had been entirely shut out from Sir Hugo’s conception. Ignorant kindness may have the effect of cruelty; but to be angry with it as if it were direct cruelty would be an ignorant *un*kindness, the most remote from Deronda’s large imaginative lenience toward others. And perhaps now, after the searching scenes of the last ten days, in which the curtain had been lifted for him from the secrets of lives unlike his own, he was more than ever disposed to check that rashness of indignation or resentment which has an unpleasant likeness to the love of punishing. When he saw Sir Hugo’s familiar figure descending from the railway carriage, the lifelong affection which had been well accustomed to make excuses, flowed in and submerged all newer knowledge that might have seemed fresh ground for blame.
“Well, Dan,” said Sir Hugo, with a serious fervor, grasping Deronda’s hand. He uttered no other words of greeting; there was too strong a rush of mutual consciousness. The next thing was to give orders to the courier, and then to propose walking slowly in the mild evening, there being no hurry to get to the hotel.
“I have taken my journey easily, and am in excellent condition,” he said, as he and Deronda came out under the starlight, which was still faint with the lingering sheen of day. “I didn’t hurry in setting off, because I wanted to inquire into things a little, and so I got sight of your letter to Lady Mallinger before I started. But now, how is the widow?”
“Getting calmer,” said Deronda.

===Chinese===

丹尼尔对雨果爵士怀着深情的感激，使他宁愿找出开脱而非责备的依据；因为原则上一丝不苟、责备时却心存温厚，原是可能的——正如看见挂歪的东西会难受，却仍能容忍那个眼里看不出歪的悬挂者。倘若雨果爵士在独身岁月里被引入了这样一种看法——孩子主要是一种产品，为使成年人的生活更惬意，处置他们时只消考虑大人的方便——那么，他所信奉的这一假设，纵然没人正式宣示，在那个世界历史的年代也正是被大规模奉行着的；而德龙达，纵然痛切记得自己少年时代经历的那些内心挣扎，也同样记得种种迹象：他这份体验，在雨果爵士的设想里是全然缺席的。无知的仁慈可能产生残酷的效果；可若因此对它发怒、当它是直接的残酷，那便是一种无知的冷酷——这与德龙达对他人那种宽厚的、设身处地的宽仁相去最远。或许，经过这十天来一幕幕拷问灵魂的场景——幕布为他揭开，露出与他全然不同的生命的秘密——他比以往任何时候都更愿意克制那种愤慨或怨怒的轻率；那种轻率同嗜罚之爱有着不愉快的相似。当他看见雨果爵士熟悉的身影从车厢里下来，那份一生惯于制造借口的爱便涌了进来，把一切新得的、似乎可作责备之据的认知都淹没了。
「好啊，丹。」雨果爵士握住德龙达的手，说得恳切而郑重。他没有再说什么寒暄的话；彼此心照不宣的洪流太急了。接着便是向随行的仆役交代事项，然后提议趁着温和的夜色慢慢散步走回去——赶去旅馆并不急。
「我一路走得从容，状态好极了。」他说着，同德龙达一道走进星光里；星光还淡淡带着白昼的余晖。「动身前我没赶急，因为想先把事情打听清楚些，所以见到了你写给马林格夫人的信。现在说说——那位遗孀怎么样？」
「渐渐安静下来了。」德龙达说。

===Original===

“She seems to be escaping the bodily illness that one might have feared for her, after her plunge and terrible excitement. Her uncle and mother came two days ago, and she is being well taken care of.”
“Any prospect of an heir being born?”
“From what Mr. Gascoigne said to me, I conclude not. He spoke as if it were a question whether the widow would have the estates for her life.”
“It will not be much of a wrench to her affections, I fancy, this loss of the husband?” said Sir Hugo, looking round at Deronda.
“The suddenness of the death has been a great blow to her,” said Deronda, quietly evading the question.
“I wonder whether Grandcourt gave her any notion what were the provisions of his will?” said Sir Hugo.
“Do you know what they are, sir?” parried Deronda.
“Yes, I do,” said the baronet, quickly. “Gad! if there is no prospect of a legitimate heir, he has left everything to a boy he had by a Mrs. Glasher; you know nothing about the affair, I suppose, but she was a sort of wife to him for a good many years, and there are three older children﻿—girls. The boy is to take his father’s name; he is Henleigh already, and he is to be Henleigh Mallinger Grandcourt. The Mallinger will be of no use to him, I am happy to say; but the young dog will have more than enough with his fourteen years’ minority﻿—no need to have had holes filled up with my fifty thousand for Diplow that he had no right to: and meanwhile my beauty, the young widow, is to put up with a poor two thousand a year and the house at Gadsmere﻿—a nice kind of banishment for her if she chose to shut herself up there, which I don’t think she will. The boy’s mother has been living there of late years. I’m perfectly disgusted with Grandcourt. I don’t know that I’m obliged to think the better of him because he’s drowned, though, so far as my affairs are concerned, nothing in his life became him like the leaving it.”
“In my opinion he did wrong when he married this wife﻿—not in leaving his estates to the son,” said Deronda, rather dryly.
“I say nothing against his leaving the land to the lad,” said Sir Hugo; “but since he had married this girl he ought to have given her a handsome provision, such as she could live on in a style fitted to the rank he had raised her to. She ought to have had four or five thousand a year and the London house for her life; that’s what I should have done for her.

「她落水又受了那么大的惊骇，原本怕她病倒，看来是躲过去了。她舅父和母亲两天前到了，她被照料得很好。」
「有希望添个继承人么？」
「照加斯科因先生对我说的，我看没有。他的口气，像是遗孀能否终身享有这些领地还在两可之间。」

「知道，我知道。」从男爵立刻说。「天哪！既然没有合法继承人的指望，他把一切都留给了一个他同格拉舍夫人生的儿子；这事你大概一无所知吧——她同他算是多年的事实夫妻，前头还有三个孩子——都是女孩。那男孩要姓父亲的姓；他已经叫亨利了，往后就叫亨利·马林格·格兰考特（Henleigh Mallinger Grandcourt）。我倒欣慰，「马林格」这姓对他没什么用处；可那小子未成年还有十四年，家业尽够他受用了——犯不着再拿我那五万镑去填迪普洛（Diplow）的窟窿，那本是他无权得的：与此同时，我的美人儿，那位年轻遗孀，只好将就一年区区两千镑，外加加兹米尔（Gadsmere）的那所宅子——她若肯把自己关在那里，倒是一种不错的放逐，不过我看她不会。那孩子的母亲近几年就住在那儿。我对格兰考特恶心透了。我不觉得他淹死了我就有义务高看他一眼；不过就我的事而论，他这一生里，没有一件事比他的死更成全他的体面。」
「依我看，他错在娶了这位妻子——而不在把领地留给儿子。」德龙达说，语气颇为干涩。

I suppose, as she was penniless, her friends couldn’t stand out for a settlement, else it’s ill trusting to the will a man may make after he’s married. Even a wise man generally lets some folly ooze out of him in his will﻿—my father did, I know; and if a fellow has any spite or tyranny in him, he’s likely to bottle off a good deal for keeping in that sort of document. It’s quite clear Grandcourt meant that his death should put an extinguisher on his wife, if she bore him no heir.”
“And, in the other case, I suppose everything would have been reversed﻿—illegitimacy would have had the extinguisher?” said Deronda, with some scorn.
“Precisely﻿—Gadsmere and the two thousand. It’s queer. One nuisance is that Grandcourt has made me an executor; but seeing he was the son of my only brother, I can’t refuse to act. And I shall mind it less if I can be of any use to the widow. Lush thinks she was not in ignorance about the family under the rose, and the purport of the will. He hints that there was no very good understanding between the couple. But I fancy you are the man who knew most about what Mrs. Grandcourt felt or did not feel﻿—eh, Dan?” Sir Hugo did not put this question with his usual jocoseness, but rather with a lowered tone of interested inquiry; and Deronda felt that any evasion would be misinterpreted. He answered gravely,
“She was certainly not happy. They were unsuited to each other. But as to the disposal of the property﻿—from all I have seen of her, I should predict that she will be quite contented with it.”
“Then she is not much like the rest of her sex; that’s all I can say,” said Sir Hugo, with a slight shrug. “However, she ought to be something extraordinary, for there must be an entanglement between your horoscope and hers﻿—eh? When that tremendous telegram came, the first thing Lady Mallinger said was, ‘How very strange that it should be Daniel who sends it!’ But I have had something of the same sort in my own life. I was once at a foreign hotel where a lady had been left by her husband without money. When I heard of it, and came forward to help her, who should she be but an early flame of mine, who had been fool enough to marry an Austrian baron with a long mustache and short affection? But it was an affair of my own that called me there﻿—nothing to do with knight-errantry, any more than you coming to Genoa had to do with the Grandcourts.”

「我料想，因为她身无分文，她的亲友们也没法坚持要一份财产约定；再说，男人婚后会立下什么样的遗嘱，实在难以逆料。连聪明人通常也要在遗嘱里渗出几分糊涂——我知道我父亲就是；一个人心里若存着怨毒或专虐，多半要在那种文书里封存起不少。明摆着，格兰考特打定了主意：倘使妻子不给他生继承人，他的死就该像罩子一样把她罩灭。」
「那么换个情形，想必一切就倒转过来——被罩灭的就是那私生子了？」德龙达说，带着几分讥诮。
「正是——加兹米尔加两千镑。说来也怪。有一桩烦人的事：格兰考特指定我做遗嘱执行人；可他是我惟一的兄弟的儿子，我没法拒绝履职。而若能帮上那位遗孀什么，做起来也就不那么硌硬。拉什认为，对这桩私底下的家事、对遗嘱的用意，她并非一无所知。他暗示这两口子感情不睦。不过我琢磨着，格兰考特夫人心里有什么、没什么，知道得最多的人该是你——呃，丹？」这一问，雨果爵士没有用他惯常的打趣口吻，倒压低了声音，是一副关切的探询；德龙达觉得再闪避就会被误解了。他郑重答道：
「她确实不幸福。他们两个彼此不合适。至于财产的处置——就我对她的全部了解，我可以断言：她会对这份处置相当知足。」
「那她可不大像她的同性；我只能这么说。」雨果爵士说着，微微一耸肩。「不过，她本该是个非凡的人物，因为你的命盘同她的命盘之间必有纠缠——呃？那封惊人的电报到时，马林格夫人口里第一句话就是：『偏偏是丹尼尔发来的，多奇怪啊！』不过我自己也遇到过类似的事。有一次我在国外一家旅馆，那里有位夫人被丈夫丢下，身无分文。我听说之后上前帮忙，你道她是谁？竟是我早年的一个相好，当年糊涂到嫁了个奥地利男爵——胡子老长，情分奇短。可把我引到那里去的，是我自己的一桩事——同游侠行径毫不相干，正如你来热那亚，同格兰考特家也毫不相干。」

===Original===

There was silence for a little while. Sir Hugo had begun to talk of the Grandcourts as the less difficult subject between himself and Deronda; but they were both wishing to overcome a reluctance to perfect frankness on the events which touched their relation to each other. Deronda felt that his letter, after the first interview with his mother, had been rather a thickening than a breaking of the ice, and that he ought to wait for the first opening to come from Sir Hugo. Just when they were about to lose sight of the port, the baronet turned, and pausing as if to get a last view, said in a tone of more serious feeling﻿—“And about the main business of your coming to Genoa, Dan? You have not been deeply pained by anything you have learned, I hope? There is nothing that you feel need change your position in any way? You know, whatever happens to you must always be of importance to me.”
“I desire to meet your goodness by perfect confidence, sir,” said Deronda. “But I can’t answer those questions truly by a simple yes or no. Much that I have heard about the past has pained me. And it has been a pain to meet and part with my mother in her suffering state, as I have been compelled to do. But it is no pain﻿—it is rather a clearing up of doubts for which I am thankful, to know my parentage. As to the effect on my position, there will be no change in my gratitude to you, sir, for the fatherly care and affection you have always shown me. But to know that I was born a Jew, may have a momentous influence on my life, which I am hardly able to tell you of at present.”
Deronda spoke the last sentence with a resolve that overcame some diffidence. He felt that the differences between Sir Hugo’s nature and his own would have, by-and-by, to disclose themselves more markedly than had ever yet been needful. The baronet gave him a quick glance, and turned to walk on. After a few moments’ silence, in which he had reviewed all the material in his memory which would enable him to interpret Deronda’s words, he said,
“I have long expected something remarkable from you, Dan; but, for God’s sake, don’t go into any eccentricities! I can tolerate any man’s difference of opinion, but let him tell it me without getting himself up as a lunatic. At this stage of the world, if a man wants to be taken seriously, he must keep clear of melodrama. Don’t misunderstand me.

===Chinese===

一时都沉默了。雨果爵士先谈起格兰考特家，是把它当作两人之间较不难启齿的话题；可他们俩都盼着克服那层不情愿，把牵动彼此关系的事谈个彻底坦白。德龙达觉得，与母亲第一次会面后他写的那封信，与其说打破了坚冰，不如说把冰加厚了；他该等雨果爵士先开口。就在港口即将隐没于视线时，从男爵转过身，停住脚，像要再看最后一眼，用一种郑重了许多的声调说——「还有，丹，你来热那亚的正事呢？你没有因为得知的事深深痛苦吧，我希望？没有什么你觉得需要改变你的地位的吧？你知道，无论你遭逢什么，对我永远都关系重大。」
「我愿以彻底的坦白来回报您的好意，爵士。」德龙达说。「可这几个问题，我没法简单地用是或不是来如实回答。我听到的许多往事，让我痛苦。而我母亲在那种苦况里，我不得不与她相见、又相别，这也是痛苦。但知道自己的血统，不是痛苦——倒是一种疑团的廓清，我为此感激。至于对我地位的影响：我对您的感激不会有任何改变，爵士，您一向待我如父亲般关爱。但知道了我生来是犹太人，这或许会对我的一生发生重大影响——这一点，我眼下还难以向您细说。」
末了一句，德龙达是以压过几分怯意的决心说出的。他感到，雨果爵士的天性同他自己的天性之间的差异，不久便要显露得比以往任何时候都更分明。从男爵迅疾地瞥了他一眼，转身继续走。片刻沉默——他在心里把记忆里可供解读德龙达这话的材料过了一遍——然后说：
「我早就料到你会干出些不寻常的事来，丹；可是看在上帝份上，可别搞什么乖僻行径！一个人见解同我不同，我都能容；但请他把见解告诉我时，别把自己装扮成个疯子。在当今这个世道，一个男人若要被人当真，就得离耸人听闻的戏码远一点。别误会我。

===Original===

I am not suspecting you of setting up any lunacy on your own account. I only think you might easily be led arm in arm with a lunatic, especially if he wanted defending. You have a passion for people who are pelted, Dan. I’m sorry for them too; but so far as company goes, it’s a bad ground of selection. However, I don’t ask you to anticipate your inclination in anything you have to tell me. When you make up your mind to a course that requires money, I have some sixteen thousand pounds that have been accumulating for you over and above what you have been having the interest of as income. And now I am come, I suppose you want to get back to England as soon as you can?”
“I must go first to Mainz to get away a chest of my grandfather’s, and perhaps to see a friend of his,” said Deronda. “Although the chest has been lying there these twenty years, I have an unreasonable sort of nervous eagerness to get it away under my care, as if it were more likely now than before that something might happen to it. And perhaps I am the more uneasy, because I lingered after my mother left, instead of setting out immediately. Yet I can’t regret that I was here﻿—else Mrs. Grandcourt would have had none but servants to act for her.”
“Yes, yes,” said Sir Hugo, with a flippancy which was an escape of some vexation hidden under his more serious speech; “I hope you are not going to set a dead Jew above a living Christian.”
Deronda colored, and repressed a retort. They were just turning into the Italia.

「我不是疑心你自己要发什么疯。我只是想，你很容易被人挽着胳膊、同一个疯子并肩走去——尤其是那疯子需要有人护卫的时候。你对挨石子的人有一种热情，丹。我也可怜他们；但要说择伴，这可是个糟糕的标准。不过，你要告诉我的事，我不催你抢在心意之前说。等你拿定了主意、要走一条需要钱的路，我这里有一万六千镑左右，是为你攒下的，此外还有你一向取息当收入的那笔。现在我人既然来了，想必你想尽快回英国去吧？」

===Original===

> But I shall say no more of this at this time; for this is to be felt and not to be talked of; and they who never touched it with their fingers may secretly perhaps laugh at it in their hearts and be never the wiser.

> The Roman Emperor in the legend put to death ten learned Israelites to avenge the sale of Joseph by his brethren. And there have always been enough of his kidney, whose piety lies in punishing who can see the justice of grudges but not of gratitude. For you shall never convince the stronger feeling that it hath not the stronger reason, or incline him who hath no love to believe that there is good ground for loving. As we may learn from the order of word-making, wherein *love* precedeth *lovable*.

===Chinese===

> 这件事此时我不愿再多说；因为这是要用心去感受、不是用嘴去谈论的；而那些从未用手指触碰过它的人，心里或许暗暗发笑，却永远不会变得更明白。

> 传说中的罗马皇帝处死了十位博学的以色列人，为约瑟被兄弟们卖掉一事报仇。与他同一副心肠的人从来不缺：他们的虔诚在于惩罚，看得见宿怨的正当、却看不见感恩的正当。因为你永远无法让较强的情感相信它没有较强的理由，也无法让没有爱心的人相信爱有充分的根据。这一点我们从造词的先后便可学到：love 先于 lovable——先有爱，才有可爱。

When Deronda presented his letter at the banking-house in the Schuster Strasse at Mainz, and asked for Joseph Kalonymos, he was presently shown into an inner room, where, seated at a table arranging open letters, was the white-bearded man whom he had seen the year before in the synagogue at Frankfort. He wore his hat﻿—it seemed to be the same old felt hat as before﻿—and near him was a packed portmanteau with a wrap and overcoat upon it. On seeing Deronda enter he rose, but did not advance or put out his hand. Looking at him with small penetrating eyes which glittered like black gems in the midst of his yellowish face and white hair, he said in German,
“Good! It is now you who seek me, young man.”
“Yes; I seek you with gratitude, as a friend of my grandfather’s,” said Deronda, “and I am under an obligation to you for giving yourself much trouble on my account.” He spoke without difficulty in that liberal German tongue which takes many strange accents to its maternal bosom.
Kalonymos now put out his hand and said cordially, “So you are no longer angry at being something more than an Englishman?”
“On the contrary. I thank you heartily for helping to save me from remaining in ignorance of my parentage, and for taking care of the chest that my grandfather left in trust for me.”
“Sit down, sit down,” said Kalonymos, in a quick undertone, seating himself again, and pointing to a chair near him. Then deliberately laying aside his hat and showing a head thickly covered, with white hair, he stroked and clutched his beard while he looked examiningly at the young face before him. The moment wrought strongly on Deronda’s imaginative susceptibility: in the presence of one linked still in zealous friendship with the grandfather whose hope had yearned toward him when he was unborn, and who, though dead, was yet to speak with him in those written memorials which, says Milton, “contain a potency of life in them to be as active as that soul whose progeny they are,” he seemed to himself to be touching the electric chain of his own ancestry; and he bore the scrutinizing look of Kalonymos with a delighted awe, something like what one feels in the solemn commemoration of acts done long ago but still telling markedly on the life of today.

===Chinese===

德龙达在美因茨（Mainz）舒斯特街的银行里递上引荐信、求见约瑟夫·卡洛尼莫斯，随即被引进一间内室；室内桌旁坐着一位白须老者，正整理着拆开的信件——正是他去年在法兰克福犹太会堂（synagogue）里见过的那个人。他头上戴着帽子——似乎还是从前那顶旧毡帽——身边放着一只收拾好的旅行箱，上面搭着围巾和大衣。见德龙达进来，他站起身，却没有迎上来，也没有伸手。他用那双细小而锐利的眼睛打量他——那眼睛在他微黄的脸庞和白发的中央，像两粒黑宝石般闪光——他用德语说：
「好！如今是你来寻我了，年轻人。」
「是；我怀着感激来寻您，作为我外祖父的朋友。」德龙达说，「您为我费了许多心力，我欠着您的情。」他说得毫不费力，用的正是德语——那宽厚的母性语言，什么样的异乡口音都揽进怀抱。
卡洛尼莫斯这才伸出手来，热忱地说：「这么说，你不再为『不止是个英国人』而恼火了？」
「恰恰相反。我衷心感激您，帮我免于对自己的血统一生无知，又替我保管了外祖父遗托给我的那口柜子。」
「坐，坐。」卡洛尼莫斯低声急促地说，自己重新坐下，指了指身旁的椅子。然后他慢条斯理摘下帽子，露出一头浓密的白发，一面捻着、拢着胡须，一面端详面前这张年轻的脸。这一刻深深撼动了德龙达善感的想象：眼前这位老者，至今还以炽热的友谊维系着那位外祖父——那希望在他尚未出生时就已渴慕着他——而外祖父虽死，却还要借那些书面的遗记同他说话；用弥尔顿的话说，那些文字「内含生命的潜能，其活跃一如孕育它们的那个灵魂」。此刻他仿佛触摸着自己血统的电流之链；他怀着欣然的敬畏承受卡洛尼莫斯的审视，那感觉有些像人们在庄严追念往昔功业时的情味——那些功业虽已久远，至今仍显著地影响着当下的人生。

===Original===

Impossible for men of duller fibre﻿—men whose affection is not ready to diffuse itself through the wide travel of imagination, to comprehend, perhaps even to credit this sensibility of Deronda’s; but it subsisted, like their own dullness, notwithstanding their lack of belief in it﻿—and it gave his face an expression which seemed very satisfactory to the observer.
He said in Hebrew, quoting from one of the fine hymns in the Hebrew liturgy, “As thy goodness has been great to the former generations, even so may it be to the latter.” Then after pausing a little he began, “Young man, I rejoice that I was not yet set off again on my travels, and that you are come in time for me to see the image of my friend as he was in his youth﻿—no longer perverted from the fellowship of your people﻿—no longer shrinking in proud wrath from the touch of him who seemed to be claiming you as a Jew. You come with thankfulness yourself to claim the kindred and heritage that wicked contrivance would have robbed you of. You come with a willing soul to declare, ‘I am the grandson of Daniel Charisi.’ Is it not so?”
“Assuredly it is,” said Deronda. “But let me say that I should at no time have been inclined to treat a Jew with incivility simply because he was a Jew. You can understand that I shrank from saying to a stranger, ‘I know nothing of my mother.’ ”
“A sin, a sin!” said Kalonymos, putting up his hand and closing his eyes in disgust. “A robbery of our people﻿—as when our youths and maidens were reared for the Roman Edom. But it is frustrated. I have frustrated it. When Daniel Charisi﻿—may his Rock and his Redeemer guard him!﻿—when Daniel Charisi was a stripling and I was a lad little above his shoulder, we made a solemn vow always to be friends. He said, ‘Let us bind ourselves with duty, as if we were sons of the same mother.’ That was his bent from first to last﻿—as he said, to fortify his soul with bonds. It was a saying of his, ‘Let us bind love with duty; for duty is the love of law; and law is the nature of the Eternal.’ So we bound ourselves. And though we were much apart in our later life, the bond has never been broken. When he was dead, they sought to rob him; but they could not rob him of me. I rescued that remainder of him which he had prized and preserved for his offspring. And I have restored to him the offspring they had robbed him of.

对于神经迟钝一些的人——那些感情不惯于随想象的远游而弥散的人——要理解、甚至要相信德龙达这份敏感是不可能的；可这份敏感并不因他们不信就不存在，正如他们的迟钝也并不因无人宣告而消失——它给他的脸添了一种神情，看在端详者眼里似乎极为熨帖。
他用希伯来语开了口，引的是希伯来礼仪书中一首优美的圣诗：「你的慈爱怎样临到先前的世代，愿它也怎样临到后来的世代。」顿了顿，他才开口：「年轻人，我很庆幸自己还没再度启程远游，你来得正巧，让我能看见我朋友年轻时的形象——不再被人带离你民族的怀抱——不再因高傲的恼怒，躲避那看似要把你认作犹太人的人的触碰。如今你自己怀着感激来认领这份亲缘与产业——那恶毒的计谋本要把它从你手里夺走。你带着甘愿的灵魂来宣告：『我是丹尼尔·查里西的外孙。』是不是这样？」
「确实如此。」德龙达说。「但请容我说一句：无论如何，我都不会仅因对方是犹太人便对他无礼。您能理解，我不愿对一个陌生人说出『我对我母亲一无所知』。」
「罪过，罪过！」卡洛尼莫斯说着，举起一只手，厌恶地闭上眼睛。「那是对我们民族的劫掠——就像我们的少年男女被养大了去归罗马的以东一样。可这劫掠落了空。是我使它落了空的。当年丹尼尔·查里西——愿他的磐石、他的救赎主守护他！——当年查里西还是个小伙子、我还是个刚过他肩头的孩子时，我们立下庄严的誓约，要做终身的朋友。他说：『让我们用义务彼此约束，如同同一位母亲所生。』这是他从始至终的秉性——用他自己的话说，用纽带加固灵魂。他有句格言：『让爱受义务的约束；因为义务是对律法的爱；而律法是永恒者的本性。』我们就这样彼此缔结了。后来的人生里我们相隔两地的时候多，这纽带却从未断过。他死后，有人想劫掠他；但他们劫不走我。我抢救下了他那一份遗存——他最珍重、特意留给后嗣的东西。我也把被人从他那里夺走的后嗣，归还给了他。我这就把柜子给你取来。」

===Original===

I will bring you the chest forthwith.”
Kalonymos left the room for a few minutes, and returned with a clerk who carried the chest, set it down on the floor, drew off a leather cover, and went out again. It was not very large, but was made heavy by ornamental bracers and handles of gilt iron. The wood was beautifully incised with Arabic lettering.
“So!” said Kalonymos, returning to his seat. “And here is the curious key,” he added, taking it from a small leathern bag. “Bestow it carefully. I trust you are methodic and wary.” He gave Deronda the monitory and slightly suspicious look with which age is apt to commit any object to the keeping of youth.
“I shall be more careful of this than of any other property,” said Deronda, smiling and putting the key in his breast-pocket. “I never before possessed anything that was a sign to me of so much cherished hope and effort. And I shall never forget that the effort was partly yours. Have you time to tell me more of my grandfather? Or shall I be trespassing in staying longer?”
“Stay yet a while. In an hour and eighteen minutes I start for Trieste,” said Kalonymos, looking at his watch, “and presently my sons will expect my attention. Will you let me make you known to them, so that they may have the pleasure of showing hospitality to my friend’s grandson? They dwell here in ease and luxury, though I choose to be a wanderer.”
“I shall be glad if you will commend me to their acquaintance for some future opportunity,” said Deronda. “There are pressing claims calling me to England﻿—friends who may be much in need of my presence. I have been kept away from them too long by unexpected circumstances. But to know more of you and your family would be motive enough to bring me again to Mainz.”
“Good! Me you will hardly find, for I am beyond my threescore years and ten, and I am a wanderer, carrying my shroud with me. But my sons and their children dwell here in wealth and unity. The days are changed for us since Karl the Great fetched my ancestors from Italy to bring some tincture of knowledge to our rough German brethren. I and my contemporaries have had to fight for it too. Our youth fell on evil days; but this we have won; we increase our wealth in safety, and the learning of all Germany is fed and fattened by Jewish brains﻿—though they keep not always their Jewish hearts.

卡洛尼莫斯出去了几分钟，带着一名职员回来；职员抱着那口柜子，把它放在地上，揭掉皮罩，又退了出去。柜子不算很大，却因饰件和镀金铁提手而颇沉。木面上刻着阿拉伯字纹，美丽精致。
「喏！」卡洛尼莫斯回到座位上说。「这把钥匙也古怪。」他又添了一句，从一只小皮囊里取出钥匙。「收仔细了。我信你是行事有章法、又谨慎的人。」他递钥匙时带着老年把任何物件托付给青年时惯有的那种告诫兼略含疑虑的神气。
「保管这个，我会比保管任何别的财物更上心。」德龙达微笑着把钥匙放进胸前口袋。「我从不曾有过一样东西，向我标示着这么多被珍爱的希望与心血。而且我永远不会忘记，那心血里也有您的一份。您可有工夫再给我讲讲我外祖父？我再待下去会不会打扰您？」
「再坐一会儿。一小时十八分钟后我就动身去的里雅斯特。」卡洛尼莫斯看看表说，「过不多时我的儿子们就要来照应我了。让我把你引见给他们好么？也好让他们有缘款待我朋友的孙儿。他们在此安居优裕，我却宁愿做个游方的人。」
「倘若您替我在他们跟前先致意，容我日后再图相见，我很乐意。」德龙达说。「有紧切的事务在召我回英国——朋友们也许正极需要我在场。意外的变故已把我耽搁得太久。但多认识您和您的家族，这本身就有足够的缘由，足以引我再来美因茨一趟。」
「好！我可就难说了，我早过了古稀之年，是个把寿衣随身带着的游方人。可我的儿子们和他们的儿女在这里安居富足、和睦同心。自查理大帝把我的祖先们从意大利请来、给我们粗悍的德意志同胞带去一点知识的底子以来，时世对我们已经变了。我和我同辈的人也曾为这知识争斗过。我们的青春落在艰难的年月里；但我们赢来了这个：我们平安地增益财富，全德意志的学问都靠犹太人的头脑饲养得膘肥体壮——尽管那些头脑并不总保有犹太人的心。你呢，年轻人——他们把你弄得对自己的民族的生活全然无知么？」

===Original===

Have you been left altogether ignorant of your people’s life, young man?”
“No,” said Deronda, “I have lately, before I had any true suspicion of my parentage, been led to study everything belonging to their history with more interest than any other subject. It turns out that I have been making myself ready to understand my grandfather a little.” He was anxious less the time should be consumed before this circuitous course of talk could lead them back to the topic he most cared about. Age does not easily distinguish between what it needs to express and what youth needs to know﻿—distance seeming to level the objects of memory; and keenly active as Joseph Kalonymos showed himself, an inkstand in the wrong place would have hindered his imagination from getting to Beyrout: he had been used to unite restless travel with punctilious observation. But Deronda’s last sentence answered its purpose.
“So﻿—you would perhaps have been such a man as he if your education had not hindered; for you are like him in features:﻿—yet not altogether, young man. He had an iron will in his face: it braced up everybody about him. When he was quite young he had already got one deep upright line in his brow. I see none of that in you. Daniel Charisi used to say, ‘Better, a wrong will than a wavering; better a steadfast enemy than an uncertain friend; better a false belief than no belief at all.’ What he despised most was indifference. He had longer reasons than I can give you.”
“Yet his knowledge was not narrow?” said Deronda, with a tacit reference to the usual excuse for indecision﻿—that it comes from knowing too much.
“Narrow? no,” said Kalonymos, shaking his head with a compassionate smile “From his childhood upward, he drank in learning as easily as the plant sucks up water. But he early took to medicine and theories about life and health. He traveled to many countries, and spent much of his substance in seeing and knowing. What he used to insist on was that the strength and wealth of mankind depended on the balance of separateness and communication, and he was bitterly against our people losing themselves among the Gentiles; ‘It’s no better,’ said he, ‘than the many sorts of grain going back from their variety into sameness.’ He mingled all sorts of learning; and in that he was like our Arabic writers in the golden time. We studied together, but he went beyond me.

===Chinese===

「不。」德龙达说，「近来——还在我对自己的血统起过一点真正的疑心之前——我已被人引着去研究与他们历史有关的一切，那份兴味比任何别的题目都浓。如今看来，我原是在不知不觉地做准备，好多少懂得一点我的外祖父。」他有些焦急，惟恐时间就这样耗掉，而这段迂回的谈话迟迟绕不回他最关心的话题。上了年纪的人，不容易分清哪些是自己需要倾诉的、哪些是青年需要知道的——距离仿佛把记忆里的物事都拉平了；约瑟夫·卡洛尼莫斯人虽老而精力弥满，可纵然如此，一只墨水台放错了位置，也足以妨碍他的想象力赶到贝鲁特：他一向是把不安分的旅行同丝毫不苟的观察结在一起的。可德龙达末了那句话起了作用。
「原来如此——倘若不是你的教育从中作梗，你说不定也会成为他那样的人；因为你眉眼像他：——不过不尽然，年轻人。他的脸上有一副铁一般的意志：那意志把身边所有人都撑得笔直。他还很年轻的时候，额头上已有了一道深深的竖纹。我在你脸上看不出这个。丹尼尔·查里西常说：『宁可一个错谬的意志，不要一个摇摆的；宁要坚定的仇敌，不要游移的朋友；宁要虚妄的信仰，不要全然无信。』他最鄙夷的是无所谓。他那些道理，比我能转述给你的深长得多。」
「那么他的见识并不偏狭？」德龙达说，暗暗针对着人们替优柔寡断辩解的惯常说法——说那是因为知道得太多。
「偏狭？不。」卡洛尼莫斯摇着头，带着怜恤的笑说。「从童年起，他吸收学问就像草木吸水一样容易。他很早便专攻医学，钻研生命与健康的道理。他游历过许多国度，把大半家财花在了见与知上。他素来坚持的一点是：人类的力量与富足，系于分立与交通的平衡；他痛切反对我们的民族在列国之中自我消融。『那不比各样谷种从各自的多样退回到一律更好。』他说。他融会各门学问；这一点上，他像我们黄金时代的那些阿拉伯作家。我们一同求学，可他远超过了我。

Though we were bosom friends, and he poured himself out to me, we were as different as the inside and outside of the bowl. And since I was a ripe man, I have been what I am now, for all but age﻿—loving to wander, loving transactions, loving to behold all things, and caring nothing about hardship. Charisi thought continually of our people’s future: he went with all his soul into that part of our religion: I, not. So we have freedom, I am content. Our people wandered before they were driven. Young man, when I am in the East, I lie much on deck and watch the greater stars. The sight of them satisfies me. I know them as they rise, and hunger not to know more. Yet we loved each other, and as he said, he bound our love with duty; we solemnly pledged ourselves to help and defend each other to the last. I have fulfilled my pledge.” Here Kalonymos rose, and Deronda, rising also, said,
“And in being faithful to him you have caused justice to be done to me. It would have been a robbery of me too that I should never have known of the inheritance he had prepared for me. I thank you with my whole soul.”
“Be worthy of him, young man. What is your vocation?” This question was put with a quick abruptness which embarrassed Deronda, who did not feel it quite honest to allege his law-reading as a vocation. He answered,
“I cannot say that I have any.”
“Get one, get one. The Jew must be diligent. You will call yourself a Jew and profess the faith of your fathers?” said Kalonymos, putting his hand on Deronda’s shoulder and looking sharply in his face.
“I shall call myself a Jew,” said Deronda, deliberately, becoming slightly paler under the piercing eyes of his questioner. “But I will not say that I shall profess to believe exactly as my fathers have believed. Our fathers themselves changed the horizon of their belief and learned of other races. But I think I can maintain my grandfather’s notion of separateness with communication.

===Chinese===

「我们虽是心腹之交，他把心里的话都倾倒给我，可我们俩就像一只钵的里面和外面那样不同。我自有两个主张：查里西的格言，我像看待树木的形状一样看待：它们在那里，用不着去争辩。到头来我们殊途同归：我们都是忠实的犹太人，庆幸自己不是外邦人。打从我成年起，除去年岁，我一直是如今这个样子——爱游历，爱做交易，爱观览万事，不把辛苦放在心上。查里西则无时不想着我们民族的将来：他把自己的整个灵魂投进了我们宗教的那一部分：我没有。我们这样便有了自由，我也知足。我们的民族在被驱赶之前，本就惯于漂泊。年轻人，我在东方（the East）的时候，常躺在甲板上看那些大星。看着它们，我就满足了。它们升起来，我都认得，也不再饥渴于知道更多。查里西却看什么都不满足，总要用之前的因由、之后的推演把它补全。然而我们彼此相爱，而且照他的话说，他用义务拴住了我们的爱；我们庄严立誓，要彼此相助相护，直到最后。我的誓言，我履行了。」说到这里卡洛尼莫斯站起身，德龙达也站起来，说：
「您对他守信，也就成全了对我的公道。倘若我永远不知道他为我备下的产业，那对我同样是一场劫掠。我以整个灵魂感谢您。」
「要配得上他，年轻人。你的志业是什么？」这问题来得急促突兀，令德龙达一时窘迫；他若拿读法律来充志业，自觉有些不诚实。他答道：
「我说不上有什么志业。」
「去得一个，去得一个。犹太人必须勤勉。你要自称犹太人、信奉列祖的信仰么？」卡洛尼莫斯把手按在德龙达肩上，锐利地看着他的脸。
「我会自称犹太人。」德龙达郑重地说，在那双逼视的眼睛下面，脸色微微发白。「但我不能说，我会宣称自己所信同列祖分毫不差。我们的列祖自己也曾移动信仰的地平线，也曾向别的族类学习。不过我想，我守得住我外祖父的信念——分立中的交通。

I hold that my first duty is to my own people, and if there is anything to be done toward restoring or perfecting their common life, I shall make that my vocation.”
It happened to Deronda at that moment, as it has often happened to others, that the need for speech made an epoch in resolve. His respect for the questioner would not let him decline to answer, and by the necessity to answer he found out the truth for himself.
“Ah, you argue and you look forward﻿—you are Daniel Charisi’s grandson,” said Kalonymos, adding a benediction in Hebrew.
With that they parted; and almost as soon as Deronda was in London, the aged man was again on shipboard, greeting the friendly stars without any eager curiosity.

===Chinese===

「我认为我的第一义务是对我自己的民族；倘若在恢复或成全他们共同生活的事上有任何可做的，我就以此为我毕生的志业。」
德龙达此刻的情形，恰如许多人经历过的：因必须开口说话，决心便划出了一个新纪元。他对发问者的敬重不容他避而不答，而由于必须作答，他为自己发现了真相。
「啊，你会推究，你会前瞻——你正是丹尼尔·查里西的外孙。」卡洛尼莫斯说，又用希伯来语添了一句祝福。
说罢两人便分手了；德龙达前脚刚到伦敦，老人后脚又已登船，向那些友善的星辰致意，不带一丝热切的好奇。

### LXI / 第六十一章
===Original===

> Within the gentle heart Love shelters him,

As birds within the green shade of the grove.

Before the gentle heart, in Nature’s scheme,

Love was not, nor the gentle heart ere Love.

===Chinese===

> 爱在温柔的心里栖身，
> 如飞鸟藏在小树林的绿荫里。
> 按造化的安排，先有温柔的心，爱才存在；
> 未有爱，也便没有温柔的心。

===Original===

There was another house besides the white house at Pennicote, another breast besides Rex Gascoigne’s, in which the news of Grandcourt’s death caused both strong agitation and the effort to repress it.
It was Hans Meyrick’s habit to send or bring in the *Times* for his mother’s reading. She was a great reader of news, from the widest-reaching politics to the list of marriages; the latter, she said, giving her the pleasant sense of finishing the fashionable novels without having read them, and seeing the heroes and heroines happy without knowing what poor creatures they were. On a Wednesday, there were reasons why Hans always chose to bring the paper, and to do so about the time that Mirah had nearly ended giving Mab her weekly lesson, avowing that he came then because he wanted to hear Mirah sing. But on the particular Wednesday now in question, after entering the house as quietly as usual with his latchkey, he appeared in the parlor, shaking the *Times* aloft with a crackling noise, in remorseless interruption of Mab’s attempt to render *Lascia ch’io pianga* with a remote imitation of her teacher. Piano and song ceased immediately; Mirah, who had been playing the accompaniment, involuntarily started up and turned round, the crackling sound, after the occasional trick of sounds, having seemed to her something thunderous; and Mab said,
“O-o-o, Hans! why do you bring a more horrible noise than my singing?”
“What on earth is the wonderful news?” said Mrs. Meyrick, who was the only other person in the room. “Anything about Italy﻿—anything about the Austrians giving up Venice?”
“Nothing about Italy, but something from Italy,” said Hans, with a peculiarity in his tone and manner which set his mother interpreting. Imagine how some of us feel and behave when an event, not disagreeable seems to be confirming and carrying out our private constructions. We say, “What do you think?” in a pregnant tone to some innocent person who has not embarked his wisdom in the same boat with ours, and finds our information flat.
“Nothing bad?” said Mrs. Meyrick anxiously, thinking immediately of Deronda; and Mirah’s heart had been already clutched by the same thought.
“Not bad for anybody we care much about,” said Hans, quickly; “rather uncommonly lucky, I think. I never knew anybody die conveniently before.

佩尼科特那座白房子之外，还有另一座房子；雷克斯·加斯科因的胸膛之外，还有另一个胸膛——格兰考特的死讯在那里同样掀起了大激动，也同样是强自按捺。
汉斯·梅里克惯于把《泰晤士报》送去或带回家给母亲读。她是读新闻的大行家，从最辽远的政治读到结婚启事栏；她说后者给她一种愉快的滋味——时尚小说没读就算读完了，还看见男女主人公个个幸福，不必知道他们其实是些多么可怜的家伙。每逢星期三，汉斯总有种种理由，偏要自己把报纸带来，而且挑的时辰，总在米拉给梅布上每周一课快结束的时候——他自认挑这时候来，是因为想听米拉唱歌。可是眼下说的这个特别的星期三，他照常用弹簧钥匙悄悄进门，一现身客厅，就把《泰晤士报》抖得哗啦啦响，毫不留情地打断了梅布的演唱——她正远远模仿着老师，试着唱《让我痛哭吧》（Lascia ch'io pianga）。琴声歌声当即停住；一直弹着伴奏的米拉不由自主地跳起来转过身——按照声音惯常的恶作剧，那哗啦声在她听来简直像什么雷霆；梅布说：
「哦哦哦，汉斯！你干吗带来一个比我的歌声更可怕的噪音？」
「到底是什么惊人的消息？」梅里克太太问；她是屋里仅有的另一个人。「意大利的事吗——奥地利人放弃威尼斯的事吗？」
「不是意大利的事，是从意大利来的事，」汉斯说，声调举止里有种说不出的特别，引得他母亲琢磨起来。试想，当一件并不讨厌的事，似乎正在证实并推进我们私心的构建时，我们有些人是什么感觉、什么做派。我们意味深长地对某个无辜的人说「你猜怎么着？」——那人没把他的智慧同我们的装在一条船上，只觉得我们的消息平淡无奇。
「不是坏事吧？」梅里克太太焦急地问，心里立刻想到德龙达；米拉的心也早被同一个念头攏住了。
「对我们疼爱的人来说不是坏事，」汉斯很快地说；「我看倒是少见地走运。我还从没见过谁死得这样恰到好处。

===Original===

Considering what a dear gazelle I am, I am constantly wondering to find myself alive.”
“Oh me, Hans!” said Mab, impatiently, “if you must talk of yourself, let it be behind your own back. What *is* it that has happened?”
“Duke Alfonso is drowned, and the Duchess is alive, that’s all,” said Hans, putting the paper before Mrs. Meyrick, with his finger against a paragraph. “But more than all is﻿—Deronda was at Genoa in the same hotel with them, and he saw her brought in by the fishermen who had got her out of the water time enough to save her from any harm. It seems they saw her jump in after her husband, which was a less judicious action than I should have expected of the Duchess. However Deronda is a lucky fellow in being there to take care of her.”
Mirah had sunk on the music stool again, with her eyelids down and her hands tightly clasped; and Mrs. Meyrick, giving up the paper to Mab, said,
“Poor thing! she must have been fond of her husband to jump in after him.”
“It was an inadvertence﻿—a little absence of mind,” said Hans, creasing his face roguishly, and throwing himself into a chair not far from Mirah. “Who can be fond of a jealous baritone, with freezing glances, always singing asides?﻿—that was the husband’s role, depend upon it. Nothing can be neater than his getting drowned. The Duchess is at liberty now to marry a man with a fine head of hair, and glances that will melt instead of freezing her. And I shall be invited to the wedding.”
Here Mirah started from her sitting posture, and fixing her eyes on Hans, with an angry gleam in them, she said, in a deeply-shaken voice of indignation,
“Mr. Hans, you ought not to speak in that way. Mr. Deronda would not like you to speak so. Why will you say he is lucky﻿—why will you use words of that sort about life and death﻿—when what is life to one is death to another? How do you know it would be lucky if he loved Mrs. Grandcourt? It might be a great evil to him. She would take him away from my brother﻿—I know she would. Mr. Deronda would not call that lucky to pierce my brother’s heart.”
All three were struck with the sudden transformation.

想想我是头多可爱的羚羊，居然还发现自己活着，我真是一直纳闷。」
「哎呀，汉斯！」梅布不耐烦地说，「你非要谈自己，也请背着你自己谈。到底出什么事了？」
「阿尔丰索公爵淹死了，公爵夫人活着，就这么点事，」汉斯说，把报纸放到梅里克太太面前，手指按着一段文字。「可要紧的还在后头——德龙达当时同他们住在热那亚同一家旅馆，亲眼看见渔夫们把她抬进来；他们把她从水里捞得及时，没受一点损伤。据说他们看见她跟着丈夫跳了下去——这可比我对公爵夫人的预想欠审慎。不管怎样，德龙达这小子真走运，正好在那里照应她。」
米拉又跌坐回琴凳上，眼睑低垂，双手紧握；梅里克太太把报纸让给梅布，说：
「可怜的人！她一定是疼她的丈夫，才会跟着跳下去。」
「那是失手——走了一会儿神，」汉斯说，脸皮顽皮地皱起来，一屁股坐进离米拉不远的椅子里。「谁能疼上一个爱吃醋的男中音，目光冷得结冰，动不动就唱旁白？——那准是丈夫的角色，错不了。他淹死得再干净利落没有了。公爵夫人如今自由了，可以嫁个头发浓密的男人，目光化得开她，而不是冻得住她。到时婚礼必定请我。」

「汉斯先生，你不该这样说话。德龙达先生不会喜欢你这样讲。你为什么偏说他走运——为什么偏拿这种字眼说生死——一个人的生，也许就是另一个人的死！你怎么知道，倘若他爱格兰考特夫人，那就是走运？那也许是他天大的祸事。她会把他从我哥哥身边夺走——我知道她会的。德龙达先生决不会把刺穿我哥哥的心叫作走运。」
三人都被这骤然的转变惊住了。

===Original===

Mirah’s face, with a look of anger that might have suited Ithuriel, pale, even to the lips that were usually so rich of tint, was not far from poor Hans, who sat transfixed, blushing under it as if he had been a girl, while he said, nervously,
“I am a fool and a brute, and I withdraw every word. I’ll go and hang myself like Judas﻿—if it’s allowable to mention him.” Even in Hans’s sorrowful moments, his improvised words had inevitably some drollery.
But Mirah’s anger was not appeased: how could it be? She had burst into indignant speech as creatures in intense pain bite and make their teeth meet even through their own flesh, by way of making their agony bearable. She said no more, but, seating herself at the piano, pressed the sheet of music before her, as if she thought of beginning to play again.
It was Mab who spoke, while Mrs. Meyrick’s face seemed to reflect some of Hans’ discomfort.
“Mirah is quite right to scold you, Hans. You are always taking Mr. Deronda’s name in vain. And it is horrible, joking in that way about his marrying Mrs. Grandcourt. Men’s minds must be very black, I think,” ended Mab, with much scorn.
“Quite true, my dear,” said Hans, in a low tone, rising and turning on his heel to walk toward the back window.
“We had better go on, Mab; you have not given your full time to the lesson,” said Mirah, in a higher tone than usual. “Will you sing this again, or shall I sing it to you?”
“Oh, please sing it to me,” said Mab, rejoiced to take no more notice of what had happened.
And Mirah immediately sang *Lascia ch’io pianga*, giving forth its melodious sobs and cries with new fullness and energy. Hans paused in his walk and leaned against the mantelpiece, keeping his eyes carefully away from his mother’s. When Mirah had sung her last note and touched the last chord, she rose and said, “I must go home now. Ezra expects me.”
She gave her hand silently to Mrs. Meyrick and hung back a little, not daring to look at her, instead of kissing her, as usual. But the little mother drew Mirah’s face down to hers, and said, soothingly, “God bless you, my dear.” Mirah felt that she had committed an offense against Mrs. Meyrick by angrily rebuking Hans, and mixed with the rest of her suffering was the sense that she had shown something like a proud ingratitude, an unbecoming assertion of superiority. And her friend had divined this compunction.

===Chinese===

米拉的脸离可怜的汉斯不远，脸上是一种连伊休利尔也当得起的怒容，苍白直漫到平日色泽丰润的唇上；汉斯呆坐在那里，被那怒容烧得满脸通红，活像个姑娘，局促地说：
「我是傻瓜，是畜生，我说的话全部收回。我这就去学犹大吊死——如果提到他不算犯忌的话。」汉斯即便在伤心的时候，脱口而出的话也免不了带几分滑稽。
可米拉的怒气并没有平息：怎么可能平息？她方才冲口而出的愤慨之言，正如剧痛中的生灵咬下去、让自己的牙关哪怕穿透自身的皮肉也要合上——为了叫那剧痛熬得下去。她没有再说，只是坐回钢琴前，按住面前的乐谱，仿佛想重新开始弹奏。
开口的是梅布；梅里克太太的脸上，似乎映出了几分汉斯的狼狈。
「米拉训你训得对，汉斯。你总是妄称德龙达先生的名字。还有，拿他娶格兰考特夫人这样的事开玩笑，太可怕了。男人的头脑一定黑得很，我看，」梅布满是不屑地收了尾。
「说得对，亲爱的，」汉斯低声说，起身一转身，朝后窗踱去。
「我们还是继续吧，梅布；你这一课还没上足时候呢，」米拉说，声调比平时高。「这支你再唱一遍，还是我唱给你听？」
「哦，请你唱给我听，」梅布说，乐得再不提方才的事。
于是米拉当即唱起《让我痛哭吧》，把它那婉转的呜咽与呼告放得格外饱满有力。汉斯踱到一半停住，倚着壁炉架，小心让自己的眼睛避开母亲的眼睛。米拉唱完最后一个音、按完最后一个和弦，便起身说：「我现在得回家了。以斯拉等着我呢。」
她默默把手伸给梅里克太太，又稍稍退缩，不敢看她，没有照往常那样亲吻她。可小妈妈把米拉的脸拉下来贴着自己的脸，抚慰地说：「上帝保佑你，亲爱的。」米拉觉得，自己怒斥汉斯，是对梅里克太太犯了过失；在她其余的痛苦里，又掺进一层感觉——仿佛自己显出了一种傲慢的忘恩，一种不得体的优越姿态。而她的朋友已看出了这份愧疚。

Meanwhile Hans had seized his wide-awake, and was ready to open the door.
“Now, Hans,” said Mab, with what was really a sister’s tenderness cunningly disguised, “you are not going to walk home with Mirah. I am sure she would rather not. You are so dreadfully disagreeable today.”
“I shall go to take care of her, if she does not forbid me,” said Hans, opening the door.
Mirah said nothing, and when he had opened the outer door for her and closed it behind him, he walked by her side unforbidden. She had not the courage to begin speaking to him again﻿—conscious that she had perhaps been unbecomingly severe in her words to him, yet finding only severer words behind them in her heart. Besides, she was pressed upon by a crowd of thoughts thrusting themselves forward as interpreters of that consciousness which still remained unaltered to herself.
Hans, on his side, had a mind equally busy. Mirah’s anger had waked in him a new perception, and with it the unpleasant sense that he was a dolt not to have had it before. Suppose Mirah’s heart were entirely preoccupied with Deronda in another character than that of her own and her brother’s benefactor; the supposition was attended in Hans’s mind with anxieties which, to do him justice, were not altogether selfish. He had a strong persuasion, which only direct evidence to the contrary could have dissipated, and that was that there was a serious attachment between Deronda and Mrs. Grandcourt; he had pieced together many fragments of observation, and gradually gathered knowledge, completed by what his sisters had heard from Anna Gascoigne, which convinced him not only that Mrs. Grandcourt had a passion for Deronda, but also, notwithstanding his friend’s austere self-repression, that Deronda’s susceptibility about her was the sign of concealed love. Some men, having such a conviction, would have avoided allusions that could have roused that susceptibility; but Hans’s talk naturally fluttered toward mischief, and he was given to a form of experiment on live animals which consisted in irritating his friends playfully. His experiments had ended in satisfying him that what he thought likely was true.

这时汉斯已抓起他那顶阔边毡帽，准备去开门。
「慢着，汉斯，」梅布说，话里其实是一种巧妙伪装的姐姐式的温柔，「你可不许送米拉回家。我敢说她宁愿你别送。你今天讨厌得吓人。」
「她不禁止我的话，我就去照应她，」汉斯说着，开了门。
米拉没有言语；他为她开了临街的门，随手带上，便得了默许似的走在她身边。她没有勇气再同他开口——自知方才的话也许严厉得有失分寸，可心底里垫着的，分明是更严厉的话。况且，一大群念头正挤上前，要给那层她自己还未看清的意识当翻译。
汉斯那边，心思也一样忙碌。米拉的怒火在他心里唤醒了一种新的知觉，随之而来的是不快：自己先前竟没有这知觉，真是块梄木。设想一下，倘若米拉的心，早被德龙达整个占据——不是作为她和她哥哥的恩人，而是换了另一种身份；这个设想在汉斯心里伴随着种种焦虑，而凭良心说，那些焦虑并不全是自私的。他有一个牢固的成见——只有相反的铁证才能驱散——那就是德龙达同格兰考特夫人之间有一段郑重的情缘；他把许多观察的碎片拼拢起来，渐渐凑成了一种认识，又经妹妹们从安娜·加斯科因那里听来的话补足，使他确信：不但格兰考特夫人对德龙达怀着激情，而且——尽管他朋友矜严自制——德龙达一提她便敏感，正是藏在心底的爱的迹象。换了别人，怀着这样的确信，多半会避开一切可能撩起这份敏感的话头；可汉斯的谈锋天生爱往祸事上扑，他还惯于拿活物做实验——方式就是嬉皮笑脸地撩惹朋友。这一番实验的结果，是让他满意地认定，他料想的事千真万确。

On the other hand, any susceptibility Deronda had manifested about a lover’s attentions being shown to Mirah, Hans took to be sufficiently accounted for by the alleged reason, namely, her dependent position; for he credited his friend with all possible unselfish anxiety for those whom he could rescue and protect. And Deronda’s insistence that Mirah would never marry one who was not a Jew necessarily seemed to exclude himself, since Hans shared the ordinary opinion, which he knew nothing to disturb, that Deronda was the son of Sir Hugo Mallinger.
Thus he felt himself in clearness about the state of Deronda’s affections; but now, the events which really struck him as concurring toward the desirable union with Mrs. Grandcourt, had called forth a flash of revelation from Mirah﻿—a betrayal of her passionate feeling on this subject which had made him melancholy on her account as well as his own﻿—yet on the whole less melancholy than if he had imagined Deronda’s hopes fixed on her. It is not sublime, but it is common, for a man to see the beloved object unhappy because his rival loves another, with more fortitude and a milder jealousy than if he saw her entirely happy in his rival. At least it was so with the mercurial Hans, who fluctuated between the contradictory states of feeling, wounded because Mirah was wounded, and of being almost obliged to Deronda for loving somebody else. It was impossible for him to give Mirah any direct sign of the way in which he had understood her anger, yet he longed that his speechless companionship should be eloquent in a tender, penitent sympathy which is an admissible form of wooing a bruised heart.
Thus the two went side by side in a companionship that yet seemed an agitated communication, like that of two chords whose quick vibrations lie outside our hearing. But when they reached the door of Mirah’s home, and Hans said “Goodbye,” putting out his hand with an appealing look of penitence, she met the look with melancholy gentleness, and said, “Will you not come in and see my brother?”
Hans could not but interpret this invitation as a sign of pardon. He had not enough understanding of what Mirah’s nature had been wrought into by her early experience, to divine how the very strength of her late excitement had made it pass more quickly into the resolute acceptance of pain.

另一方面，德龙达每逢流露对向米拉献殷勤的追求者的敏感，汉斯都拿那句托出的理由去充分解释——即她寄人篱下的处境；因为他相信朋友对一切他能搭救、能护佑的人，怀有一切可能的无私关切。而德龙达坚称米拉绝不嫁非犹太人，这在汉斯看来必然把自己排除在外——因为他同世人一样认定德龙达是雨果·马林格爵士的儿子，也没有任何消息动摇过这个认定。
于是他自觉把德龙达的感情状况看得清清楚楚；可是现在，那桩在他看来正促成德龙达同格兰考特夫人好事的一系列事件，却从米拉身上引出了一道天启——她在这一题旨上的炽烈感情泄露无遗，害得他既为自己、也为她黯然——不过总的说来，比设想德龙达的心思系在她身上要好受些。看见心爱的人因情敌另有所爱而不幸，男人能比看见她同情敌十分美满时更坚忍、醋意更温和——这算不得崇高，却是常情。至少，善变的汉斯就是这样：他在两种矛盾的心情间摇摆，一面因米拉受伤而受伤，一面几乎要感激德龙达爱了别人。他无法给米拉任何直接的表示，说明他已读懂她的怒火；却渴望自己无言的相伴能雄辩地说出一种温柔的、悔罪的同情——那是对一颗受了伤的心求爱的可行方式。
两人就这样并肩走着，这相伴却像一场激动的交流，好比两根琴弦，急速的颤动落在我们的听觉之外。可走到米拉家门口，汉斯说声「再见」，伸出手来，眼里带着恳求的悔意；她迎着那目光，忧郁而温柔地说：「你不进来看看我哥哥吗？」
汉斯不能不把这邀请当作宽恕的记号。他对米拉早年经历把她天性历练成的样子懂得太少，猜不到方才那阵激动的强烈，恰恰使它更快地化作了对痛苦的坚忍承受。

When he had said, “If you will let me,” and they went in together, half his grief was gone, and he was spinning a little romance of how his devotion might make him indispensable to Mirah in proportion as Deronda gave his devotion elsewhere. This was quite fair, since his friend was provided for according to his own heart; and on the question of Judaism Hans felt thoroughly fortified:﻿—who ever heard in tale or history that a woman’s love went in the track of her race and religion? Muslim and Jewish damsels were always attracted toward Christians, and now if Mirah’s heart had gone forth too precipitately toward Deronda, here was another case in point. Hans was wont to make merry with his own arguments, to call himself a Giaour, and antithesis the sole clue to events; but he believed a little in what he laughed at. And thus his birdlike hope, constructed on the lightest principles, soared again in spite of heavy circumstances.
They found Mordecai looking singularly happy, holding a closed letter in his hand, his eyes glowing with a quiet triumph which in his emaciated face gave the idea of a conquest over assailing death. After the greeting between him and Hans, Mirah put her arm round her brother’s neck and looked down at the letter in his hand, without the courage to ask about it, though she felt sure that it was the cause of his happiness.
“A letter from Daniel Deronda,” said Mordecai, answering her look. “Brief﻿—only saying that he hopes soon to return. Unexpected claims have detained him. The promise of seeing him again is like the bow in the cloud to me,” continued Mordecai, looking at Hans; “and to you it must be a gladness. For who has two friends like him?”
While Hans was answering Mirah slipped away to her own room; but not to indulge in any outburst of the passion within her.

待他说过「你若允许」，两人一同进了门，他的悲伤已去了一半，正自编织一段小小的传奇：德龙达的深情既然投向别处，他的忠诚便可以按比例地使自己成为米拉少不了的人。这十分公道，因为朋友已各随己心得其所哉；而在犹太教这个问题上，汉斯自觉武装到了牙齿：——传说里、史书里，谁听说过女人的爱沿着她种族和宗教的旧辙走？穆斯林和犹太的少女，从来总是被基督徒吸引去的；如今米拉的心倘若向德龙达奔得太急，这不过是又一个现成的例子。汉斯惯于拿自己的论据打趣，管自己叫异教徒，说「对立」是解开盘根错节的唯一线头；可他对自己嘲笑的东西，也信上几分。于是他那只鸟儿似的希望——凭着最轻飘的原理搭成——不顾沉重的情势，又飞起来了。
他们看见末底改显出少有的快乐，手里握着一封封好的信，眼里燃着一种静静的得胜之光——在他枯槁的脸上，那光让人觉得他打了一场击退死神的胜仗。他同汉斯寒暄过后，米拉挞住哥哥的脖子，低头看他手里的信，不敢问起，虽然她确信那正是他快乐的原因。
「丹尼尔·德龙达来的信，」末底改回答她的目光说。「很短——只说他盼望不久归来。意外的事由把他绊住了。能再见他的应许，于我就像云中的虹，」末底改望着汉斯继续说；「于你也必定是一喜。谁有过两个像他这样的朋友呢？」
汉斯应答的当儿，米拉悄悄溜进了自己的房间；却不是去放任胸中的激情倾泻一空。

If the angels, once supposed to watch the toilet of women, had entered the little chamber with her and let her shut the door behind them, they would only have seen her take off her hat, sit down and press her hands against her temples as if she had suddenly reflected that her head ached; then rise to dash cold water on her eyes and brow and hair till her backward curls were full of crystal beads, while she had dried her brow and looked out like a freshly-opened flower from among the dewy tresses of the woodland; then give deep sighs of relief, and putting on her little slippers, sit still after that action for a couple of minutes, which seemed to her so long, so full of things to come, that she rose with an air of recollection, and went down to make tea.
Something of the old life had returned. She had been used to remember that she must learn her part, must go to rehearsal, must act and sing in the evening, must hide her feelings from her father; and the more painful her life grew, the more she had been used to hide. The force of her nature had long found its chief action in resolute endurance, and today the violence of feeling which had caused the first jet of anger had quickly transformed itself into a steady facing of trouble, the well-known companion of her young years. But while she moved about and spoke as usual, a close observer might have discerned a difference between this apparent calm, which was the effect of restraining energy, and the sweet genuine calm of the months when she first felt a return of her infantine happiness.
Those who have been indulged by fortune and have always thought of calamity as what happens to others, feel a blind incredulous rage at the reversal of their lot, and half believe that their wild cries will alter the course of the storm. Mirah felt no such surprise when familiar Sorrow came back from brief absence, and sat down with her according to the old use and wont. And this habit of expecting trouble rather than joy, hindered her from having any persistent belief in opposition to the probabilities which were not merely suggested by Hans, but were supported by her own private knowledge and long-growing presentiment. An attachment between Deronda and Mrs. Grandcourt, to end in their future marriage, had the aspect of a certainty for her feeling.

倘若那些天使——从前被认为专门看顾女人梳妆的——随她进了小屋，由她关上门，他们也只会看见她摘下帽子，坐下，双手按住两侧太阳穴，仿佛这才想起自己头疼；随后起身，用冷水扑眼睛、扑额头、扑头发，直扑得后脑的发卷挂满晶亮的水珠；她已擦干额头，从林间带露的发丝中间探出脸来，像一朵初绽的花；然后深深吐出几口宽慰的气，穿上小小的拖鞋，在那动作之后再静坐两分钟——那两分钟在她觉来那样长，那样满装着未来的事，以致她终于带着回过神来的神气起身，下楼泡茶去了。

一向被命运宠惯、总把灾祸当作他人之事的人，一旦命运翻覆，会感到一种盲目的、难以置信的狂怒，并且半信着自己的狂呼乱喊能叫风暴改道。米拉却没有这份惊讶：当熟识的忧愁小别归来，照老规矩在她身边坐下时，她并不诧异。而这种宁盼麻烦、不盼欢喜的习惯，也使她无法固执地不信那些可能——它们不仅有汉斯的言语作引，更有她自己私下的所见与日久生成的预感作靠。德龙达同格兰考特夫人的一段情，以日后成婚作结——在她的感觉里，已具有确凿的面目。

There had been no fault in him: facts had ordered themselves so that there was a tie between him and this woman who belonged to another world than hers and Ezra’s﻿—nay, who seemed another sort of being than Deronda, something foreign that would be a disturbance in his life instead of blending with it. Well, well﻿—but if it could have been deferred so as to make no difference while Ezra was there! She did not know all the momentousness of the relation between Deronda and her brother, but she had seen, and instinctively felt enough to forebode its being incongruous with any close tie to Mrs. Grandcourt; at least this was the clothing that Mirah first gave to her mortal repugnance. But in the still, quick action of her consciousness, thoughts went on like changing states of sensation unbroken by her habitual acts; and this inward language soon said distinctly that the mortal repugnance would remain even if Ezra were secured from loss.
“What I have read about and sung about and seen acted, is happening to me﻿—this that I am feeling is the love that makes jealousy;” so impartially Mirah summed up the charge against herself. But what difference could this pain of hers make to anyone else? It must remain as exclusively her own, and hidden, as her early yearning and devotion to her lost mother. But unlike that devotion, it was something that she felt to be a misfortune of her nature﻿—a discovery that what should have been pure gratitude and reverence had sunk into selfish pain, that the feeling she had hitherto delighted to pour out in words was degraded into something she was ashamed to betray﻿—an absurd longing that she who had received all and given nothing should be of importance where she was of no importance﻿—an angry feeling toward another woman who possessed the good she wanted. But what notion, what vain reliance could it be that had lain darkly within her and was now burning itself into sight as disappointment and jealousy? It was as if her soul had been steeped in poisonous passion by forgotten dreams of deep sleep, and now flamed out in this unaccountable misery. For with her waking reason she had never entertained what seemed the wildly unfitting thought that Deronda could love her.

他没有错处：事实自行排布成这样——他同这个女人之间有了牵系；而这女人属于另一个世界，不是她同以斯拉的世界——不，她在米拉眼里简直是另一种生灵，同德龙达隔着一层，只会成为他生活里的搅扰，而不能与之交融。也罢，也罢——可它就不能缓一缓，缓到以斯拉在世时无妨无碍吗！她并不知道德龙达同她哥哥之间那份关系的全部分量，可她见过的、下意识感到的，已足够让她预感：那关系同任何与格兰考特夫人的亲密牵系都不能相容；至少，米拉起先给她那份切骨的憎嫌穿上的，是这样一件衣裳。可是在她意识那静而迅疾的运转里，思绪如种种变换的感官状态般持续着，不被她惯常的动作打断；这内心的语言很快便说得明白：即便以斯拉保住不失，那份切骨的憎嫌也仍会在。
「我在书里读到过、唱到过、在台上看到过的事，正发生在我身上——我此刻感到的，就是生出嫉妒的爱；」米拉这样毫不含糊地给自己立了案。可她这份痛，于别人又能改变什么？它必须照旧全然归她私有、藏起，像她对失散母亲的早年孺慕与挚爱一样。只是同那份挚爱不同，她感到这是她天性中的一桩不幸——一桩发现：本该是纯粹的感激与敬重，竟沉沦为自私的痛楚；她一向乐于倾吐在言语里的那份感情，竟堕成她耻于吐露的东西——一桩荒唐的渴念：她这个受尽一切、未给分毫的人，竟想在人家眼里举足轻重——一股对另一个女人的怒意：那人占有着她想要的好。可那埋在她心底幽暗处、此刻正烧得显形的，究竟是个什么念头、什么虚妄的指望，化作失望与嫉妒？仿佛她的灵魂在深睡遗忘的梦里浸透了毒性的激情，如今便在这场无从解释的苦楚里烧出火来。因为她凭着醒着的理性，从未怀过那样一个念头——那个看来全然不称的念头：德龙达会爱她。
