> 啊，欢迎，目色纯净的信，素手的望，

你这位盘旋的天使，束着金色的翅膀！

应格温多琳新的召唤，德龙达并非心无波澜。不是虚荣，而是他那敏锐的同情，使他易受这样一种危险的侵扰：另一颗心对他提出的要求，可能超出他所能满足的；而格温多琳的灵魂正以怎样炽热的需要依恋着他的灵魂，这在他已不是可以推敲的事，而是洞穿人心的知觉。一个声音里颤动的怒气或轻蔑，我们并不推论它的存在；我们只是感到它，而它不容辩驳。德龙达感到这个女人的命运正悬在他身上，悬在绝望的悬崖之上。了解他的人，对他这番内心的自白都不会诧异：倘若这一切发生在仅仅一年多以前，他多半不会先问自己爱不爱她；推动他、决定他的，将是那股炽烈的冲动——救她脱于忧患，护她一生永不再受孤独的险，把那始于项链之警戒救赎的搭救，贯彻到底。可如今，爱与义务已把别的纽带缠上他身，那股冲动再不能决定他的一生；可它仍在他心里，化作悲悯的渴念，化作一阵阵痛楚的颤栗——只消想到要一遍又一遍迎对她眼睛与话语的恳求。而正是那条纽带的坚韧、那决心的笃定——它们把他同她隔开——使他在远处凝望她的命运时，怀着愈发锥心的怜悯。
他在后客厅里等她来——那是那片银白与绯红的一部分；在那场音乐聚会上，两人曾一同坐在那里，格温多琳在那里头一回说出：她的命运系于他不抛弃她；而她的恳求仿佛融进了那句旋律的哀呼——Per pietà non dirmi addio（怜悯我，莫对我说离别）。可那旋律，原是从米拉亲爱的嗓音里流出来的。
这间屋子他多年来烂熟于心；他在其中踱来踱去，怀着一种奇异的感觉——自己的人生已然换了形。

===Original===

The familiar objects around him, from Lady Mallinger’s gently smiling portrait to the also human and urbane faces of the lions on the pilasters of the chimneypiece, seemed almost to belong to a previous state of existence which he was revisiting in memory only, not in reality; so deep and transforming had been the impressions he had lately experienced, so new were the conditions under which he found himself in the house he had been accustomed to think of as a home﻿—standing with his hat in his hand awaiting the entrance of a young creature whose life had also been undergoing a transformation﻿—a tragic transformation toward a wavering result, in which he felt with apprehensiveness that his own action was still bound up.
But Gwendolen was come in, looking changed; not only by her mourning dress, but by a more satisfied quietude of expression than he had seen in her face at Genoa. Her satisfaction was that Deronda was there; but there was no smile between them as they met and clasped hands; each was full of remembrance﻿—full of anxious prevision. She said, “It was good of you to come. Let us sit down,” immediately seating herself in the nearest chair. He placed himself opposite to her.
“I asked you to come because I want you to tell me what I ought to do,” she began, at once. “Don’t be afraid of telling me what you think is right, because it seems hard. I have made up my mind to do it. I was afraid once of being poor; I could not bear to think of being under other people; and that was why I did something﻿—why I married. I have borne worse things now. I think I could bear to be poor, if you think I ought. Do you know about my husband’s will?”
“Yes, Sir Hugo told me,” said Deronda, already guessing the question she had to ask.
“Ought I to take anything he has left me? I will tell you what I have been thinking,” said Gwendolen, with a more nervous eagerness. “Perhaps you may not quite know that I really did think a good deal about my mother when I married. I *was* selfish, but I did love her, and feel about her poverty; and what comforted me most at first, when I was miserable, was her being better off because I had married.

===Chinese===

四周那些熟悉的物件——从马林格夫人含着浅笑的画像，到壁炉柱上那几只也颇通人性、和蔼可亲的狮子脸——几乎像属于他前世的一段存在，如今他只是在记忆里重访，而不是在现实里；他新近领受的印象是这样深、这样翻覆人心；他在这所一向被自己当作家的宅子里，处境竟这样一新——手里拿着帽子，等候一个年轻生灵进来；那生灵的生命也正经历着一场蜕变——一场趋向未定之局的悲剧性蜕变，而他怀着忧惧感到，自己的行动仍系在那局里。
格温多琳进来了，样子变了；不只是因一身丧服，还因她脸上的神情比热那亚时多了一种安顿了的宁静。她的满足在于德龙达在那里；可两人相见握手时谁也没有笑；各人都满怀回忆——满怀焦灼的前瞻。她说：「你能来真好。我们坐吧。」随即在最近的一把椅子上坐下。他在她对面落座。
「我请你来，是因为要你告诉我，我该做什么。」她开门见山地说。「你觉得对的事，别怕告诉我，哪怕听着严苛。我已经打定主意照办了。我从前怕穷；一想到要仰人鼻息就受不了；所以我做了那件事——所以嫁了人。更糟的事如今我都受过了。倘若你认为我该穷着，我想我受得了。我丈夫的遗嘱，你知道么？」
「知道，雨果爵士告诉过我。」德龙达说，已猜到她要问什么。
「他留给我的东西，我该拿么？我把我的想法告诉你。」格温多琳说，带着更紧张的急切。「也许你不大知道，我出嫁时，心里确实把母亲掂得很重。我是自私，可我确实爱她，也确实心疼她的贫穷；起初我最痛苦的时候，最安慰我的，就是因我出嫁，她的日子好过了。

===Original===

The thing that would be hardest to me now would be to see her in poverty again; and I have been thinking that if I took enough to provide for her, and no more﻿—nothing for myself﻿—it would not be wrong; for I was very precious to my mother﻿—and he took me from her﻿—and he meant﻿—and if she had known﻿—”
Gwendolen broke off. She had been preparing herself for this interview by thinking of hardly anything else than this question of right toward her mother; but the question had carried with it thoughts and reasons which it was impossible for her to utter, and these perilous remembrances swarmed between her words, making her speech more and more agitated and tremulous. She looked down helplessly at her hands, now unladen of all rings except her wedding-ring.
“Do not hurt yourself by speaking of that,” said Deronda, tenderly. “There is no need; the case is very simple. I think I can hardly judge wrongly about it. You consult me because I am the only person to whom you have confided the most painful part of your experience: and I can understand your scruples.” He did not go on immediately, waiting for her to recover herself. The silence seemed to Gwendolen full of the tenderness that she heard in his voice, and she had courage to lift up her eyes and look at him as he said, “You are conscious of something which you feel to be a crime toward one who is dead. You think that you have forfeited all claim as a wife. You shrink from taking what was his. You want to keep yourself from profiting by his death. Your feeling even urges you to some self-punishment﻿—some scourging of the self that disobeyed your better will﻿—the will that struggled against temptation. I have known something of that myself. Do I understand you?”
“Yes﻿—at least, I want to be good﻿—not like what I have been,” said Gwendolen. “I will try to bear what you think I ought to bear. I have tried to tell you the worst about myself. What ought I to do?”
“If no one but yourself were concerned in this question of income,” said Deronda, “I should hardly dare to urge you against any remorseful prompting; but I take as a guide now, your feeling about Mrs. Davilow, which seems to me quite just. I cannot think that your husband’s dues even to yourself are nullified by any act you have committed. He voluntarily entered into your life, and affected its course in what is always the most momentous way.

===Chinese===

「如今最叫我受不了的，就是眼见她再陷进贫穷；我一直在想，倘若我只拿够供养她的那一份，多一分也不要——自己分文不取——那便不算错；因为我在母亲心里是极珍贵的——是他把我从她身边夺走的——他存心——倘若她知道了——」
格温多琳说不下去了。为这场会面做准备的这些天，她心里翻来覆去几乎只有这桩对母亲的是非；可这问题牵连着的思绪与缘由，她无法出口；那些凶险的记忆在她的字句间蜂拥，使她的话越说越激动、越说越颤。她无助地低头看自己的手——如今除了结婚戒指，所有戒指都已卸尽。
「别再提那个，免得伤了自己。」德龙达温言道。「不必了；事情很简单。我想我不会断错的。你来问我，因为我是惟一知道你经历中最惨痛部分的人：你的顾虑，我懂。」他没有立刻说下去，等她自己平复。在格温多琳听来，那沉默同他声音里的温存一样满；她鼓起勇气抬眼看他，听他说：「你心里存着一件事，你觉得那是对一个死者的罪。你以为自己丧失尽了一切做妻子的权利。你畏于取用他的东西。你要使自己不得益于他的死。你的情感甚至催你去自罚——去鞭笞那个违背了你更好的意志的自我——那意志曾同诱惑搏斗。这种滋味，我自己也尝过一些。我懂你么？」
「是——至少，我想变好——不再是从前的我。」格温多琳说。「你认为我该承受什么，我就尽力承受。我尽力把最坏的我告诉了你。我该怎么办？」
「倘若这进项的问题只关你一个人，」德龙达说，「那任何出于悔恨的驱使，我都不敢劝你违逆；可如今我引为向导的，是你对戴维洛太太的那份心意，在我看来它相当正当。我不认为你丈夫对你本人应尽的一切，会因你做过的任何事而一笔勾销。是他自愿走进你的生命，又以人间最关紧要的方式改动了它的航向。

===Original===

But setting that aside, it was due from him in his position that he should provide for your mother, and he of course understood that if this will took effect she would share the provision he had made for you.”
“She has had eight hundred a year. What I thought of was to take that and leave the rest,” said Gwendolen. She had been so long inwardly arguing for this as a permission, that her mind could not at once take another attitude.
“I think it is not your duty to fix a limit in that way,” said Deronda. “You would be making a painful enigma for Mrs. Davilow; an income from which you shut yourself out must be embittered to her. And your own course would become too difficult. We agreed at Genoa that the burden on your conscience is one what no one ought to be admitted to the knowledge of. The future beneficence of your life will be best furthered by your saving all others from the pain of that knowledge. In my opinion you ought simply to abide by the provisions of your husband’s will, and let your remorse tell only on the use that you will make of your monetary independence.”
In uttering the last sentence Deronda automatically took up his hat which he had laid on the floor beside him. Gwendolen, sensitive to his slightest movement, felt her heart giving a great leap, as if it too had a consciousness of its own, and would hinder him from going: in the same moment she rose from her chair, unable to reflect that the movement was an acceptance of his apparent intention to leave her; and Deronda, of course, also rose, advancing a little.
“I will do what you tell me,” said Gwendolen, hurriedly; “but what else shall I do?” No other than these simple words were possible to her; and even these were too much for her in a state of emotion where her proud secrecy was disenthroned: as the childlike sentences fell from her lips they reacted on her like a picture of her own helplessness, and she could not check the sob which sent the large tears to her eyes. Deronda, too, felt a crushing pain; but imminent consequences were visible to him, and urged him to the utmost exertion of conscience. When she had pressed her tears away, he said, in a gently questioning tone,
“You will probably be soon going with Mrs. Davilow into the country.”
“Yes, in a week or ten days.” Gwendolen waited an instant, turning her eyes vaguely toward the window, as if looking at some imagined prospect.

===Chinese===

「可撇开这层不谈，以他的身份，供养你的母亲本是他分内之责；他当然明白，这遗嘱一旦生效，她自会分享他为你做的这一份安排。」
「她一向有八百镑一年。我想的就是把这份拿下来，其余都不要。」格温多琳说。她在心里为这方案争辩得太久，把它当成了一种许可，一时转不过别的立场来。
「我认为，用这种方式划一条界线，不是你的义务。」德龙达说。「那等于给戴维洛太太造一个痛苦的哑谜；一份你自己拒绝沾边的进项，在她嘴里必是苦的。而你自己的路也会变得太难。我们在热那亚已商定：你良心上的重负，是不容任何人知晓的。你日后一生为善，最好的成全，就是使旁人全都免于知晓的痛苦。依我看，你只应照你丈夫遗嘱的条款办，让你的悔恨只在你如何使用这份钱财自由上说话。」
说最后一句时，德龙达下意识地拾起了搁在脚边地上的帽子。格温多琳对他的最细微的动静都敏感，只觉心口猛地一跳，仿佛那颗心也有自己的知觉，要拦住他走；同一瞬间她从椅子里站起来，来不及细想这一动已是默认了他明显的告辞之意；德龙达自然也站了起来，向前挪了半步。
「你吩咐什么，我就做什么。」格温多琳急急地说；「可除了这个，我还能做什么？」她只说得出这几句简单的话；而在她那傲守的缄默已被掳下宝座的心绪里，连这几句也嫌太多：那天真的句子一出口，便像一幅她自己无助的画像反照回她身上，她止不住那声呜咽，大颗的泪涌上眼睛。德龙达也感到一阵碾压般的痛；可即将到来的后果在他眼里清晰可见，逼着他把良知用尽。等她拭去了泪，他用轻声探询的语调说：
「你们大概不久就要同戴维洛太太下乡去了吧。」
「是，一周或十天之内。」格温多琳顿了顿，茫然把眼睛转向窗子，像在眺望某个想象中的前景。

===Original===

“I want to be kind to them all﻿—they can be happier than I can. Is that the best I can do?”
“I think so. It is a duty that cannot be doubtful,” said Deronda. He paused a little between his sentences, feeling a weight of anxiety on all his words. “Other duties will spring from it. Looking at your life as a debt may seem the dreariest view of things at a distance; but it cannot really be so. What makes life dreary is the want of motive: but once beginning to act with that penitential, loving purpose you have in your mind, there will be unexpected satisfactions﻿—there will be newly-opening needs﻿—continually coming to carry you on from day to day. You will find your life growing like a plant.”
Gwendolen turned her eyes on him with the look of one athirst toward the sound of unseen waters. Deronda felt the look as if she had been stretching her arms toward him from a forsaken shore. His voice took an affectionate imploringness when he said,
“This sorrow, which has cut down to the root, has come to you while you are so young﻿—try to think of it not as a spoiling of your life, but as a preparation for it. Let it be a preparation﻿—” Anyone overhearing his tones would have thought he was entreating for his own happiness. “See! you have been saved from the worst evils that might have come from your marriage, which you feel was wrong. You have had a vision of injurious, selfish action﻿—a vision of possible degradation; think that a severe angel, seeing you along the road of error, grasped you by the wrist and showed you the horror of the life you must avoid. And it has come to you in your springtime. Think of it as a preparation. You can, you will, be among the best of women, such as make others glad that they were born.”
The words were like the touch of a miraculous hand to Gwendolen. Mingled emotions streamed through her frame with a strength that seemed the beginning of a new existence, having some new power or other which stirred in her vaguely. So pregnant is the divine hope of moral recovery with the energy that fulfills it. So potent in us is the infused action of another soul, before which we bow in complete love. But the new existence seemed inseparable from Deronda: the hope seemed to make his presence permanent. It was not her thought, that he loved her, and would cling to her﻿—a thought would have tottered with improbability; it was her spiritual breath.

===Chinese===

「我想好好待他们所有的人——他们能比我幸福。这是我能做的最好的事么？」
「我想是的。这是一桩无可置疑的义务。」德龙达说。他句与句之间略作停顿，感到每个字都压着焦虑。「别的义务会从它里面长出来。把一生看作一笔偿债，远远望去似乎是最灰暗的看法；其实不会真是这样。使人生灰暗的是动机的匮乏：而一旦照你心里那个悔罪的、爱的宗旨行动起来，自有意外的满足——自有新开的需索——源源而来，把你从一天载往下一天。你会发现你的生命像一株植物那样生长。」
格温多琳把眼睛转向他，那目光，像渴极的人望向看不见的水声。德龙达感到那目光，仿佛她正从一座被遗弃的岸上向他伸张双臂。他的声音带上了深情的恳求，当他说：
「这场悲伤斩到了根上，却来得这样早——试着别把它看作对你一生的败坏，而看作对它的预备。就让它是一场预备——」旁人若听见他的声调，必以为他在恳求自己的幸福。「你看！你已从那桩你自知错误的婚姻可能带来的最坏的祸患里被救出来了。你看见了损人利己的行为——看见了可能堕落的下场；你就想：一位严厉的天使，望见你走在错路上，一把攥住你的手腕，指给你看你必须避开的那种生活的可怖。而这一切临到你，是在你的春天。就把它当作预备吧。你能——你将会——跻身于最好的女人之列，那种女人，叫别人庆幸自己生在世上。」
这些话于格温多琳，像一只神迹之手的抚触。交织的情感涌过她的全身，带着一种仿佛新生命开端的力量，内里有某种新的能力在她身上朦胧地萌动。道德新生的神圣希望，原是这样孕育着成就它的精力。另一个灵魂注入我们心里的行动，原是这样有力，令我们以全然的爱向它俯首。可这新生命仿佛同德龙达分不开：那希望仿佛使他的在场成了恒久。这并非她想「他爱我、会守着我」——一个念头会被荒唐压垮；这是她灵性的呼吸。

===Original===

For the first time since that terrible moment on the sea a flush rose and spread over her cheek, brow and neck, deepened an instant or two, and then gradually disappeared. She did not speak.
Deronda advanced and put out his hand, saying, “I must not weary you.”
She was startled by the sense that he was going, and put her hand in his, still without speaking.
“You look ill yet﻿—unlike yourself,” he added, while he held her hand.
“I can’t sleep much,” she answered, with some return of her dispirited manner. “Things repeat themselves in me so. They come back﻿—they will all come back,” she ended, shudderingly, a chill fear threatening her.
“By degrees they will be less insistent,” said Deronda. He could not drop her hand or move away from her abruptly.
“Sir Hugo says he shall come to stay at Diplow,” said Gwendolen, snatching at previously intended words which had slipped away from her. “You will come too.”
“Probably,” said Deronda, and then feeling that the word was cold, he added, correctively, “Yes, I shall come,” and then released her hand, with the final friendly pressure of one who has virtually said goodbye.
“And not again here, before I leave town?” said Gwendolen, with timid sadness, looking as pallid as ever.
What could Deronda say? “If I can be of any use﻿—if you wish me﻿—certainly I will.”
“I must wish it,” said Gwendolen, impetuously; “you know I must wish it. What strength have I? Who else is there?” Again a sob was rising.
Deronda felt a pang, which showed itself in his face. He looked miserable as he said, “I will certainly come.”
Gwendolen perceived the change in his face; but the intense relief of expecting him to come again could not give way to any other feeling, and there was a recovery of the inspired hope and courage in her.
“Don’t be unhappy about me,” she said, in a tone of affectionate assurance. “I shall remember your words﻿—every one of them. I shall remember what you believe about me; I shall try.”
She looked at him firmly, and put out her hand again as if she had forgotten what had passed since those words of his which she promised to remember. But there was no approach to a smile on her lips. She had never smiled since her husband’s death. When she stood still and in silence, she looked like a melancholy statue of the Gwendolen whose laughter had once been so ready when others were grave.

===Chinese===

自海上那可怕的一刻以来，一团红晕头一回升起来，漫过她的脸颊、额头和脖颈，深了一两瞬，又渐渐褪去。她没有说话。
德龙达上前伸出手，说：「我不能叫你累了。」
惊觉他就要走了，她把手放进他手里，仍没有说话。
「你气色还是不好——不像你。」他握着她的手又添了一句。
「我睡不多。」她答道，蔫蔫的神气又回到身上。「事情总在我心里一遍遍重演。它们回来——它们全会回来的。」她末了打着颤说，一股寒凛的恐惧向她逼来。
「慢慢地，它们就不会这样步步紧逼了。」德龙达说。他不能骤然撒开她的手、骤然离开她。
「雨果爵士说要来迪普洛住。」格温多琳说，赶忙抓住那句早想好、却已溜走的话。「你也会来的。」
「大概。」德龙达说，随即觉得这字眼太冷，又补正道：「会，我会来的。」然后放开她的手，带着最后一握的友善——那已是实际上的道别。
「我离城之前，不再来这里了么？」格温多琳说，怯怯的悲伤，脸色同先前一样苍白。
德龙达还能说什么呢？「若我能派上用场——若你需要我——我一定来。」
「我需要。」格温多琳急促地说；「你知道我需要。我还有什么力气？除了你还有谁？」呜咽又要涌上来。
德龙达感到一阵刺痛，痛意浮上了脸。他说「我一定来」时，神色凄然。
格温多琳看见了他脸上的变化；可盼到他再来的那种强烈的宽解容不下别的感觉，她心里那受启的希望与勇气又回来了。
「别为我难过。」她说，声调里是深情的笃定。「我会记住你的话——每一句。我会记住你对我的信心；我会努力的。」
她坚定地望着他，又伸出手来，仿佛已忘记自他那几句她允诺记住的话以后的一切。可她的唇边没有一丝将笑未笑的意思。自丈夫死后，她再没有笑过。她静立无语时，像一尊忧郁的雕像——雕的是从前的格温多琳，那个旁人一正色她便笑靥立现的格温多琳。

===Original===

It is only by remembering the searching anguish which had changed the aspect of the world for her that we can understand her behavior to Deronda﻿—the unreflecting openness, nay, the importunate pleading, with which she expressed her dependence on him. Considerations such as would have filled the minds of indifferent spectators could not occur to her, any more than if flames had been mounting around her, and she had flung herself into his open arms and clung about his neck that he might carry her into safety. She identified him with the struggling regenerative process in her which had begun with his action. Is it any wonder that she saw her own necessity reflected in his feeling? She was in that state of unconscious reliance and expectation which is a common experience with us when we are preoccupied with our own trouble or our own purposes. We diffuse our feeling over others, and count on their acting from our motives. Her imagination had not been turned to a future union with Deronda by any other than the spiritual tie which had been continually strengthening; but also it had not been turned toward a future separation from him. Lovemaking and marriage﻿—how could they now be the imagery in which poor Gwendolen’s deepest attachment could spontaneously clothe itself? Mighty Love had laid his hand upon her; but what had he demanded of her? Acceptance of rebuke﻿—the hard task of self-change﻿—confession﻿—endurance. If she cried toward him, what then? She cried as the child cries whose little feet have fallen backward﻿—cried to be taken by the hand, lest she should lose herself.
The cry pierced Deronda. What position could have been more difficult for a man full of tenderness, yet with clear foresight? He was the only creature who knew the real nature of Gwendolen’s trouble: to withdraw himself from any appeal of hers would be to consign her to a dangerous loneliness. He could not reconcile himself to the cruelty of apparently rejecting her dependence on him; and yet in the nearer or farther distance he saw a coming wrench, which all present strengthening of their bond would make the harder.
He was obliged to risk that. He went once and again to Park Lane before Gwendolen left; but their interviews were in the presence of Mrs. Davilow, and were therefore less agitating.

===Chinese===

惟有记得那场改变了整个世界面目的拷问般的苦痛，我们才能理解她对德龙达的举止——那种不加思索的敞开，甚至是纠缠不休的恳求，她就这样表明自己倚赖着他。那些足以占满漠然旁观者心思的种种计较，在她根本无从发生，就像烈焰四起时，一个人纵身投入他张开的怀抱、搂住他的脖颈，好让他把自己抱出险境——那时还有什么计较。她已把他同自己身上那场挣扎中的新生合为一体——那新生，正是始于他的作为。她在他情感里照见自己的必需，又何足为奇？她正处在那种不自觉的倚赖与期待之中——当我们被自身的祸事或自身的目的占满时，这是我们共有的经验：我们把自己的情感敷在别人身上，指望他们凭我们的动机行事。她的想象，从未借任何别的名目转向同德龙达的未来结合——除了那条不断加固的心灵纽带；可它也从未转向同他的未来分离。求爱与婚嫁——如今它们还怎么能充作衣裳，让可怜的格温多琳最深的依恋自然而然地穿上？大能的爱已把手按在她身上；可他向她要了什么？领受责备——自我改变的苦功——忏悔——忍耐。倘若她朝他哭喊，那又是什么？她哭，像那小脚倒绊跌了的孩子那样哭——哭着要人牵住手，惟恐自己走失。
这哭声刺穿了德龙达。一个满怀柔情、却又目光清明的人，还有什么处境比这更难？他是惟一知道格温多琳苦况底细的人：从她的任何恳求前抽身，都等于把她交给一种凶险的孤独。他不忍让自己做出那看似拒绝她倚赖的残忍；然而或远或近，他望见一场行将到来的撕裂，而此刻对两人纽带的每一分加固，都只会使那撕裂更疼。
他只得冒这个险。格温多琳离城之前，他到公园巷去过一两回；但会面都有戴维洛太太在场，因而少了些激荡。

===Original===

Gwendolen, since she had determined to accept her income, had conceived a project which she liked to speak of: it was to place her mother and sisters with herself in Offendene again, and, as she said, piece back her life unto that time when they first went there, and when everything was happiness about her, only she did not know it. The idea had been mentioned to Sir Hugo, who was going to exert himself about the letting of Gadsmere for a rent which would more than pay the rent of Offendene. All this was told to Deronda, who willingly dwelt on a subject that seemed to give some soothing occupation to Gwendolen. He said nothing and she asked nothing, of what chiefly occupied himself. Her mind was fixed on his coming to Diplow before the autumn was over; and she no more thought of the Lapidoths﻿—the little Jewess and her brother﻿—as likely to make a difference in her destiny, than of the fermenting political and social leaven which was making a difference in the history of the world. In fact poor Gwendolen’s memory had been stunned, and all outside the lava-lit track of her troubled conscience, and her effort to get deliverance from it, lay for her in dim forgetfulness.

===Chinese===

格温多琳自打定主意接受那份进项，便酝酿起一项她爱挂在嘴边的计划：带着母亲和妹妹们重新搬回奥芬迪恩（Offendene），而且照她的说法，把自己的人生重新拼回初搬去的那段时光——那时她四周事事是幸福，只是她自己不知道。这想法已对雨果爵士提过；爵士打算张罗着把加兹米尔（Gadsmere）租出去，租金尽敷奥芬迪恩的租钱且有余。这些都说给了德龙达听；这话题似乎能给格温多琳一点抚慰的事做，他也乐于顺着它谈。至于他自己心头的大事，他一字未提，她也一无所问。她一心惦着的，是秋尽之前他会来迪普洛；至于拉皮多特家的人——那个小小的犹太姑娘和她哥哥——可能给她的命运带来什么改变，她同想不到那正在改写世界历史的、发酵着的政治与社会的酵素一样，全然想不到。事实上，可怜的格温多琳的记忆已被震麻；在她那被良知煎熬的熔岩照亮的轨迹之外——连同她求得解脱的努力之外——的一切，都躺在她昏沉的遗忘里。

### LXVI / 第六十六章
===Original===

> One day still fierce ’mid many a day struck calm.

Meanwhile Ezra and Mirah, whom Gwendolen did not include in her thinking about Deronda, were having their relation to him drawn closer and brought into fuller light.
The father Lapidoth had quitted his daughter at the doorstep, ruled by that possibility of staking something in play or betting which presented itself with the handling of any sum beyond the price of staying actual hunger, and left no care for alternative prospects or resolutions. Until he had lost everything he never considered whether he would apply to Mirah again or whether he would brave his son’s presence. In the first moment he had shrunk from encountering Ezra as he would have shrunk from any other situation of disagreeable constraint; and the possession of Mirah’s purse was enough to banish the thought of future necessities. The gambling appetite is more absolutely dominant than bodily hunger, which can be neutralized by an emotional or intellectual excitation; but the passion for watching chances﻿—the habitual suspensive poise of the mind in actual or imaginary play﻿—nullifies the susceptibility of other excitation. In its final, imperious stage, it seems the unjoyous dissipation of demons, seeking diversion on the burning marl of perdition.
But every form of selfishness, however abstract and unhuman, requires the support of at least one meal a day; and though Lapidoth’s appetite for food and drink was extremely moderate, he had slipped into a shabby, unfriendly form of life in which the appetite could not be satisfied without some ready money. When, in a brief visit at a house which announced “Pyramids” on the window-blind, he had first doubled and trebled and finally lost Mirah’s thirty shillings, he went out with her empty purse in his pocket, already balancing in his mind whether he should get another immediate stake by pawning the purse, or whether he should go back to her giving himself a good countenance by restoring the purse, and declaring that he had used the money in paying a score that was standing against him. Besides, among the sensibilities still left strong in Lapidoth was the sensibility to his own claims, and he appeared to himself to have a claim on any property his children might possess, which was stronger than the justice of his son’s resentment.

===Chinese===

> 多少个日子被击打得风平浪静，独有一日，犹自狂烈。

与此同时，以斯拉和米拉——格温多琳想到德龙达时从没把他们算进去——同他的关系，却在拉近，也在显出更完全的光亮。
父亲拉皮多思在门口台阶上把女儿撤下之后，便由那可能性支配着——只要手里过手的钱超过果腹的价钱，拿点什么去赌去押的可能便自己出现，其余的前景与决心一概无暇顾及。不到输光一切，他从不考虑要不要再去求米拉、要不要硬着头皮面对儿子。起初那一刻，他躲着不见以斯拉，就像躲任何一处难受的拘束；而米拉那只钱袋在手，足以把日后的需用逐出念头。赌瘾比饥肠更绝对地主宰人——饥肠尚可被一阵情绪或思想的兴奋中和；而盯注输赢的激情——心智在实际或想象的赌局里那种悬而不决的架势——把其余一切兴奋的敏感都取消了。到了它最后那专横的阶段，它简直像魔鬼们那种毫无欢趣的消遣，在毁灭的烧灼的泥灰岩上寻开心。
可一切形式的自私，无论多么抽象、多么非人，一天至少也得有一顿饭撑着；拉皮多思虽然吃喝的胃口极有节制，却也滑进了一种寒酸而无友的生活形态——没有点现钱，那胃口便满足不了。在一处窗帘上写着「金字塔」的人家短暂逗留时，他把米拉那三十先令翻了一倍、又翻了一倍，末了输了个精光；他揣着她那只空钱袋走出来，心里已在盘算：是立刻把这只钱袋当掉、再弄一笔赌本呢，还是回到她那里去，把钱袋还她、装出一副好面孔，声明那笔钱拿去还了他欠下的一笔旧账？况且，拉皮多思身上尚存的敏感里，还有一层对自己权利的敏感；他觉得自己对儿女可能拥有的任何财物都有一份权利，这权利比儿子怨恨他的那份公道还要硬。

===Original===

After all, to take up his lodging with his children was the best thing he could do; and the more he thought of meeting Ezra the less he winced from it, his imagination being more wrought on by the chances of his getting something into his pocket with safety and without exertion, than by the threat of a private humiliation. Luck had been against him lately; he expected it to turn﻿—and might not the turn begin with some opening of supplies which would present itself through his daughter’s affairs and the good friends she had spoken of? Lapidoth counted on the fascination of his cleverness﻿—an old habit of mind which early experience had sanctioned: and it is not only women who are unaware of their diminished charm, or imagine that they can feign not to be worn out.
The result of Lapidoth’s rapid balancing was that he went toward the little square in Brompton with the hope that, by walking about and watching, he might catch sight of Mirah going out or returning, in which case his entrance into the house would be made easier. But it was already evening﻿—the evening of the day next to that which he had first seen her; and after a little waiting, weariness made him reflect that he might ring, and if she were not at home he might ask the time at which she was expected. But on coming near the house he knew that she was at home: he heard her singing.
Mirah, seated at the piano, was pouring forth “*Herz, mein Herz*,” while Ezra was listening with his eyes shut, when Mrs. Adam opened the door, and said in some embarrassment,
“A gentleman below says he is your father, miss.”
“I will go down to him,” said Mirah, starting up immediately and looking at her brother.
“No, Mirah, not so,” said Ezra, with decision. “Let him come up, Mrs. Adam.”
Mirah stood with her hands pinching each other, and feeling sick with anxiety, while she continued looking at Ezra, who had also risen, and was evidently much shaken. But there was an expression in his face which she had never seen before; his brow was knit, his lips seemed hardened with the same severity that gleamed from his eye.
When Mrs. Adam opened the door to let in the father, she could not help casting a look at the group, and after glancing from the younger man to the elder, said to herself as she closed the door, “Father, sure enough.”

===Chinese===

说到底，到儿女那里去落脚，是他能行的最好一步；见以斯拉这件事，他想得越多，越不怕了——打动他想象的，与其说是私下受辱的威胁，不如说是平平安安、不费力气往口袋里弄进点什么的机会。近来手气一直同他作对；他指望它转——这转机，兴许就从女儿的事、从她说起的那几位好朋友那里开出一条财路开始呢？拉皮多思指望靠自己聪明的魅惑——一种早年经历曾经认可过的旧心习：对自己的魅力减退了还浑然不觉的，或者自以为装一装就不显破败的，又何止是女人。
拉皮多思一番飞快的权衡，结果是朝布朗普顿那个小广场走去，指望四下走走、盯着点，或许能撞见米拉出门或回家——那样，他进那栋房子便顺当些。可天已经黑了——那已是他初见她的第二天晚上；等了一小会儿，倦意叫他想起，不妨按铃；她若不在家，可以问问她几时回来。可走到房子近前，他知道她在家：他听见她在唱歌。
米拉正坐在钢琴前倾吐着《心啊，我的心》（Herz, mein Herz），以斯拉闭目听着；这时亚当太太开了门，有点窘地说：
「楼下有位先生，说是您的父亲，小姐。」
「我下楼去见他，」米拉说着立刻起身，望着哥哥。
「不，米拉，不能这样，」以斯拉决然说。「请他上来吧，亚当太太。」
米拉站着，两只手互相掐着，焦虑得心里发呕，眼睛仍旧望着以斯拉；以斯拉也已起身，显然大为震动。可他脸上有一种她从未见过的表情：眉头锁着，嘴唇仿佛同眼里闪出的那股严酷凝在了一起。
亚当太太开门放父亲进来时，忍不住朝这一家人看了一眼，从年轻的望到年长的，关上门时自语道：「真是父子，错不了。」

===Original===

The likeness was that of outline, which is always most striking at the first moment; the expression had been wrought into the strongest contrasts by such hidden or inconspicuous differences as can make the genius of a Cromwell within the outward type of a father who was no more than a respectable parishioner.
Lapidoth had put on a melancholy expression beforehand, but there was some real wincing in his frame as he said,
“Well, Ezra, my boy, you hardly know me after so many years.”
“I know you﻿—too well﻿—father,” said Ezra, with a slow biting solemnity which made the word father a reproach.
“Ah, you are not pleased with me. I don’t wonder at it. Appearances have been against me. When a man gets into straits he can’t do just as he would by himself or anybody else, *I*’ve suffered enough, I know,” said Lapidoth, quickly. In speaking he always recovered some glibness and hardihood; and now turning toward Mirah, he held out her purse, saying, “Here’s your little purse, my dear. I thought you’d be anxious about it because of that bit of writing. I’ve emptied it, you’ll see, for I had a score to pay for food and lodging. I knew you would like me to clear myself, and here I stand﻿—without a single farthing in my pocket﻿—at the mercy of my children. You can turn me out if you like, without getting a policeman. Say the word, Mirah; say, ‘Father, I’ve had enough of you; you made a pet of me, and spent your all on me, when I couldn’t have done without you; but I can do better without you now,’﻿—say that, and I’m gone out like a spark. I shan’t spoil your pleasure again.” The tears were in his voice as usual, before he had finished.
“You know I could never say it, father,” answered Mirah, with not the less anguish because she felt the falsity of everything in his speech except the implied wish to remain in the house.
“Mirah, my sister, leave us!” said Ezra, in a tone of authority.
She looked at her brother falteringly, beseechingly﻿—in awe of his decision, yet unable to go without making a plea for this father who was like something that had grown in her flesh with pain. She went close to her brother, and putting her hand in his, said, in a low voice, but not so low as to be unheard by Lapidoth, “Remember, Ezra﻿—you said my mother would not have shut him out.”
“Trust me, and go,” said Ezra.

===Chinese===

那相像只在轮廓——轮廓的相像总在初见的一刻最惊人；表情却已被造成最强的对照，靠的正是那些藏着的、不起眼的差异——正是这样的差异，能在一个不过体面教民的父亲的外形里，造出一个克伦威尔的天才。
拉皮多思事先给自己敷上了一副愁苦的表情，可开口时，身子里也真有几分畏缩：
「哎，以斯拉，我的孩子，隔了这么多年，你几乎认不得我啦。」
「我认得你——太认得了——父亲，」以斯拉说，字字迟缓、带咬啮的严峻，把「父亲」两个字说成了一句责斥。
「啊，你对我不得劲。我不奇怪。外表都同我作对。人一落到窘境，自己也好、别人也好，就由不得自己做主了。我受够了苦，我知道，」拉皮多思很快地说。一开口，他总能找回几分流利和胆气；这时他转向米拉，递出她的钱袋，说：「你的小钱袋在这儿，亲爱的。我想你会为它着急的，因为里头那张小字条。我把它倒空了，你会看到的——我欠着一笔食宿的账，得还。我知道你愿意我把账还清；我如今站在这儿——口袋里连一个铜子也没有——全凭儿女发落。你们高兴，尽可以把我撵出去，用不着叫警察。说一声吧，米拉；你说：『父亲，我受够你了；你从前把我当宝贝疼，把你的全部花在我身上，那时我没你不行；可如今没有你，我倒更好过』——你这样说，我就像个火星子似的熄掉走人。我再不会搅了你们的快活。」不等说完，他嗓音里照例已经带了泪。
「你知道我永远说不出这样的话，父亲，」米拉答道；她感到他话里的一切都是假的，只有那层想留下的意思不是假的——这并不使她的痛苦减轻分毫。
「米拉，我的妹妹，你出去！」以斯拉用权威的声调说。
她望着哥哥，迟疑、哀恳——慑于他的决断，却又不能不为这个父亲讨一句情；这父亲像一块长在她肉里的东西，长时带疼。她走到哥哥跟前，把手放进他手里，低声——却没低到拉皮多思听不见——说：「记住，以斯拉——你说过，我母亲是不会把他关在门外的。」
「信我，去吧，」以斯拉说。

===Original===

She left the room, but after going a few steps up the stairs, sat down with a palpitating heart. If, because of anything her brother said to him, he went away﻿—
Lapidoth had some sense of what was being prepared for him in his son’s mind, but he was beginning to adjust himself to the situation and find a point of view that would give him a cool superiority to any attempt at humiliating him. This haggard son, speaking as from a sepulchre, had the incongruity which selfish levity learns to see in suffering, and until the unrelenting pincers of disease clutch its own flesh. Whatever preaching he might deliver must be taken for a matter of course, as a man finding shelter from hail in an open cathedral might take a little religious howling that happened to be going on there.
Lapidoth was not born with this sort of callousness: he had achieved it.
“This home that we have here,” Ezra began, “is maintained partly by the generosity of a beloved friend who supports me, and partly by the labors of my sister, who supports herself. While we have a home we will not shut you out from it. We will not cast you out to the mercy of your vices. For you are our father, and though you have broken your bond, we acknowledge ours. But I will never trust you. You absconded with money, leaving your debts unpaid; you forsook my mother; you robbed her of her little child and broke her heart; you have become a gambler, and where shame and conscience were there sits an insatiable desire; you were ready to sell my sister﻿—you had sold her, but the price was denied you. The man who has done these things must never expect to be trusted any more. We will share our food with you﻿—you shall have a bed, and clothing. We will do this duty to you, because you are our father. But you will never be trusted. You are an evil man: you made the misery of our mother. That such a man is our father is a brand on our flesh which will not cease smarting. But the Eternal has laid it upon us; and though human justice were to flog you for crimes, and your body fell helpless before the public scorn, we would still say, ‘This is our father; make way, that we may carry him out of your sight.’ ”
Lapidoth, in adjusting himself to what was coming, had not been able to foresee the exact intensity of the lightning or the exact course it would take﻿—that it would not fall outside his frame but through it.

她出了房门，上楼梯走了几级，便坐了下来，心砰砰地跳。倘若因为哥哥对他说了什么，他走了——
拉皮多思多少觉出儿子心里正为他备下什么，可他已开始把自己调适到这个局面里，找好一个视角，好教自己冷冷地凌驾于任何羞辱他的图谋之上。这个形容枯槁、声如出自坟墓的儿子，在自私的轻浮看来，正有一种「不合适」——轻浮的人就是在苦难里也学会看见这种不合适，直到疾病那不松口的铁钳夹住他自己的肉。
这种麻木，拉皮多思不是生来就有的：是他修炼成的。
「我们在这里的这一个家，」以斯拉开言道，「一部分靠一位挚友的慷慨扶持着，一部分靠我妹妹的劳作——她自食其力。只要我们还有家，就不会把你关在门外。我们不会把你抛出去任凭你的恶习发落。因为你是我们的父亲；你虽然毁了你那一方的约，我们这一方的，我们认。可我永远不会信任你。你卷款潜逃，欠债不还；你抛弃了我的母亲；你夺走她的小女儿，伤碎了她的心；你做了赌徒，在羞耻和良心原先坐镇的地方，如今坐着的是填不满的贪欲；你随时肯卖掉我的妹妹——你已经把她卖了，只是价钱没有如你的愿。做过这些事的人，永远别指望再被信任。我们的食物分你一份——你会有床铺，有衣穿。这分义务我们对你尽，因为你是我们的父亲。可你永远不会再被信任。你是个恶人：我们母亲的苦难是你造的。这样的人竟是我们的父亲，这是我们肉上的一块烙印，火辣辣地永不停歇。可这是永恒者加在我们身上的；哪怕人间的公义为你的罪鞭打你，你的身子当众倒在人人的鄙夷之下，我们仍会说：『这是我们的父亲；让开路，让我们把他抬出你们的视线。』」
拉皮多思对将临的事一路调适，却没能预见这闪电确切的烈度、确切的走向——它不会落在他身框的外面，而要贯穿而过。

===Original===

He could not foresee what was so new to him as this voice from the soul of his son. It touched that spring of hysterical excitability which Mirah used to witness in him when he sat at home and sobbed. As Ezra ended, Lapidoth threw himself into a chair and cried like a woman, burying his face against the table﻿—and yet, strangely, while this hysterical crying was an inevitable reaction in him under the stress of his son’s words, it was also a conscious resource in a difficulty; just as in early life, when he was a bright-faced curly young man, he had been used to avail himself of this subtly-poised physical susceptibility to turn the edge of resentment or disapprobation.
Ezra sat down again and said nothing﻿—exhausted by the shock of his own irrepressible utterance, the outburst of feelings which for years he had borne in solitude and silence. His thin hands trembled on the arms of the chair; he would hardly have found voice to answer a question; he felt as if he had taken a step toward beckoning Death. Meanwhile Mirah’s quick expectant ear detected a sound which her heart recognized: she could not stay out of the room any longer. But on opening the door her immediate alarm was for Ezra, and it was to his side that she went, taking his trembling hand in hers, which he pressed and found support in; but he did not speak or even look at her. The father with his face buried was conscious that Mirah had entered, and presently lifted up his head, pressed his handkerchief against his eyes, put out his hand toward her, and said with plaintive hoarseness, “Goodbye, Mirah; your father will not trouble you again. He deserves to die like a dog by the roadside, and he will. If your mother had lived, she would have forgiven me﻿—thirty-four years ago I put the ring on her finger under the *Chuppa*, and we were made one. She would have forgiven me, and we should have spent our old age together. But I haven’t deserved it. Goodbye.”
He rose from the chair as he said the last “goodbye.” Mirah had put her hand in his and held him. She was not tearful and grieving, but frightened and awestruck, as she cried out,
“No, father, no!” Then turning to her brother, “Ezra, you have not forbidden him?﻿—Stay, father, and leave off wrong things. Ezra, I cannot bear it. How can I say to my father, ‘Go and die!’ ”
“I have not said it,” Ezra answered, with great effort.

===Chinese===

他预见不到的，是这样一种他全然生疏的东西——发他儿子灵魂深处来的这个声音。它触动了那根歇斯底里的兴奋之弦——米拉从前常在家里看见他坐着呜咽时发作的那一根。以斯拉话音一落，拉皮多思便瘫进椅子里，像个女人似的哭出声，把脸埋在桌上——然而奇怪的是，这歇斯底里的哭，既是他受不住儿子那番话时必然的反应，也是他身处难题时自觉的一件法宝；正如年轻的时候——那时他是个脸色明亮、头发鬈曲的小伙子——他惯于利用这份拿捉得微妙的身体易感性，来磨掉别人的愤懑与非难。
以斯拉重新坐下，一言不发——被自己那番压抑不住的言辞的震动耗尽了；那是他多年孤独缄默中承受的感情，此刻迸发了出来。他枯瘦的手在椅臂上发抖；有人问一句话，他几乎找不出声音来答；他觉得自己像是朝死神招了招手，又挨近了一步。这时，米拉那竖着的耳朵捕捉到一个她的心一听便认出的声音：她再也待不在门外了。可一开门，她先惊的是以斯拉，径直奔到他身边，把他颤抖的手握在自己手里；他握了握，从中得了支撑；却一言不发，甚至不看她。埋着脸的父亲觉出米拉进来了，随即抬起头，把手帕按在眼睛上，朝她伸出手，用哀怨的沙哑说：「再见了，米拉；你父亲不会再搅扰你了。他合该像条狗一样死在路边，他也会那样死的。你母亲要是活着，她会饶了我的——三十四年前，我在婚棚（Chuppa）下把戒指戴上她的手指，我们结为一体。她会饶了我的，我们本可以一起过完晚年。可我不配。再见了。」
说最后一声「再见」时，他从椅子里起身。米拉已把手放进他手里，拉住他。她没有流泪悲泣，而是又惊又惧，喊道：
「不，父亲，不！」随即转向哥哥：「以斯拉，你没有不许他留下吧？——留下吧，父亲，别再干坏事了。以斯拉，我受不住。我怎么能对自己的父亲说：『去死吧！』」
「我没有那样说，」以斯拉费了大劲才答出。

===Original===

“I have said, stay and be sheltered.”
“Then you will stay, father﻿—and be taken care of﻿—and come with me,” said Mirah, drawing him toward the door.
This was really what Lapidoth wanted. And for the moment he felt a sort of comfort in recovering his daughter’s dutiful attendance, that made a change of habits seem possible to him. She led him down to the parlor below, and said,
“This is my sitting-room when I am not with Ezra, and there is a bedroom behind which shall be yours. You will stay and be good, father. Think that you are come back to my mother, and that she has forgiven you﻿—she speaks to you through me.” Mirah’s tones were imploring, but she could not give one of her former caresses.
Lapidoth quickly recovered his composure, began to speak to Mirah of the improvement in her voice, and other easy subjects, and when Mrs. Adam came to lay out his supper, entered into converse with her in order to show her that he was not a common person, though his clothes were just now against him.
But in his usual wakefulness at night, he fell to wondering what money Mirah had by her, and went back over old Continental hours at Roulette, reproducing the method of his play, and the chances that had frustrated it. He had had his reasons for coming to England, but for most things it was a cursed country.
These were the stronger visions of the night with Lapidoth, and not the worn frame of his ireful son uttering a terrible judgment. Ezra did pass across the gaming-table, and his words were audible; but he passed like an insubstantial ghost, and his words had the heart eaten out of them by numbers and movements that seemed to make the very tissue of Lapidoth’s consciousness.

===Chinese===

「我说的是：留下，受庇护。」
「那你就留下，父亲——有人照应你——跟我来，」米拉说着，把他往门口引。
这其实正中拉皮多思的下怀。那一刻，他重新得到女儿恭顺的伺候，竟觉出一种安慰，仿佛改一改习惯于他也并非不可能。她领他到楼下的客厅，说：
「我不在以斯拉那里的时候，就坐在这间屋里；后面有一间卧室，归你。你留下，学好吧，父亲。就当你是回到我母亲跟前，就当她饶了你了——她借我的口同你说话。」米拉的声调是恳求的，可她再给不出从前那种亲昵的爱抚了。
拉皮多思很快恢复了镇定，开始同米拉谈起她嗓音的长进，和别的轻松话题；亚当太太来摆晚饭时，他又同她攀谈起来，好叫她明白他不是个寻常人——尽管他这身衣裳眼下同他作对。
可夜里照例睡不着，他渐渐琢磨起米拉手边有多少钱，又把大陆上那些轮盘赌的旧时光一一翻回，重温自己下注的路数、拆了它的台的那些运气。他到英国来自有他的缘故，可就大多数事而言，这是个可咒的国家。
夜里在拉皮多思眼前占上风的，是这些景象，而不是他那盛怒的儿子那枯槁的身架、那可怕的判词。以斯拉确也掠过赌台上空，他的话也听得见；可他像一个虚浮的鬼影掠过，他的话被数字与动向吃掉了心——那些数字与动向，仿佛就是拉皮多思意识的组织本身。

### LXVII / 第六十七章
===Original===

> The godhead in us wrings our noble deeds

From our reluctant selves.

It was an unpleasant surprise to Deronda when he returned from the Abbey to find the undesirable father installed in the lodgings at Brompton. Mirah had felt it necessary to speak of Deronda to her father, and even to make him as fully aware as she could of the way in which the friendship with Ezra had begun, and of the sympathy which had cemented it. She passed more lightly over what Deronda had done for her, omitting altogether the rescue from drowning, and speaking of the shelter she had found in Mrs. Meyrick’s family so as to leave her father to suppose that it was through these friends Deronda had become acquainted with her. She could not persuade herself to more completeness in her narrative: she could not let the breath of her father’s soul pass over her relation to Deronda. And Lapidoth, for reasons, was not eager in his questioning about the circumstances of her flight and arrival in England. But he was much interested in the fact of his children having a beneficent friend apparently high in the world.
It was the brother who told Deronda of this new condition added to their life. “I am become calm in beholding him now,” Ezra ended, “and I try to think it possible that my sister’s tenderness, and the daily tasting a life of peace, may win him to remain aloof from temptation. I have enjoined her, and she has promised, to trust him with no money. I have convinced her that he will buy with it his own destruction.”
Deronda first came on the third day from Ladipoth’s arrival. The new clothes for which he had been measured were not yet ready, and wishing to make a favorable impression, he did not choose to present himself in the old ones. He watched for Deronda’s departure, and, getting a view of him from the window, was rather surprised at his youthfulness, which Mirah had not mentioned, and which he had somehow thought out of the question in a personage who had taken up a grave friendship and hoary studies with the sepulchral Ezra. Lapidoth began to imagine that Deronda’s real or chief motive must be that he was in love with Mirah. And so much the better; for a tie to Mirah had more promise of indulgence for her father than a tie to Ezra: and Lapidoth was not without the hope of recommending himself to Deronda, and of softening any hard prepossessions.

===Chinese===

> 我们身上的神性，硬从迟疑的

自我手中拧出高贵的作为。

德龙达从修道院府回来，发现那位不受欢迎的父亲已在布朗普顿的寓所里安顿下来——这对他是一桩不快的意外。米拉觉得有必要对父亲说起德龙达，甚至尽可能让他明白：她同以斯拉的交情是怎样开始的，又是靠怎样的相知结成的。德龙达为她做的事，她说得轻描淡写，落水获救一节全然略去；说到在梅里克夫人家得到收留，也只顺着说，好让父亲以为是经由这些朋友，德龙达才同她相识。她说服不了自己把事情讲得更全：她不能容父亲灵魂的气息，吹过她同德龙达的关系。而拉皮多特自有缘故，也不急于细问她出逃和来到英国的情形。但他的儿女有这样一位乐善好施、看样子位分很高的朋友——这个事实他大感兴趣。
把这桩新添进他们生活里的境况告诉德龙达的，是哥哥。「如今我见到他，已经能平静了。」以斯拉末了说，「我竭力想让自己相信：妹妹的温柔，加上日日尝到平安生活的滋味，或许能引得他远离诱惑。我已叮嘱她不许把钱托付给他，她也答应了。我使她信了：他拿那钱，买到的只会是自己的毁灭。」
拉皮多特到后的第三天，德龙达头一回上门。量体制的新衣还没有做好；他既想留个好印象，便不愿穿着旧衣见客。他守着等德龙达离开，从窗口望了他一眼，倒吃了一惊——那人竟这样年轻；米拉没提过，而他不知怎么总觉得，一个肯同坟墓气派的以斯拉结下郑重的友谊、共修古老学问的人物，年轻是不可能的。拉皮多特渐渐想：德龙达真正的、或者说主要的动机，必是爱上了米拉。那就更好；因为系在米拉身上的纽带，比系在以斯拉身上的，更许给她父亲纵容的指望；而且拉皮多特并非没有希望博得德龙达的好感，把可能有的成见软化几分。

===Original===

He was behaving with much amiability, and trying in all ways at his command to get himself into easy domestication with his children﻿—entering into Mirah’s music, showing himself docile about smoking, which Mrs. Adam could not tolerate in her parlor, and walking out in the square with his German pipe, and the tobacco with which Mirah supplied him. He was too acute to offer any present remonstrance against the refusal of money, which Mirah told him that she must persist in as a solemn duty promised to her brother. He was comfortable enough to wait.
The next time Deronda came, Lapidoth, equipped in his new clothes, and satisfied with his own appearance, was in the room with Ezra, who was teaching himself, as a part of his severe duty, to tolerate his father’s presence whenever it was imposed. Deronda was cold and distant, the first sight of this man, who had blighted the lives of his wife and children, creating in him a repulsion that was even a physical discomfort. But Lapidoth did not let himself be discouraged, asked leave to stay and hear the reading of papers from the old chest, and actually made himself useful in helping to decipher some difficult German manuscript. This led him to suggest that it might be desirable to make a transcription of the manuscript, and he offered his services for this purpose, and also to make copies of any papers in Roman characters. Though Ezra’s young eyes he observed were getting weak, his own were still strong. Deronda accepted the offer, thinking that Lapidoth showed a sign of grace in the willingness to be employed usefully; and he saw a gratified expression in Ezra’s face, who, however, presently said, “Let all the writing be done here; for I cannot trust the papers out of my sight, lest there be an accident by burning or otherwise.” Poor Ezra felt very much as if he had a convict on leave under his charge. Unless he saw his father working, it was not possible to believe that he would work in good faith. But by this arrangement he fastened on himself the burden of his father’s presence, which was made painful not only through his deepest, longest associations, but also through Lapidoth’s restlessness of temperament, which showed itself the more as he become familiarized with his situation, and lost any awe he had felt of his son.

===Chinese===

他表现得极为和蔼，千方百计想在儿女中间混出一份自在的家庭生活——兴致勃勃地听米拉的音乐；抽烟上也很听话，亚当夫人的客厅容不得烟味，他便揣着德国烟斗、抽着米拉供给他的烟草，到广场上去溜达。米拉告诉他，拒不给钱这件事，她必须坚持下去，那是应承哥哥的神圣义务；他太精明，不肯当场就这一点发半句怨言。他日子过得够舒坦，等得起。
德龙达再来时，拉皮多特已披挂上新衣，对自己的仪表颇为满意，正同以斯拉待在屋里；以斯拉正在训练自己——当作严峻义务的一部分——忍受父亲每每强加于他的在场。
德龙达冷淡而疏远；一眼看见这个毁掉了妻儿生活的男人，他心里生出的憎恶甚至成了身体上的不适。可拉皮多特不气馁，请求留下旁听旧柜中文稿的诵读，还真派上了用场，帮忙辨读了几页艰涩的德文手稿。由此他提议，不妨把手稿誊录一份，他愿意效劳，凡罗马字母写成的文稿，他都可抄录。他注意到以斯拉那双还算年轻的眼睛已渐昏花，而自己的眼力还健。德龙达应允了，心想拉皮多特甘愿做点有用的事，总算露出一线善性；他也看见以斯拉脸上一副欣慰的神情——不过以斯拉随即说：「誊抄都在这里做；文稿出了我的眼皮我不放心，怕失火或出别的意外。」
可怜的以斯拉，觉得自己简直像看守一个放风取保的罪犯。不亲眼看着父亲干活，就没法相信他会实心实意地干。可这么一安排，他便把父亲在场的重负锁在了自己身上；那重负之苦，不仅来自他最深最久的种种联想，也来自拉皮多特坐立不安的性子——随着他对处境日渐熟惯、对儿子仅存的一点敬畏日渐消失，那性子显露得越发充分。

===Original===

The fact was, he was putting a strong constraint on himself in confining his attention for the sake of winning Deronda’s favor; and like a man in an uncomfortable garment he gave himself relief at every opportunity, going out to smoke, or moving about and talking, or throwing himself back in his chair and remaining silent, but incessantly carrying on a dumb language of facial movement or gesticulation: and if Mirah were in the room, he would fall into his old habit of talk with her, gossiping about their former doings and companions, or repeating quirks and stories, and plots of the plays he used to adapt, in the belief that he could at will command the vivacity of his earlier time. All this was a mortal infliction to Ezra; and when Mirah was at home she tried to relieve him, by getting her father down into the parlor and keeping watch over him there. What duty is made of a single difficult resolve? The difficulty lies in the daily unflinching support of consequences that mar the blessed return of morning with the prospect of irritation to be suppressed or shame to be endured. And such consequences were being borne by these, as by many other heroic children of an unworthy father﻿—with the prospect, at least to Mirah, of their stretching onward through the solid part of life.
Meanwhile Lapidoth’s presence had raised a new impalpable partition between Deronda and Mirah﻿—each of them dreading the soiling inferences of his mind, each of them interpreting mistakenly the increased reserve and diffidence of the other. But it was not very long before some light came to Deronda.
As soon as he could, after returning from his brief visit to the Abbey, he had called at Hans Meyrick’s rooms, feeling it, on more grounds than one, a due of friendship that Hans should be at once acquainted with the reasons of his late journey, and the changes of intention it had brought about. Hans was not there; he was said to be in the country for a few days; and Deronda, after leaving a note, waited a week, rather expecting a note in return.

===Chinese===

实情是：为博德龙达的欢心，他正强自约束着注意力；像穿一件不合身衣裳的人，一有机会便要松快松快——出去抽口烟，或者起身走动、说话，或者仰进椅子里默不作声，脸上的肌肉和手势却不停地说着一套哑语：米拉若在屋里，他便同她聊起旧日的习惯来，絮叨从前的事和从前的人，或者讲些俏皮话、小故事、他当年改编过的戏的情节，自信还能随意召来年轻时的那股活气。这一切对于以斯拉是致命的酷刑；米拉在家时便想法替他解围，把父亲引到楼下的客厅去，在那儿看着他。
哪有一桩义务是靠一次艰难的决心就做成的？难就难在日复一日、毫不畏缩地承担后果——它们糟蹋了清晨可祝福的归来，带来的是要压下的烦躁、要忍受的羞辱。这样的后果，兄妹俩正承受着，正如许多不配为父者的高尚儿女承受着的一样——而且照前景看，至少对米拉，这承受还要绵延下去，贯穿人生殷实的年月。
与此同时，拉皮多特的存在在德龙达和米拉之间竖起了一道新的无形的隔墙——两人都惧怕他脑子里那些沾泥带水的推想，又都把对方愈见的缄默与羞怯误会了。但没过多久，德龙达便得了些光亮。
那次去修道院府的短访归来后，他尽早去了汉斯·梅里克（Hans Meyrick）的住处；他觉得，出于不止一层的情谊，汉斯都该立刻知道他此番远行的缘由，以及由此带来的志向的改变。汉斯不在；说是下乡去了几天；德龙达留下便条，等了一个星期，颇盼着回一张。

===Original===

But receiving no word, and fearing some freak of feeling in the incalculably susceptible Hans, whose proposed sojourn at the Abbey he knew had been deferred, he at length made a second call, and was admitted into the painting-room, where he found his friend in a light coat, without a waistcoat, his long hair still wet from a bath, but with a face looking worn and wizened﻿—anything but country-like. He had taken up his palette and brushes, and stood before his easel when Deronda entered, but the equipment and attitude seemed to have been got up on short notice.
As they shook hands, Deronda said, “You don’t look much as if you had been in the country, old fellow. Is it Cambridge you have been to?”
“No,” said Hans, curtly, throwing down his palette with the air of one who has begun to feign by mistake; then pushing forward a chair for Deronda, he threw himself into another, and leaned backward with his hands behind his head, while he went on, “I’ve been to I-don’t-know-where﻿—No man’s land﻿—and a mortally unpleasant country it is.”
“You don’t mean to say you have been drinking, Hans,” said Deronda, who had seated himself opposite, in anxious survey.
“Nothing so good. I’ve been smoking opium. I always meant to do it some time or other, to try how much bliss could be got by it; and having found myself just now rather out of other bliss, I thought it judicious to seize the opportunity. But I pledge you my word I shall never tap a cask of that bliss again. It disagrees with my constitution.”
“What has been the matter? You were in good spirits enough when you wrote to me.”
“Oh, nothing in particular. The world began to look seedy﻿—a sort of cabbage-garden with all the cabbages cut. A malady of genius, you may be sure,” said Hans, creasing his face into a smile; “and, in fact, I was tired of being virtuous without reward, especially in this hot London weather.”
“Nothing else? No real vexation?” said Deronda.
Hans shook his head.
“I came to tell you of my own affairs, but I can’t do it with a good grace if you are to hide yours.”
“Haven’t an affair in the world,” said Hans, in a flighty way, “except a quarrel with a bric-à-brac man. Besides, as it is the first time in our lives that you ever spoke to me about your own affairs, you are only beginning to pay a pretty long debt.”

可音信全无，他又担心起那位敏感得无以测算的汉斯闹什么情绪上的别扭——他知道汉斯原定的修道院府小住已经推迟——终于第二次登门，被让进画室；只见朋友穿着薄外套，没穿背心，长发刚洗过还湿着，一张脸却憔悴干缩——怎么也不像从乡下来的样子。德龙达进来时，他已抓起调色板和画笔，站在画架前；可那副行头和架势，怎么看都像是仓促摆出来的。

Deronda felt convinced that Hans was behaving artificially, but he trusted to a return of the old frankness by-and-by if he gave his own confidence.
“You laughed at the mystery of my journey to Italy, Hans,” he began. “It was for an object that touched my happiness at the very roots. I had never known anything about my parents, and I really went to Genoa to meet my mother. My father has been long dead﻿—died when I was an infant. My mother was the daughter of an eminent Jew; my father was her cousin. Many things had caused me to think of this origin as almost a probability before I set out. I was so far prepared for the result that I was glad of it﻿—glad to find myself a Jew.”
“You must not expect me to look surprised, Deronda,” said Hans, who had changed his attitude, laying one leg across the other and examining the heel of his slipper.
“You knew it?”
“My mother told me. She went to the house the morning after you had been there﻿—brother and sister both told her. You may imagine we can’t rejoice as they do. But whatever you are glad of, I shall come to be glad of in the end﻿—*when* exactly the end may be I can’t predict,” said Hans, speaking in a low tone, which was as usual with him as it was to be out of humor with his lot, and yet bent on making no fuss about it.
“I quite understand that you can’t share my feeling,” said Deronda; “but I could not let silence lie between us on what casts quite a new light over my future. I have taken up some of Mordecai’s ideas, and I mean to try and carry them out, so far as one man’s efforts can go. I dare say I shall by and by travel to the East and be away for some years.”
Hans said nothing, but rose, seized his palette and began to work his brush on it, standing before his picture with his back to Deronda, who also felt himself at a break in his path embarrassed by Hans’s embarrassment.
Presently Hans said, again speaking low, and without turning, “Excuse the question, but does Mrs. Grandcourt know of all this?”
“No; and I must beg of you, Hans,” said Deronda, rather angrily, “to cease joking on that subject. Any notions you have are wide of the truth﻿—are the very reverse of the truth.”
“I am no more inclined to joke than I shall be at my own funeral,” said Hans. “But I am not at all sure that you are aware what are my notions on that subject.”
“Perhaps not,” said Deronda.

“I don’t know that I have ever betrayed *my* feeling to her,” said Hans, as if he were vindicating himself.

They are not likely to make any pleasant difference to myself under present circumstances. Now the father is there﻿—did you know that the father is there?”

Hans turned on his heel and threw himself into his chair, looking up at Deronda with an expression the reverse of tender. Something like a shock passed through Deronda, and, after an instant, he said,

“I am not in a good-natured mood. I assure you I found the fact disagreeable when it was thrust on me﻿—all the more, or perhaps all the less, because I believed then that your heart was pledged to the duchess. “Tell me what convinced you﻿—there’s a good fellow,” said Deronda, distrusting a delight that he was unused to.
“Don’t ask. Little mother was witness. The upshot is, that Mirah is jealous of the duchess, and the sooner you relieve her mind the better. There! I’ve cleared off a score or two, and may be allowed to swear at you for getting what you deserve﻿—which is just the very best luck I know of.”
“God bless you, Hans!” said Deronda, putting out his hand, which the other took and wrung in silence.

### LXVIII / 第六十八章
===Original===

> All thoughts, all passions, all delights,

Whatever stirs this mortal frame,

All are but ministers of Love,

And feed his sacred flame.

Deronda’s eagerness to confess his love could hardly have had a stronger stimulus than Hans had given it in his assurance that Mirah needed relief from jealousy. He went on his next visit to Ezra with the determination to be resolute in using﻿—nay, in requesting﻿—an opportunity of private conversation with her. If she accepted his love, he felt courageous about all other consequences, and as her betrothed husband he would gain a protective authority which might be a desirable defense for her in future difficulties with her father. Deronda had not observed any signs of growing restlessness in Lapidoth, or of diminished desire to recommend himself; but he had forebodings of some future struggle, some mortification, or some intolerable increase of domestic disquietude in which he might save Ezra and Mirah from being helpless victims.
His forebodings would have been strengthened if he had known what was going on in the father’s mind. That amount of restlessness, that desultoriness of attention, which made a small torture to Ezra, was to Lapidoth an irksome submission to restraint, only made bearable by his thinking of it as a means of by-and-by securing a well-conditioned freedom. He began with the intention of awaiting some really good chance, such as an opening for getting a considerable sum from Deronda; but all the while he was looking about curiously, and trying to discover where Mirah deposited her money and her keys. The imperious gambling desire within him, which carried on its activity through every other occupation, and made a continuous web of imagination that held all else in its meshes, would hardly have been under the control of a contracted purpose, if he had been able to lay his hands on any sum worth capturing. But Mirah, with her practical clear-sightedness, guarded against any frustration of the promise she had given to Ezra, by confiding all money, except what she was immediately in want of, to Mrs. Meyrick’s care, and Lapidoth felt himself under an irritating completeness of supply in kind as in a lunatic asylum where everything was made safe against him.

===Chinese===

> 一切思想，一切激情，一切欢愉，
> 凡拨动这凡人身躯的，
> 都只是爱的臣仆，
> 都喂养着它神圣的火焰。

德龙达急于求诉爱情的这颗心，几乎再得不到比汉斯更强的刺激了——汉斯一口咬定，米拉需要从嫉妒里解脱出来。下一次去访以斯拉，他打定主意，要坚决地利用——不，要主动请求——一个同她单独交谈的机会。倘若她接受他的爱，他对其余一切后果都有了勇气；而作为她的未婚夫，他将取得一种保护的权柄，日后她同父亲起了难处，这权柄便是她可贵的屏障。拉皮多思身上日益增长的躁动、见人就讨好的热劲有没有减退，德龙达并没有看出来；可他预感到将来会有一场争斗、一场屈辱、或一场忍无可忍的家宅不宁——到那时，他可以救以斯拉和米拉，不至做束手的牺牲。
倘若他知道那位父亲心里正转着什么念头，这预感还要重些。那一分躁动、那注意力的涣散，落在以斯拉身上是一场小小的酷刑；落在拉皮多思身上，却是受约束的难受，全靠想着这是换取日后一份体面自由的手段，才熬得住。他起初打定主意，要等一个真正的好机会——比如一个从德龙达那里弄到一大笔钱的口子；可他无时不在四下窥探，想摸清米拉把她的钱和钥匙收在哪里。他心里那专横的赌欲，穿透一切旁的事务运转，织出一张连绵不绝的想象之网、把其余的一切都网在网眼里；倘若他真把手按上任何一笔值得下手的钱，这赌欲是几乎不受任何收缩的目标节制的。可米拉有她务实的老练眼光，防着自己对以斯拉的许诺落空——除了手边即用的，所有的钱都托给了梅里克太太；拉皮多思觉得自己活在一种气人的周全供应里，像在疯人院里，样样都被收拾得叫他无从下手。

===Original===

To have opened a desk or drawer of Mirah’s, and pocketed any banknotes found there, would have been to his mind a sort of domestic appropriation which had no disgrace in it; the degrees of liberty a man allows himself with other people’s property being often delicately drawn, even beyond the boundary where the law begins to lay its hold﻿—which is the reason why spoons are a safer investment than mining shares. Lapidoth really felt himself injuriously treated by his daughter, and thought that he ought to have had what he wanted of her other earnings as he had of her apple-tart. But he remained submissive; indeed, the indiscretion that most tempted him, was not any insistence with Mirah, but some kind of appeal to Deronda. Clever persons who have nothing else to sell can often put a good price on their absence, and Lapidoth’s difficult search for devices forced upon him the idea that his family would find themselves happier without him, and that Deronda would be willing to advance a considerable sum for the sake of getting rid of him. But, in spite of well-practiced hardihood, Lapidoth was still in some awe of Ezra’s imposing friend, and deferred his purpose indefinitely.
On this day, when Deronda had come full of a gladdened consciousness, which inevitably showed itself in his air and speech, Lapidoth was at a crisis of discontent and longing that made his mind busy with schemes of freedom, and Deronda’s new amenity encouraged them. This preoccupation was at last so strong as to interfere with his usual show of interest in what went forward, and his persistence in sitting by even when there was reading which he could not follow. After sitting a little while, he went out to smoke and walk in the square, and the two friends were all the easier. Mirah was not at home, but she was sure to be in again before Deronda left, and his eyes glowed with a secret anticipation: he thought that when he saw her again he should see some sweetness of recognition for himself to which his eyes had been sealed before. There was an additional playful affectionateness in his manner toward Ezra.
“This little room is too close for you, Ezra,” he said, breaking off his reading. “The week’s heat we sometimes get here is worse than the heat in Genoa, where one sits in the shaded coolness of large rooms. You must have a better home now.

「这间小屋对你太闷了，以斯拉，」他中断诵读说。「我们这里有时一热一个礼拜，比热那亚还难受——在那儿，人坐在宽敞房间的荫凉里。你如今该有个更好的家了。

I shall do as I like with you, being the stronger half.” He smiled toward Ezra, who said,

“Oh, the country would be a banishment while you are here,” said Deronda, rising and walking round the double room, which yet offered no long promenade, while he made a great fan of his handkerchief. “This is the happiest room in the world to me. Besides, I will imagine myself in the East, since I am getting ready to go there some day. Only I will not wear a cravat and a heavy ring there,” he ended emphatically, pausing to take off those superfluities and deposit them on a small table behind Ezra, who had the table in front of him covered with books and papers.
“I have been wearing my memorable ring ever since I came home,” he went on, as he reseated himself. “But I am such a Sybarite that I constantly put it off as a burden when I am doing anything. I understand why the Romans had summer rings﻿—*if* they had them. Now then, I shall get on better.”
They were soon absorbed in their work again. Deronda was reading a piece of rabbinical Hebrew under Ezra’s correction and comment, and they took little notice when Lapidoth reentered and took a seat somewhat in the background.
His rambling eyes quickly alighted on the ring that sparkled on the bit of dark mahogany. During his walk, his mind had been occupied with the fiction of an advantageous opening for him abroad, only requiring a sum of ready money, which, on being communicated to Deronda in private, might immediately draw from him a question as to the amount of the required sum: and it was this part of his forecast that Lapidoth found the most debatable, there being a danger in asking too much, and a prospective regret in asking too little. His own desire gave him no limit, and he was quite without guidance as to the limit of Deronda’s willingness. But now, in the midst of these airy conditions preparatory to a receipt which remained indefinite, this ring, which on Deronda’s finger had become familiar to Lapidoth’s envy, suddenly shone detached and within easy grasp.

Its value was certainly below the smallest of the imaginary sums that his purpose fluctuated between; but then it was before him as a solid fact, and his desire at once leaped into the thought (not yet an intention) that if he were quietly to pocket that ring and walk away he would have the means of comfortable escape from present restraint, without trouble, and also without danger; for any property of Deronda’s (available without his formal consent) was all one with his children’s property, since their father would never be prosecuted for taking it. The details of this thinking followed each other so quickly that they seemed to rise before him as one picture. Lapidoth had never committed larceny; but larceny is a form of appropriation for which people are punished by law; and, take this ring from a virtual relation, who would have been willing to make a much heavier gift, would not come under the head of larceny. Still, the heavier gift was to be preferred, if Lapidoth could only make haste enough in asking for it, and the imaginary action of taking the ring, which kept repeating itself like an inward tune, sank into a rejected idea. He satisfied his urgent longing by resolving to go below, and watch for the moment of Deronda’s departure, when he would ask leave to join him in his walk and boldly carry out his meditated plan. He rose and stood looking out of the window, but all the while he saw what lay beyond him﻿—the brief passage he would have to make to the door close by the table where the ring was. However he was resolved to go down; but﻿—by no distinct change of resolution, rather by a dominance of desire, like the thirst of the drunkard﻿—it so happened that in passing the table his fingers fell noiselessly on the ring, and he found himself in the passage with the ring in his hand. It followed that he put on his hat and quitted the house. The possibility of again throwing himself on his children receded into the indefinite distance, and before he was out on the square his sense of haste had concentrated itself on selling the ring and getting on shipboard.
Deronda and Ezra were just aware of his exit; that was all. But, by-and-by, Mirah came in and made a real interruption.

She had not taken off her hat; and when Deronda rose and advanced to shake hands with her, she said, in a confusion at once unaccountable and troublesome to herself,
“I only came in to see that Ezra had his new draught. I must go directly to Mrs. Meyrick’s to fetch something.”
“Pray allow me to walk with you,” said Deronda urgently. “I must not tire Ezra any further; besides my brains are melting. I want to go to Mrs. Meyrick’s: may I go with you?”
“Oh, yes,” said Mirah, blushing still more, with the vague sense of something new in Deronda, and turning away to pour out Ezra’s draught; Ezra meanwhile throwing back his head with his eyes shut, unable to get his mind away from the ideas that had been filling it while the reading was going on. Deronda for a moment stood thinking of nothing but the walk, till Mirah turned round again and brought the draught, when he suddenly remembered that he had laid aside his cravat, and saying﻿—“Pray excuse my deshabille﻿—I did not mean you to see it,” he went to the little table, took up his cravat, and exclaimed with a violent impulse of surprise, “Good heavens, where is my ring gone?” beginning to search about on the floor.
Ezra looked round the corner of his chair. Mirah, quick as thought, went to the spot where Deronda was seeking, and said, “Did you lay it down?”
“Yes,” said Deronda, still unvisited by any other explanation than that the ring had fallen and was lurking in shadow, indiscernable on the variegated carpet. He was moving the bits of furniture near, and searching in all possible and impossible places with hand and eyes.
But another explanation had visited Mirah and taken the color from her cheeks. She went to Ezra’s ear and whispered “Was my father here?” He bent his head in reply, meeting her eyes with terrible understanding. She darted back to the spot where Deronda was still casting down his eyes in that hopeless exploration which we are apt to carry on over a space we have examined in vain. “You have not found it?” she said, hurriedly.
He, meeting her frightened gaze, immediately caught alarm from it and answered, “I perhaps put it in my pocket,” professing to feel for it there.
She watched him and said, “It is not there?﻿—you put it on the table,” with a penetrating voice that would not let him feign to have found it in his pocket; and immediately she rushed out of the room.

「请一定让我陪你走一趟，」德龙达恳切地说。「我不能再累以斯拉了；再说我的脑子都快化了。我正要去梅里克太太家：能同你一起走吗？」
「哦，好的，」米拉说，脸红得更深了，模糊地觉出德龙达身上有了什么新的东西，一边转过身去倒以斯拉的药水；以斯拉仰着头闭着眼，满脑子还盘桓着诵读时充塞其中的那些观念。德龙达有一会儿只想着那趟同行，什么也没想；直到米拉转身把药水端来，他才猛然记起自己解下了领巾，说声「请原谅我这身随便——我本不想让你看见的」，走到小桌前拿起领巾，随即带着一阵猛烈的惊愕喊道：「天哪，我的戒指哪儿去了？」开始在地上四处找。
以斯拉从椅角上望过来。米拉快如念头，走到德龙达寻找的地方，问：「您刚才放在这儿了？」

可另一个解释已经找上了米拉，把她颊上的血色都带走了。她凑到以斯拉耳边低声问：「我父亲来过吗？」他点头作答，迎着她的目光，带着可怕的会意。她奔回德龙达还在低头呆找的地方——徒劳搜索过一遍的地方，我们还偏要在那里没指望地来回找。「还没找到吗？」她急急地说。
他迎上她惊惶的目光，立刻被那目光吓着了，答道：「也许我揣进口袋了，」装模作样往口袋里摸。
她盯着他，说：「不在口袋里吧？——您放在桌上了。」那声音有种穿透力，不许他假装在口袋里摸到了；话音未落，她已冲出房间。

Deronda followed her﻿—she was gone into the sitting-room below to look for her father﻿—she opened the door of the bedroom to see if he were there﻿—she looked where his hat usually hung﻿—she turned with her hands clasped tight and her lips pale, gazing despairingly out of the window. Then she looked up at Deronda, who had not dared to speak to her in her white agitation. She looked up at him, unable to utter a word﻿—the look seemed a tacit acceptance of the humiliation she felt in his presence. But he, taking her clasped hands between both his, said, in a tone of reverent adoration,
“Mirah, let me think that he is my father as well as yours﻿—that we can have no sorrow, no disgrace, no joy apart. I will rather take your grief to be mine than I would take the brightest joy of another woman. Say you will not reject me﻿—say you will take me to share all things with you. Say you will promise to be my wife﻿—say it now. I have been in doubt so long﻿—I have had to hide my love so long. Say that now and always I may prove to you that I love you with complete love.”
The change in Mirah had been gradual. She had not passed at once from anguish to the full, blessed consciousness that, in this moment of grief and shame, Deronda was giving her the highest tribute man can give to woman. With the first tones and the first words, she had only a sense of solemn comfort, referring this goodness of Deronda’s to his feeling for Ezra. But by degrees the rapturous assurance of unhoped-for good took possession of her frame: her face glowed under Deronda’s as he bent over her; yet she looked up still with intense gravity, as when she had first acknowledged with religious gratitude that he had thought her “worthy of the best;” and when he had finished, she could say nothing﻿—she could only lift up her lips to his and just kiss them, as if that were the simplest “yes.” They stood then, only looking at each other, he holding her hands between his﻿—too happy to move, meeting so fully in their new consciousness that all signs would have seemed to throw them farther apart, till Mirah said in a whisper: “Let us go and comfort Ezra.”

德龙达跟了下去——她已进了楼下的起居室找父亲——她推开卧室的门看他在不在——她看了看他惯常挂帽子的地方——她转过身来，双手紧握，嘴唇发白，绝望地望着窗外。随后她抬头望德龙达——她惨白激动，他一直不敢对她说话。她仰望着他，一个字也吐不出——那目光仿佛默默领下了她在他面前感到的那份羞辱。可他把她紧握的双手拢在自己两手之间，用一种虔敬爱慕的声调说：
「米拉，让我把他当作我的父亲，如同你的父亲——让我们的悲哀、我们的耻辱、我们的欢乐，再没有分开的。我宁肯把你的悲伤当作我的，也不肯要另一个女人最明亮的欢乐。说你不会拒绝我——说你肯让我与你分担一切。说你肯答应做我的妻子——现在就说。我疑惑了这么久——我把我的爱藏了这么久。说吧，从今以后、时时刻刻，让我向你证明：我用完整无缺的爱爱你。」
米拉的变化是渐渐来的。她并不是一下子从苦痛跳进那圆满的、有福的意识——意识到在这个悲与耻的时刻，德龙达正把男人能给女人的最高的敬意给她。头几声、头几句，她只觉出一种庄重的安慰，把德龙达这份善良，归到他对照以斯拉的情分上。可渐渐地，那不望之喜的狂喜的确信占据了她的身心：他俯身向她时，她的脸在他脸下泛起红光；她仰望时仍带着极度的郑重，像她最初怀着宗教的感激领受「配得上最好的」那句品评时一样；等他说完，她说不出话——只能仰起嘴唇，轻轻碰一碰他的唇，仿佛那就是最简单的一声「是」。两人于是站着，只是对望，他把她的手拢在自己的两手间——幸福得动弹不得，在各自新的意识里相遇得这样满，任何表示倒像要把他们推远了；直到米拉低声说：「我们去安慰以斯拉吧。」

In earth, the widely scattered wreck sublime

Sir Hugo carried out his plan of spending part of the autumn at Diplow, and by the beginning of October his presence was spreading some cheerfulness in the neighborhood, among all ranks and persons concerned, from the stately home of Brackenshaw and Quetcham to the respectable shop-parlors in Wanchester. For Sir Hugo was a man who liked to show himself and be affable, a Liberal of good lineage, who confided entirely in reform as not likely to make any serious difference in English habits of feeling, one of which undoubtedly is the liking to behold society well fenced and adorned with hereditary rank. Hence he made Diplow a most agreeable house, extending his invitations to old Wanchester solicitors and young village curates, but also taking some care in the combination of the guests, and not feeding all the common poultry together, so that they should think their meal no particular compliment. Easygoing Lord Brackenshaw, for example, would not mind meeting Robinson the attorney, but Robinson would have been naturally piqued if he had been asked to meet a set of people who passed for his equals. On all these points Sir Hugo was well informed enough at once to gain popularity for himself and give pleasure to others﻿—two results which eminently suited his disposition. The rector of Pennicote now found a reception at Diplow very different from the haughty tolerance he had undergone during the reign of Grandcourt. It was not that the baronet liked Mr. Gascoigne; it was that he desired to keep up a marked relation of friendliness with him on account of Mrs. Grandcourt, for whom Sir Hugo’s chivalry had become more and more engaged. Why? The chief reason was one that he could not fully communicate, even to Lady Mallinger﻿—for he would not tell what he thought one woman’s secret to another, even though the other was his wife﻿—which shows that his chivalry included a rare reticence.
Deronda, after he had become engaged to Mirah, felt it right to make a full statement of his position and purposes to Sir Hugo, and he chose to make it by letter. He had more than a presentiment that his fatherly friend would feel some dissatisfaction, if not pain, at this turn of his destiny. In reading unwelcome news, instead of hearing it, there is the advantage that one avoids a hasty expression of impatience which may afterward be repented of.

雨果爵士照他的计划，把一部分秋天安顿在迪普洛；十月初，他的到来已给邻近各处散布了些喜气——各等各样的人，从布雷肯肖和奎彻姆气派的府邸，到旺彻斯特体面的店铺客厅。雨果爵士是个喜欢露面、喜欢和气的人，一位家世很好的自由派，对改革抱着全盘的信任——相信它不至于给英国人的感情习惯带来什么大变动；那些习惯之一，无疑便是喜欢看见社会用世袭的等级围好、装饰好。于是他把迪普洛办成了一处再惬意不过的宅邸，请客连旺彻斯特的老律师、村里的年轻副牧师都一并在内；只是对客人的搭配也留几分心，不把寻常的家禽一齐喂养，免得它们觉得那顿食算不得什么特别的抬举。比方说，好性子的布雷肯肖勋爵不在乎遇见律师鲁滨逊；可要是请鲁滨逊来会一桌在他被当作同等的人，他自然要憋一肚子气。在这一切分寸上，雨果爵士都消息灵通得恰到好处，一面替自己赢得人望，一面给别人送去快活——这两个结果，同他的性子再相配不过。佩尼科特的牧师如今在迪普洛受到的接待，同格兰考特当政时他忍受的那种傲慢的宽容，大不一样了。这倒不是从男爵喜欢上了加斯科因先生；而是他有意同他维持一种显著的友好关系——为了格兰考特夫人，雨果爵士的骑士肝肠已为她越系越深。为什么？主要的缘故，是他连对马林格夫人也不能和盘托出——他不愿把一个女人心里的秘密讲给另一个女人，哪怕那另一个是他的妻子——可见他的骑士气里还带着一种难得的缄默。
德龙达同米拉订婚之后，觉得理应向雨果爵士把自己的处境和打算作一番完整的陈明，并选择用信来说。他不止预感到：这位父亲般的朋友对他的命运这一转，纵不痛，也要不快。读不受欢迎的消息，比听它多一样好处——可以免去一声日后追悔的急躁。

Deronda dreaded that verbal collision which makes otherwise pardonable feeling lastingly offensive.
And Sir Hugo, though not altogether surprised, was thoroughly vexed. His immediate resource was to take the letter to Lady Mallinger, who would be sure to express an astonishment which her husband could argue against as unreasonable, and in this way divide the stress of his discontent. And in fact when she showed herself astonished and distressed that all Daniel’s wonderful talents, and the comfort of having him in the house, should have ended in his going mad in this way about the Jews, the baronet could say,
“Oh, nonsense, my dear! depend upon it, Dan will not make a fool of himself. He has large notions about Judaism﻿—political views which you can’t understand. No fear but Dan will keep himself head uppermost.”
But with regard to the prospective marriage she afforded him no counterirritant. The gentle lady observed, without rancor, that she had little dreamed of what was coming when she had Mirah to sing at her musical party and give lessons to Amabel. After some hesitation, indeed, she confessed it *had* passed through her mind that after a proper time Daniel might marry Mrs. Grandcourt﻿—because it seemed so remarkable that he should be at Genoa just at that time﻿—and although she herself was not fond of widows she could not help thinking that such a marriage would have been better than his going altogether with the Jews. But Sir Hugo was so strongly of the same opinion that he could not correct it as a feminine mistake; and his ill-humor at the disproof of his disagreeable conclusions on behalf of Gwendolen was left without vent. He desired Lady Mallinger not to breathe a word about the affair till further notice, saying to himself, “If it is an unkind cut to the poor thing (meaning Gwendolen), the longer she is without knowing it the better, in her present nervous state. And she will best learn it from Dan himself.” Sir Hugo’s conjectures had worked so industriously with his knowledge, that he fancied himself well informed concerning the whole situation.
Meanwhile his residence with his family at Diplow enabled him to continue his fatherly attentions to Gwendolen; and in these Lady Mallinger, notwithstanding her small liking for widows, was quite willing to second him.

德龙达怕的正是那种言语的相撞——它会把原本可恕的情绪，撞成长久的冒犯。
雨果爵士呢，虽不全然意外，却也着着实实恼了。他的头一步对策，是把信拿给马林格夫人——她准会表示一番惊诧，做丈夫的正好可以驳她不讲道理，这样把自己的一肚子不快分掉一半。果然，她显出又惊又痛：丹尼尔那许多了不起的才具、宅子里有他的那份慰藉，到头来竟落到为犹太人发这样的疯！从男爵便可以说：
「哦，胡说，亲爱的！你放心，丹不会作践自己。他对犹太教有大见识——你不懂的政治眼光。丹保持脑袋朝上，这不用怕。」
可说到那桩眼看要来的婚事，她就给不了他什么反刺激了。温良的夫人不怀怨气地议论道：当初请米拉来她的音乐会上唱歌、教阿玛贝尔功课时，她哪里想到会有今日。迟疑了一阵，她竟也招认：她脑子里确实闪过——等过了合宜的时日，丹尼尔兴许会娶格兰考特夫人——因为他恰好在那个时候出现在热那亚，实在太蹊跷——而且尽管她自己不喜欢寡妇，也不免觉得那样的婚姻，总比他整个儿跟犹太人走强。可雨果爵士同她的意见一致得太厉害，没法把这当作女人的错见来纠正；他为格温多琳下的那些不祥结论既已被证伪，这一腔闷气便没了出口。他嘱咐马林格夫人在另行通知之前对此事一个字不许漏，心里想着：「这对那可怜人（指格温多琳）若是狠心一刀，那么以她如今的神经过敏，越晚知道越好。而且，这件事由丹亲口告诉她最好。」雨果爵士的种种猜测同他的知识勤劳地合作了一场，竟使他自以为对全局了如指掌。
与此同时，他携家小住在迪普洛，得以继续他对格温多琳的父辈般的关切；在这一层上，马林格夫人尽管不喜欢寡妇，也全然乐意同他唱和。

The plan of removal to Offendene had been carried out; and Gwendolen, in settling there, maintained a calm beyond her mother’s hopes. She was experiencing some of that peaceful melancholy which comes from the renunciation of demands for self, and from taking the ordinary good of existence, and especially kindness, even from a dog, as a gift above expectation. Does one who has been all but lost in a pit of darkness complain of the sweet air and the daylight? There is a way of looking at our life daily as an escape, and taking the quiet return of morn and evening﻿—still more the starlike out-glowing of some pure fellow-feeling, some generous impulse breaking our inward darkness﻿—as a salvation that reconciles us to hardship. Those who have a self-knowledge prompting such self-accusation as Hamlet’s, can understand this habitual feeling of rescue. And it was felt by Gwendolen as she lived through and through again the terrible history of her temptations, from their first form of illusory self-pleasing when she struggled away from the hold of conscience, to their latest form of an urgent hatred dragging her toward its satisfaction, while she prayed and cried for the help of that conscience which she had once forsaken. She was now dwelling on every word of Deronda’s that pointed to her past deliverance from the worst evil in herself, and the worst infliction of it on others, and on every word that carried a force to resist self-despair.
But she was also upborne by the prospect of soon seeing him again: she did not imagine him otherwise than always within her reach, her supreme need of him blinding her to the separateness of his life, the whole scene of which she filled with his relation to her﻿—no unique preoccupation of Gwendolen’s, for we are all apt to fall into this passionate egoism of imagination, not only toward our fellow-men, but toward God. And the future which she turned her face to with a willing step was one where she would be continually assimilating herself to some type that he would hold before her. Had he not first risen on her vision as a corrective presence which she had recognized in the beginning with resentment, and at last with entire love and trust? She could not spontaneously think of an end to that reliance, which had become to her imagination like the firmness of the earth, the only condition of her walking.

迁往奥芬迪恩的计划已经办妥；格温多琳在那里安顿下来，保持着的平静，超出了母亲的指望。她正尝着一种安详的忧郁——它来自对自我索求的放弃，来自把生存寻常的好意、尤其是善意——哪怕一条狗的善意——当作高于期望的礼物来领受。一个在黑暗深坑里几乎丧命的人，会抱怨甜美的空气和白昼吗？有这样一种日日看待自己生活的方式：把它当作一场逃脱，把清晨与黄昏静静的回还——更把某种纯净的同情的星光般的放光、某种把我们内心黑暗划破的慷慨冲动——当作使我们同苦难和解的救赎。凡有哈姆雷特那种引人自讼的自知的人，都懂得这种习常的获救之感。格温多琳正怀着它，把她那部诱惑的可怕历史从头到尾重新活了一遍——从最初那种幻觉的自我取悦（她那时挣脱了良心的把持），到最后那种急迫的仇恨（它拖着她去讨满足，她一面祈祷、一面哭喊，求那曾被她抛下的良心救助）。此刻她流连于德龙达说过的每一句话——凡指向她过去得救、免于自身最深的恶、免于把它加于他人的，凡带着抵抗自弃的力量的，她都一一反刍。
可支撑着她的，还有不久便可见到他的指望：她想象不出他会不在她够得着的地方；她对他的至高需要，使她看不见他生活的另立一隅——那生活的整个场景，都被她用他同她的关系填满了。这并非格温多琳独有的心事：我们都容易坠入这种想象的热情的利己主义——不仅对人，也对上帝。而她愿意举步迎去的未来，是一个她将不断把自己同化于他举在她面前的某个榜样的未来。他起初出现在她眼前时，不正是一个矫正的临在么——起初她怀着怨怼认出他，最后怀着全然的爱与信托？她无法自然而然地想到那份倚靠会有尽头；那份倚靠，在她的想象里已如大地的坚固，是她行走唯一的条件。
